News.title: Madeleine McCann suspect Christian Brueckner ‘physically attacks’ police outside supermarket leaving one injured
News.content:
THE suspect in the disappearance of Madeleine McCann has been accused of scuffling with police officers outside a supermarket in Germany.

Christian Brueckner – who has never been charged in the 2007 case and to this day, maintains his innocence – was involved in a “physical attack” on cops in the city of Kiel on June 6.



Since his release from prison last year, he has been under round-the-clock police surveillance, with the force tracking his every move.

The incident is understood to have happened as he refused to hand over his phone after the officers spotted that he was taking a photo of them, Der Spiegel reported.



“During the course of the police intervention, a physical assault or act of resistance against law enforcement officers occurred,” a spokesperson for the police said.

The officers involved were apparently not part of the team monitoring Brueckner and happened to be at the scene by chance.

One of them even suffered a knee injury during the scrap.

Brueckner’s lawyer, Philipp Marquort, confirmed the incident but said the police response was excessive.

“The photo was taken from a distance of more than 40 metres and was innocuous,” he added.

“This amounts to the persecution of an innocent man.”



The paedophile was also investigated by Kiel police over a fight involving a British man in April.

This comes just weeks after The Sun reported that the watch, intended for public safety and to guard him from vigilantes, is set to be scrapped after a court ruled it was no longer required.

But Brueckner is still expected to wear an electronic ankle monitoring tag.



Police are understood to have appealed the ruling. The guard will remain in place until a court makes a final decision.

A post online in Germany, confirmed by police, said: “A surveillance order for the German suspect in the case of British girl Madeleine ‘Maddie’ McCann, who disappeared in 2007, has not been renewed, according to police in Kiel.

“The police headquarters in the Schleswig-Holstein state capital announced this on Wednesday.

“They have already filed an appeal with the district court, and a decision is still pending.”

The German national has multiple previous convictions for sex offences and other crimes including theft, drug trafficking, assault and sexual abuse of children.



He was recently released from prison after serving seven years for raping an American pensioner in Praia da Luz, Portugal.

Brueckner was expected to be behind bars right now for verbally abusing a prison officer in 2023.

But the court case that would have seen him jailed was scrapped last week – leaving him free to cycle to his local garden centre.



Three-year-old Maddie, of Rothley, Leics., vanished from the Ocean Club, in Praia da Luz, Portugal on May 3, 2007, while on holiday with her family.

Brueckner was named as the prime suspect in the disappearance and murder of the tot in 2020 by German cops.

Police have been able to confirm his phone was near Ocean Club, where the McCanns were staying, around the time Madeleine vanished on May 3, 2007.

The Metropolitan Polcie are pushing for the suspect to stand trial in the UK for the toddler’s abduction and murder.

The force reportedly wants to charge him ahead of the 20th anniversary of her disappearance next year.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

But the German government has pointed to strict rules preventing it from extraditing suspects to non-EU countries.

Criminal suspects can only be sent to fellow EU member states under the European Arrest Warrant (EAW).

News.title: Two killers of PC Harper made sneering comments about grieving widow as they went to court, ex-guard reveals
News.content:
TWO killers of PC Andrew Harper made sneering comments about his grieving widow as they were escorted to court — and are “the last who should be considered for early release”, an ex-guard has said.

Vile Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers laughed and joked their way through their Old Bailey trial and carried on causing chaos after they were jailed, the source revealed.



A former prison officer who dealt with the duo said they showed no remorse and mocked PC Harper’s widow Lissie before being jailed for manslaughter in July 2020.

He said: “I saw their behaviour first-hand. They thought the whole thing was a joke and had no respect for PC Harper or his widow.



“One day they were being taken to the Bailey, they were making derogatory comments about Lissie and a custody officer told them to show some respect — and they laughed in his face.”

Cole and Bowers were moved from a young offenders’ institution in Yorkshire to Feltham in West London in 2020 for their trial and held on separate units so they could not discuss the case.

But our source said: “They went in the same van to the Old Bailey every day and there was nothing officers could do to stop them talking. They openly discussed blaming Henry for the death.

“It was obvious they knew PC Harper was being dragged along the road.

“They made comments about him and his widow that made officers sick.

“They thought the whole thing was funny and did not have an ounce of remorse.



“They were laughing and joking in the dock as well.”

At the court, they were held in category A units used for prisoners such as Wayne Couzens and Manchester Arena terrorist Hashem Abedi.

Our source said: “The suite has emergency bells they kept ringing. Officers — from Belmarsh Prison — kept running in. But they would just say things like, ‘Mate can I have a cup of tea, two sugars?’



”The officers couldn’t understand how the Feltham staff put up with the pair.”

After the case they were sent to HMP Feltham before going on to adult jails.

Our source said: “Jessie Cole was on an enhanced unit. He was a restricted prisoner but got extra gym and more money for the canteen. Bowers stayed on an induction unit and had all the privileges too.

“Cole was the most disruptive inmate I have known at Feltham. He was an accomplished boxer and people were terrified of him.

“There were lots of gangsters in there but they were no use without weapons and Cole and Bowers knew how to fight. Cole beat a few lads up in the showers — they’d say they’d fallen over.



“Bowers was less violent but had a menacing aura and was from a serious family.

“We were all very relieved when they got moved.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He added: “Anyone who saw them at trial or in jail would think it’s utterly wrong they could get early release. They are the last people who should be considered for it.”

The Ministry of Justice did not comment.

News.title: People pleaser Burnham’s vibes won’t tackle Britain’s REAL problems… We need PM with a plan rather than kumbaya rhetoric
News.content:
LESS than a week into the job and our new Prime Minister has been exposed as The Man With No Plan.

Just days after turfing Sir Keir Starmer out of office, it is already painfully obvious that, just like his predecessor, Andy ­Burnham has spent far more time thinking about how he could become PM than he has thinking about what he was going to do once he finally got the top job.



Judging by his first few announcements — the daily 6am good news story — it’s abundantly clear that most of us put more thought into planning (and paying for) our summer holiday than Burnham has put into how he will run the country.

Sure, there have been lots of feelgood words and buzz phrases about “hope” and “change” and all that “good growth” he wants to deliver (but none of that “bad growth” we apparently don’t want).



But despite feverish chatter among the leftie lanyard classes about the Burnham “vibe”, and a clear Labour bounce in the polls, there is nothing so far to suggest that he has an actual programme for government to sort out ANY of the key problems afflicting our country.

We’ve had no shortage of policy announcements since Monday: £340million spent to tackle rough sleeping, £850million on cutting VAT from domestic electricity bills, £500million on cutting the cap on bus fares to £2, and £100million to cut 20 per cent off business rates for pubs and clubs.

While they are exactly the sort of popular — some might even say “populist” — policies that we would expect from a people pleaser like Andy Burnham, they don’t even begin to touch the sides of the REAL change this country needs.

Equally, his decision to “pause” the early release of prisoners while he conducts an “urgent review” has betrayed the fact that he hasn’t given a moment’s thought to prison overcrowding before this week.

This isn’t governing — it’s doing the easy stuff.

Like the eminently personable Burnham himself, this is all about easy PR with no real substance.



I’m all for cutting energy bills (although I still haven’t decided how to spend my 86 pence a week saving), helping the homeless and hospitality businesses, and lower bus fares too, but these policies are far too meagre to matter — and many of them have turned out to be unfunded.

If the new PM and his team haven’t worked out how they’re going to pay for a bus fare cap, how will they find the funding for everything else Burnham says he wants to do — from devolution, a huge council house-building programme and reforming social care, to the renationalisation of many utilities — which will cost hundreds of billions.

Those are just some of the priorities Burnham has talked about, but he is still yet to mention any of the major problems and issues that urgently need to be addressed by the new PM.

He refused to tell us what his big policy plans were before he won the Makerfield by-election, then he refused to tell us them before he became PM.

Even his first statement outside No10 was just empty kumbaya rhetoric.



Now he says he will tell us about his Ten-Year Plan in the autumn.

Let’s hope his team can Google and type up some policy ideas quickly, eh?

To this day, we still don’t know how he plans to deliver growth or reindustrialise our nation, while we have the highest energy prices in the Western world thanks to the insane Net Zero policies.



Yes, Burnham has plans to allow more drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea but his new Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is even more of a climate-change zealot than Ed Miliband.

We have not heard a single word about what Burnham plans to do about immigration — whether that’s the mass legal influx or the illegal Channel boat arrivals.

But I guess that means we know who will be living in all those new council houses.

There has been no hint about his strategy to cut our almost £1trillion in Government debt or how he will tackle the ballooning working-age benefit bill, or a blueprint for funding the desperately needed boost to defence spending.

While Burnham is far more likeable than his predecessor, and talks like a normal person, he is quickly going to discover there’s far more to being the leader of a G7 nation than just being someone people might like to go to the pub with.



I hate to be the one to burst the Burnham bubble, but vibes don’t deliver growth. Vibes don’t build council houses.

Vibes don’t provide plentiful secure energy. Vibes don’t build warships or missiles.

Vibes don’t stop the Channel migrant boats or keep our streets safe.

We don’t need a people pleaser as our Prime Minister.

We need a PM who is able and willing to make the tough choices our country needs.



We need a man with a plan.

LINEKER TAXES MY PATIENCE

WHILE one million extra people are being dragged into paying income tax or a higher rate over the next year, please spare a thought for those of us who just don’t get to pay ENOUGH tax.

I am talking, of course, about the pitiful ranks of the “super-rich” who are apparently DESPERATE to pay more of their hard-earned wealth into Treasury coffers.

So keen are they to pay more, they’ve even written a letter to the new Prime Minister BEGGING for the chance to do so.



Gary Lineker and 150 other British millionaires told Andy Burnham that “millionaires are a patriotic bunch” and “proud to pay”, pleading: “We want you to tax us – the super-rich.

“We can afford it.”

The former England footballer, turned crisp salesman, doesn’t just want us all to know how rich he is.

He wants us to know how super he is, too.

Our Gary loves to virtue-signal about the latest “progressive” cause, whether it’s defending Channel migrants, LGBTQ rights in Qatar, taking in Syrian refugees or the plight of the Palestinians.



But his fine words are rarely backed up by his actions.

He’s had his own battles with the Inland Revenue over a claim for millions in unpaid tax due to his off-payroll freelance status at the BBC.

And he was revealed in the Panama Papers to have used an offshore company set up in the British Virgin Islands to avoid tax on his luxury villa in Barbados.

There’s no need for millionaires like Lineker to beg to pay extra tax.

They can voluntarily pay more at any time simply by clicking on a link on the HMRC website.



Or Gary and his super-rich chums can email accounts- receivable@hmtreasury.gov.uk to request to make a donation.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Either way, we’d all be grateful for the extra dosh to pay for public services.

But we’d be even more grateful if Gary Lineker and his super-rich chums would pay up and then shut up.

News.title: Landlords will toast our Save Our Sups win but Burnham must scrap business rates for independent shops to boost growth
News.content:
Sup and away

RELIEVED landlords will today be toasting The Sun’s Save Our Sups victory.

It’s great to see the PM recognise the massive stress local boozers have been under over the past 12 months.



His decision to cut business rates by 20 per cent — an average £1,100 boost — is proof that community pubs DO matter.

In Andy Burnham’s words, it’s a small step — and the estimated £100million cost remains unfunded for now.



No10 will know that some bars were hit in April with rate rises of over 75 per cent, so still face massive pain.

Ex-Chancellor Rachel Reeves was also drawing up mean-spirited plans to target successful big countryside venues — known as the “nice pub tax” — which the PM should rule out.

The hard-up trade is now asking Mr Burnham to honour his pledge to cut their VAT to ten per cent, bringing them into line with European countries.

They will have to wait until the Autumn Budget to find out if he agrees.

But if Mr Burnham wants to turbo-charge growth he could do a lot worse than scrapping business rates altogether for independent high street shops.

Sugar crush

YESTERDAY Britain’s oldest sugar factory shut down after being undone by crippling electricity prices.



It’s been the same story for heavy industry across the country.

British exports are becoming chronically uncompetitive on global markets because of energy costs driven up by insane Net Zero policies.

Andy Burnham says he can fix the nation’s finances through a massive re-industrialisation programme.

But he has no chance of delivering it if he allows new Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to pursue the same policies as her mentor Ed Miliband.

Mr Burnham has also just appointed three Miliband disciples — all eco obsessives — to the Energy Department.



So the chances of sense prevailing and Net Zero being unpicked are minuscule.

The PM has to realise he can’t have it both ways.

Fuel duty

THE new Chancellor was drafted in as an experienced and safe pair of hands.

John Healey will know that ALL of his predecessors over the last 14 years have agreed with The Sun’s relentless campaign to keep fuel duty down.

Yesterday Tory leader Kemi Badenoch reminded him of the vital importance of fuel costs to ordinary families.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Drivers and businesses are facing a planned 5p rise in January, which will put a big dent in incomes and drive up inflation on transported goods like food.

With the war on Iran pushing up oil prices again, another fuel duty increase makes no sense at all.

News.title: Saudi prince found dead in luxury London hotel is pictured after cocktail of party drugs in system
News.content:
TRAGIC END Saudi prince found dead in luxury London hotel is pictured after cocktail of party drugs in system

THE SAUDI prince found dead in a luxury London hotel has been pictured for the first time after a cocktail of party drugs was found in his system.

Prince Abdullah bin Fahad bin Abdullah bin Abdulaziz bin Jalawi al Saud, 29, was discovered on the bathroom floor of his £600-a-night room at the Marriott Hotel in Kensington on November 25.



It was found that the Saudi royal had suffered a cardiac arrest after consuming a cocktail of drugs and alcohol, including party drug GBH.

The young prince had arrived at the hotel on November 19 for a week-long stay, Inner West London Coroner’s Court heard.



It was revealed that his body was found by a cleaner who had entered his fifth-floor room.

Paramedics raced to the luxury hotel but, despite their best efforts, he was sadly pronounced dead at the scene.



A source told Taroudant Press that Prince Abdullah was a “quiet and well-liked figure within the royal family and was “known for his discreet philanthropic contributions to societal projects”.

They added his passing came “when the Al Saud family is undergoing a period of internal renewal, with a focus on domestic stability and economic development”.



The Saudi Royal Court later issued an official statement on December 2 officially announcing Prince Abdullah death.

It read: “Prince Abdullah bin Fahd bin Abdullah bin Abdulaziz bin Musaid bin Jalawi Al Saud has passed away to the mercy of Almighty God, outside the Kingdom.”

The statement added that a funeral prayer was to take place at the Imam Turki bin Abdullah Mosque in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia – a mosque which usually holds funeral ceremonies for VIPs.

According to Saudi media reports at the time, the funeral prayer was to be attended by a high number of princes and officials to reflect the family’s unity.

Following a toxicology test, it was uncovered that Prince Abdullah had a blood alcohol level of 222mg per 100ml of blood.



With almost three times England’s legal drink-drive limit of 80mg in his system, the inquest heard this alone could have caused a coma.

It was also found that he had a fatal level of Gamma-hydroxybutyrate, commonly known as GHB, in his system.

Tests revealed he also had traces of cannabis and multiple anti-anxiety medications including Xanax.

The prince had struggled with alcohol misuse and Xanax before his death, the court heard.

He was admitted to the Priory Clinic in Roehampton in south-west London in August last year.



During his stay, he underwent detoxification from alcohol, benzodiazepines and the anti-anxiety drug pregabalin.

Consultant psychiatrist Dr Victoria Chamorro said: “He was assessed as having symptoms of low mood and anxiety on admission.

“When he was discharged he was considered not to be at risk of suicide. He was discharged with a friend but then failed to attend scheduled Zoom appointments.

“Nevertheless there was no concern for him. He engaged well and completed his treatment.”

The inquest heard he was also diagnosed with an upper respiratory tract infection before recovering and leaving the clinic.



Assistant Coroner Jean Harkin said that there was nothing to suggest the prince intended to end his life.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Concluding the inquest, Harkin recorded the death by misadventure, with the medical cause of death given as multi-drug ingestion.

She added: “I would like to offer my sincere condolences to the family of Abdullah.”

News.title: Kemi Badenoch urges Andy Burnham to ditch looming 5p fuel duty rise or risk hammering hard-up drivers
News.content:
KEMI Badenoch has called on Andy Burnham to axe the looming 5p fuel duty hike as one of his next cost-of-living measures.

She warned that the increase due to come in next year will hammer drivers and increase inflation.



The Tory Party leader also ­challenged Labour’s new Prime Minister to rule out tax rises to pay for his spending spree.

Asked by The Sun if Mr Burnham should axe the fuel duty hike, she said: “The Conservatives froze fuel duty throughout the 14 years we were in office.



“There is a cost of living crisis and increasing fuel duty will only make that worse.

“And it’s not just going to make it worse for drivers. It will make it worse for anyone who relies on deliveries and anything that relies on transport to do their business.



“It will increase inflation. It is not necessary. So that’s the sort of thing which he should be finding the money for.”

Ms Badenoch made the comments in a speech in which she likened Mr Burnham to Tory PM Liz Truss.

She said: “He needs to rule out tax rises to pay for his spending spree.”

A Labour Party spokesperson hit back at Ms Badenoch saying the “economy-crashing Tories haven’t got a clue”.



They added: “Andy Burnham is bringing back hope after Kemi Badenoch’s Tory Party nearly broke Britain.

“More of the same failed Tory politics that let people down for years is a recipe for disaster and will only hold Britain back.”

News.title: Drunkest driver ‘ever seen’ set for early jail release after he killed pedestrian and mowed down teen girl
News.content:
SOFT JUSTICE Drunkest driver ‘ever seen’ set for early jail release after he killed pedestrian and mowed down teen girl

A MAN who was branded the “drunkest driver ever seen” after he killed a university student could be set for early release.

Malcolm Waite, 72, was four times over the legal limit and found with a half-drunk bottle of vodka after he hit Fenella Hawes, 20.



Waite’s car mounted the pavement before smashing into two pedestrians, Fenella and a teenage girl.

The Lancaster University student was walking with a bunch of sunflowers for her mum Margaret when Waite hit her and she died at the scene.



Waite then failed to stop and drove on for a mile, only coming to a halt when his Lexus RX SUV collided with a road sign and a tree.

Officers later found him slumped in the driver’s seat smelling strongly of alcohol.

He was jailed for eight years in 2022 after pleading guilty to causing death by dangerous driving after the crash on the A149 in Norfolk.

PC Callum Walchester told Norwich Crown Court at the time: “I’ve been a PC for 10 years and worked in roads policing for almost six years, and he was the drunkest person I have ever seen behind the wheel of a car.”



But the killer driver could be released after serving only half his sentence under the government’s attempts to reduce prison overcrowding.

The controversial early release scheme has been paused after it was revealed two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers could have been freed within weeks.

After mounting pressure, Andy Burnham said: “Keeping the public safe will always be my top priority.

“I am working closely with the new Justice Secretary and have instructed my team to put a pause on the changes that were due to start in September.

“No prisoners will be let out under this policy until we have conducted an urgent review and done everything we can to minimise risk to the public.



“Where changes are needed, we will not hesitate to make them.”

This means no prisoners will be released under the policy until ministers have completed the review.

If the scheme goes ahead, Waite could be one of more than 5,000 offenders, including killers, rapists and violent criminals, released on September 2.

Fenella’s family have said the thought of seeing him on the streets is “petrifying”.

They have called for anyone who has caused a death to be exempt from the scheme and added that an early release would be “no deterrent”.



Speaking to The Telegraph, Fenella’s sister said a four-year-long sentence would be no “equivalent to Fenella’s life at all”.

She continued: “She was 20 years old and had a whole life ahead of her. It doesn’t correlate.

“It’s not a deterrent for anyone else to not drink drive because they can run someone over and only have to do four years for killing someone.”

While he was in custody at Great Yarmouth Police Investigation Centre, some four hours after hitting the two women, Waite was recorded as having 120 micrograms of alcohol in his breath.

Officers calculated this would have been approximately 158 micrograms if taken at the roadside after the crash.



The legal limit is 35 micrograms per 100 millilitres.

A police investigation established Waite’s car was not faulty and the weather and road conditions were clear and fine on July 31, 2022.

During police interviews, Waite answered no comment to every question.

Fenella’s mum told the court in her victim personal statement: “Every day I sob, when I wake up, throughout the day at random times with seemingly no reason, and when I go to bed at night.

“I picture her walking along, so happy carrying sunflowers for me and then being hit by the car.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I sob because I will never see Fenella again, I will never see her radiant smile or hear her laugh.”

She continued: “I sob because she was so happy: she was so lovely inside and out she was so alive and now she isn’t here, and never will be again. I never had a chance to say goodbye.”

News.title: 'We must give all kids water-safety lessons to stop more tragedies like the Mersea Island one'
News.content:
'We must give all kids water-safety lessons to stop more tragedies like the Mersea Island one'

The Rahman family hoped to enjoy a happy day out in the 21C sunshine — instead they're now grieving Samiha Rahman, 15, and her mother, Shelina, after the tragedy at West Mersea beach in Essex

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

The deaths of Samiha Rahman and her mother, Shelina, are a tragedy beyond words. Samiha was 15 when she tried to save her seven-year-old cousin as the tide swept in at West Mersea. Her courage was extraordinary. The loss suffered by this family is unbearable. Which is why it must force Britain to confront a deadly inequality. Children from African, Caribbean and Asian backgrounds are three-and-a-half times more likely to drown. Too many families lack access to affordable swimming lessons, while too many youngsters reach summer without basic survival skills. That is why the Mirror’s Save Lives for Sam campaign matters. We are demanding compulsory water-safety lessons, a national awareness drive, proper rescue equipment at dangerous waters and Sam’s Law to make those protections permanent. Swimming is not a luxury or a sporting extra. It is a life skill. Samiha died trying to save someone she loved. Her bravery must now be matched by action that saves other families from the same devastation.

‌



Iran’s chilling threat against Britain is a sobering reminder of how quickly this country can be dragged into a conflict that is not ours. The use of RAF Fairford by American bombers may be presented as defensive, but to Tehran, it makes UK soil part of the battlefield. That puts our bases, service personnel and nearby communities in the firing line for decisions made in Washington. There can be no excuse for threats from Iran’s Revolutionary Guard, whose record of violence and intimidation is well known. Britain must defend itself and stand firmly against aggression. But ministers also owe the public honesty. Allowing US forces to launch operations from Britain carries consequences. Parliament and the country deserve to know the risks before we are pulled deeper into a war not directly of our making.

Britain’s pubs have been battered by soaring costs, closures and falling trade, so Andy Burnham’s rates cut is a welcome start. A 20 per cent cut in business rates will not transform every struggling local overnight, but it will help protect jobs, keep venues open and back the beating heart of communities.

News.title: M6 traffic live: Massive offal spillage near Stafford sparks 90 minute delays
News.content:
Unclear when M6 will fully reopen

In response to a driver, National Highways explained teams are unsure when the M6 will be fully open again.

The full response, sent at 6.32pm, read: "Good afternoon, and thank you for your message. Lanes 2, 3, and 4 (of 4) remain closed on the M6 northbound between J14 and J15 due to the spillage.

"Contractors have arrived on scene, but they are unable to tackle the spillage without specialist equipment.

"Due to delays in getting this equipment to the site, alternative arrangements have been made and is expected to arrive within the hour.

"There are currently delays of 110 minutes on approach to the incident, with 9 miles of congestion and queuing traffic starting between J12 and J13.

"Unfortunately we are unable to give any further updates on the road reopening. I sincerely apologise for any inconvenience this causes."

News.title: Gangs of youths with machetes terrorise Liverpool city centre as fights break out
News.content:
Gangs of youths with machetes terrorise Liverpool city centre as fights break out

Police in Liverpool city centre now have extra stop and search powers after gangs of youths armed with machetes became involved in fights and assaults

View 2 Images Merseyside Police have been given extra stop and search powers (Image: Andrew Teebay Liverpool Echo)

Groups of youths armed with machetes have terrorised Liverpool city centre with police now granted emergency powers to keep the peace.

‌



A section 60 order came into force at 3pm today following a series of reported fights and assaults involving youths in the area.

‌



The special powers police no longer need "reasonable grounds" to stop and search anyone they reasonably suspect may be involved in violence, criminality or disorder in the affected area.

‌



The authorisation applies to males and females aged between 12 and 30 who officers believe may be involved in criminal activity, the Liverpool Echo reports.

View 2 Images A Section 60 Order has been introduced in Liverpool city centre (Image: Merseyside Police)

‌



Southport killer Axel Rudakabana moved from prison to Broadmoor secure hospital READ MORE :

Mum killed in crash while on way to identify her son's body after tragedy READ MORE :

Chief Inspector Chris Ruane said: “This order is not designed to disrupt people going about their lawful business in the area.

“It will instead be used to deter and disrupt those involved in criminality. We aim to ensure that people who live, work and visit the area can carry on with as little disruption as possible.

“Officers have been deployed across the city centre following these incidents and I hope that the increased presence of our officers is reassuring to those who are within the city centre.

‌



“Some of these offences have included teenage offenders. We would appeal to parents and carers to know where your child is and what they are doing.

"For young people, involvement in crime and anti-social behaviour can have life changing or life limiting consequences.

"We want our young people to enjoy our vibrant city centre safely and with due consideration for others and would ask that all the community plays their part in this.”

News.title: Soho stabbing horror as police swarm London tourist area and 'everyone panicking'
News.content:
Emergency services have rushed to the Greek Street and Soho Square areas in central London, with one man seen being stretchered into an ambulance

A man in his 30s has been stabbed in London's Soho in a broad daylight attack sparking a major emergency services response.

A police cordon is in place on Manette Street, an alley between Greek Street and Charing Cross Road. Several 999 crews can be seen inside the cordon, including paramedics, while footage shows a man being stretchered into an ambulance.

A Met Police statement said the man had been stabbed in the leg. It said: "Urgent enquiries are ongoing. At this early stage of the investigation no arrests have been made."

Inspector Hannah Woodfield, who polices central west London, said it was believed to be an isolated incident, with no further threat to the public.

News.title: Charles and Camilla emerge from Tardis at Commonwealth Games opening ceremony
News.content:
Charles and Camilla emerge from Tardis at Commonwealth Games opening ceremony

King Charles and Queen Camilla attended the opening ceremony for the Commonwealth Games that will see 3,000 athletes from 74 nations compete in events over the next two weeks

View 3 Images The King and Queen emerged from a Tardis (Image: Getty Images)

King Charles and Queen Camilla made an out-of-this world entrance at the opening ceremony of the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

‌



The pair emerged from the Doctor Who Tardis - the time travelling machine used in the long-running science fiction TV series - to huge cheers at the centre of the Hydro stadium in Glasgow. The Tardis, based on a police box designed by Scottish architect Gilbert Mackenzie, was seen rushing through space and time taking in famous local landmarks such as Loch Ness - famously home to 'Nessie,' the Loch Ness Monster - Edinburgh Castle, The Kelpies, the Victorian Glenfinnan Viaduct, and the Highlands during the Jurassic period.

‌



The Ceremony began with the theme of nature, featuring a magical garden reflecting Scotland’s extraordinary landscapes. It also pays tribute to one of Glasgow’s defining moments - the 1988 Garden Festival, in the same way organisers hope Glasgow 2026 is a defining moment for the Commonwealth Games.

‌



View 3 Images King Charles and Queen Camilla made a dramatic entrance at the Glasgow venue (Image: Andrew Milligan/PA Wire)

The Tardis - which stands for Time And Relative Dimension In Space - was also flown over the University of Glasgow, where the TV Doctor graduated from. Viewers from around the world and inside the stadium witnessed the time travelling machine going on a journey round Scotland, almost accidentally operated by one of Scotland’s greatest athletes Sir Chris Hoy and Scottish actor Greg McHugh, much to the confusion of the Seventh Doctor, Sylvester McCoy.

‌



Materialising at various famous landmarks of Scotland, the TARDIS finally arrived at Balmoral Castle, the home of the Royal Family in the Highlands. The Games will take place across multiple venues in the city.

View 3 Images King Charles mingled ahead of the opening ceremony (Image: Getty Images)

The Games will welcome 3,000 athletes from 74 nations and territories, supported by 3,000 volunteers and hundreds of thousands of fans from across Glasgow and beyond.

Article continues below

The 14,300-capacity Hydro stadium, modelled on the great amphitheatres of Greece and Rome, will also host the closing ceremony on Sunday, August 2. The scaled-back games will see 10 sports being played at the event, down from 17 at the 2022 Birmingham games.

Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said he wanted to see athletes compete with pride and passion. Swinney said he was certain of "an absolutely outstanding opening ceremony" in front of Charles and Camilla.

News.title: Southport killer Axel Rudakabana moved from prison to Broadmoor secure hospital
News.content:
Southport killer Axel Rudakabana moved from prison to Broadmoor secure hospital

People in psychiatric units such as Broadmoor are treated as patients rather than prisoners so the move could well anger the families of Rudakabana's victims

View 3 Images Axel Rudakubana has been transferred to Broadmoor (Image: PA)

Southport killer Axel Rudakabana has been transferred to Broadmoor secure hospital, the Ministry of Justice has said.

‌



People in psychiatric units such as Broadmoor are treated as patients rather than prisoners. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said he would remain locked up and is unlikely to ever be released.

‌



The move is likely to anger many of the families of his victims because he was assessed as fit to stand trial in January 2025.

‌



Rudakubana, now 19, from Banks, Lancashire, was jailed for life in January 2025, with a minimum sentence of 52 years, for the murders of Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and nine-year-old Alice da Silva Aguiar.

The tragic girls died after Rudakubana's horrific knife attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance party in Southport on July 29 of the previous year.

View 3 Images Bebe King, Elsie Dot Stancombe and Alice da Silva Aguiar were all tragically killed (Image: Merseyside Police/PA Wire)

‌



He also pleaded guilty to the attempted murders of Leanne Lucas and Jonathan Hayes and admitted the possession of a bladed article in a public place, namely a kitchen knife with a curved blade.

Officials approved the transfer on behalf of ministers, but a spokesperson for the Ministry of Justice stressed it does not alter his 52-year sentence.

The spokesperson said: "The families of those murdered and injured in Southport will be in this country’s heart forever and our thoughts remain with them.

Article continues below

View 3 Images The Southport killer has been moved to Broadmoor psychiatric hospital (Image: PA)

"Any decision to transfer an offender is made following an independent, clinical assessment, under the Mental Health Act. Following rigorous security checks, the offender has been transferred to a high-security psychiatric unit, where he will remain until assessed fit to return to prison.

"Officials have approved this transfer, on behalf of Ministers. This transfer does not change his sentence – which remains at 52 years – and of which he will serve every single day."

News.title: Trump considers 'biggest ever' attack on Iran - 'they haven't had enough pain'
News.content:
Trump considers 'biggest ever' attack on Iran - 'they haven't had enough pain'

Donald Trump is reportedly 'considering a massive attack' on Iran that would dwarf previous US strikes

View Image In an interview today Trump reportedly said the US was all set for a new massive offensive (file photo) (Image: AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Donald Trump has said he is giving serious thought to restarting major combat operations in Iran.

‌



News website Axios reported the US president as saying he was considering a "massive attack" and that would be "bigger than ever before" and that he was "close to making a decision".

‌



Trump said the Iranians "want to negotiate" according to the news site, but they were not ready to make a deal at the present time. "They haven't received enough pain yet," he reportedly said. His words come amid a surge of US military to the Middle East with more US Special Forces are heading to the region as are extra squadrons of fighter jets.

‌



In a post on social media US Central Command said this morning that US forces had “completed another round of strikes against Iran for the 12th consecutive night.”

"I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before. I am close to making a decision. We are all set for it," Axios reported the president as saying. The outlet said it had heard from military sources that no final decisions have been made and no new orders have been issued to US armed forces.

‌



The Iranians "want to negotiate," Trump reportedly insisted but he added that the reason they were not yet ready to make a deal was that "They haven't received enough pain yet".

Meanwhile The Houthis, an armed Islamist group aligned with Iran, struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea last night (Wednesday) after announcing a blockade of the Bab al Mandeb Strait on Tuesday. These latest attacks have seen oil prices soar, oil topping $100 a barrel for the first time since May.

The Houthis announced a a blockade of the Bab al Mandeb strait on Tuesday. The strait, at the southern entrance to the Red Sea, is a chokepoint for oil tankers and cargo vessels moving goods across the world.

Article continues below

Iran's Revolutionary Guard today issued a chilling warning to the British Royal Family and threatened military bases in the UK after the US launched an attack involving what Tehran claims was a mission from RAF Fairford.

An IRGC press release said "any base used to invade Iranian territory is our legitimate target" before warning the "British monarchy".

The statement claimed the monarchy is "the main cause of the misfortunes of the people of our region" and urged that it shouldn't "burden its case any further."

News.title: Motorcyclist, 28, dead in horror Romford collision where car driver fled scene
News.content:
Motorcyclist, 28, dead in horror Romford collision where car driver fled scene

Met Police have released an image of 45-year-old Lee Culleton, who officers are looking to speak to in connection with the fatal crash on the A12, Whalebone Lane in Romford last Sunday

View 2 Images The Met Police rushed to the scene in Romford (stock image) (Image: Nick Wilkinson/Birmingham Live)

Detectives are "urgently" hunting for a man in connection with a fatal crash between a car and a motorbike where they say the car driver fled the scene.

‌



The Metropolitan Police have named the man they want to speak to following the deadly collision in Romford as Lee Culleton.

‌



Cops responded to reports of the crash involving a car and a motorbike on Sunday, July 19, at 9.20pm, the force said.

‌



Police, along with the London Ambulance Service, Air Ambulance and London Fire Brigade raced to the scene on the A12 Whalebone Lane in Romford.

Paramedics battled to save the 28-year-old motorcyclist at the scene but sadly he was pronounced dead. Specialist officers are supporting his loved-ones.

The driver of the car fled the scene on foot, in the direction of Chadwell Heath, the Met said in a statement.

‌



Police say they have been following “several lines of enquiry” and are now asking for the public’s help in tracking down Lee Culleton.

View 2 Images Police are keen to speak with 45-year-old Lee Culleton (Image: Met Police)

The force said the 45-year-old is described as being approximately 5”9’-5”10’ in height, with a medium to large build.

‌



Culleton is known to frequent Canvey Island, Essex.

Detective Inspector Mark Braithwaite, who is leading the investigation, said: "We are keen to speak with Mr Culleton in connection with this incident, which has resulted in a man tragically losing his life. If any members of the public see Culleton, we strongly advise you not to approach him and to call 999 as soon as possible."

Detectives ask that any sightings or information about Lee Culleton are reported by calling 999 citing reference CAD 7142/19JUL.

Article continues below

Anonymous reports can be submitted via Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Burnham pauses plan to release some prisoners early from September
News.content:
Andy Burnham has announced he is pausing a scheme which would have seen thousands of prisoners in England and Wales eligible to be released early.

It came after criticism of the scheme from survivors and victims' families, including the widow of PC Andrew Harper who described the possibility of his killers' early release as "deplorable".

The Sentencing Act, which was due to come into effect in September, would have seen some offenders let out at varying stages in a bid to ease prison overcrowding.

The new Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the pause aimed to "give victims and survivors certainty" and the government wanted to make sure it got "the implementation of this policy right".

He added a review would also look at the information given to survivors and victims' families as part of the early release process.

Burnham earlier said: "No prisoners will be let out under this policy until we have conducted an urgent review and done everything we can to minimise risk to the public."

He added: "Where changes are needed, we will not hesitate to make them."

Under the act, some offenders would have been let out after serving a third of their sentence, rather than half.

The rest of their sentence would be spent in the community, where they would be monitored and could be returned to prison if they offended again.

More serious offenders would have been released after serving half of their sentence, rather than two-thirds.

The policy was brought in to ease overcrowding in the prison system but has been criticised by opposition parties, as well as victims and their families.

The scheme would have seen around 700 prisoners released in early September, the BBC understands.

The decision to pause the scheme came after criticism from the family of Thames Valley Police officer Andrew Harper, who was killed in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road by three teenagers.

Two of the killers of PC Harper, who were both sentenced to 13 years in prison, would have benefited from the scheme from June 2027, when the longest fixed sentences would have been added to the scheme.

PC Harper's widow, Lissie, called the plans "deplorable" and said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.

His mother, meanwhile, said her son had not been given "proper justice" and "every victim will be feeling the same" about the early prison release scheme.

Thousands of letters had been sent to victims in recent weeks, warning them that the early release scheme was coming in September.

Norris, who voted in support of the Sentencing Act under Starmer's government, later said the decision to pause was made after "listening to victims" and he hoped to provide them "certainty as soon as we can".

He said: "The prime minister and I have heard from victims and survivors and from people across the country about their concerns about the implementation of some very important elements of the Sentencing Act."

One element the government needed to get right was the information provided to victims before prisoners were released, Norris added.

Norris refused to be drawn on why he did not raise concerns when the Sentencing Act was first introduced but said Burnham was "quite right" to review the scheme.

Jade Belgrove, a survivor of sexual assault who has been campaigning against the early release scheme, said it was "such a relief that we've been heard".

She told BBC News that when she received a letter informing her that her attacker might be released early "it was horrific".

Belgrove said it even led her to question whether reporting the assault in the first place was worth it.

News.title: Mum and daughter who died at beach were trying to save boy, 7
News.content:
A woman and her 15-year-old daughter who died after getting into difficulty in the water on the Essex coast were trying to help a seven-year-old boy, police have said.

The child remains in a critical condition in hospital after the incident at West Mersea near Colchester on Wednesday evening. Three others were taken to hospital.

The victims have been named by a family member as Shally Rahman, 41, and teenager Samiha Rahman. Police said all the people involved knew each other.

Shally's brother-in-law Matiur Rahman said the family was enjoying a seaside holiday when a "big wave came and took them".

"My whole family, we are, like, speechless," said Matiur Rahman, who used to live in Bradford, but spoke to the BBC from Bangladesh.

"We are very shocked. We can't explain [what has happened]."

He said his niece was a "very, very good person" and his sister-in-law was "a very helpful person".

News.title: Senior ministers and aides set to work from No 10 North
News.content:
Senior ministers and aides close to Andy Burnham are expecting to regularly work from No 10 North, which the prime minister has said will be the "dominant driver of the UK's economy".

Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Louise Haigh, who is overseeing No 10 North in her role as Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, are planning to work there.

The new branch of Downing Street is currently operating from Heron House in Manchester city centre, whilst a brownfield site is redeveloped.

A blueprint for No 10 North produced by the think tank Re:State recommends a workforce of as many as 300 staff within 18 months.

Burnham aims to base himself at No 10 North at least one day a week and is expected to start work there for the first time in coming days.

He will be joined by his closest adviser, Kevin Lee, the director of his mayoral office, who will move to No 10 North after next week's Greater Manchester mayoral election.

Lee is one of at least seven Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) employees, including four senior managers, to have been recruited by Burnham and are already moving into No 10 North.

Chief executive Caroline Simpson is moving to become Downing Street deputy chief of staff based at No 10 North, Directors John Wrathmell and Claire Norman will also move across.

Some London-based civil servants have voiced concerns about the uncertainty surrounding the plans, with most details expected to be announced in the weeks ahead.

In the weeks before Burnham became prime minister, the BBC has been told that senior officials were summoned to calls informing them that a significant programme to move staff out of London was being developed.

News.title: Rayner rules out repaying severance cash after making cabinet return
News.content:
A lump sum, equivalent of 25% of the annual ministerial salary, is payable when a minister stops holding office. Departing ministers who are aged over 65 or are reappointed within three weeks do not qualify.

The 2025/26 accounts, external for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government record the severance payment for Rayner.

In her first interview since returning to government, Rayner was pressed on whether she would return the money.

She told Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live: "No, my severance payment was given to me at the time, I had worked in government for a period of time and then I came out of government for just under a year."

She added: "I will be delivering in government again."

Rayner earlier said her criticism of the Conservatives over severance payments came at a time when there was a "revolving door" which saw ministers return to government "after 40-odd days".

The Conservatives earlier this week said Rayner had "quit in disgrace and took a Â£17k payout" last year.

The party added: "Now she's got her old job back, will she return the cash? Or is it one rule for Labour, and another for everyone else?"

Rayner's departure last September came after the prime minister's ethics adviser, Sir Laurie Magnus, said she had "acted with integrity" but concluded that she had breached the ministerial code.

Sir Laurie said she did get legal advice when buying the property, but failed to seek further expert tax advice as recommended.

In May, Rayner resolved her tax affairs with HMRC following an investigation, settling Â£40,000 in unpaid stamp duty.

The MP for Ashton-under-Lyne said she had been "exonerated" of the accusation that she had "deliberately sought to avoid tax".

Rayner told Matt Chorley: "The situation I went through last year was really difficult, it was difficult for my family, but I felt I'd let people down and I never want to let people down, I want to fight for them."

Rayner also said she has "unfinished business" in government, including on building council houses and supporting local government.

Burnham has said he wants to deliver "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period".

Asked for details to explain what this will look like, Rayner said she would not provide an "exact figure" or provide a date for when she considers the post-war period to have ended.

She said: "We want to aspire to get as far as possible and what we've done as a government is put more investment in that, the Â£39bn for social and affordable housing grant funding that we want to get out the door."

News.title: Wildfires and record dry conditions trigger drought in parts of Wales
News.content:
"We've had really dry weather but also it's been really hot - and those things combined if you're a livestock farmer means excessive pressure on livestock," said Abi Reader, president of NFU Cymru.

"You have to make sure they have enough water and shade, and we are getting farms with springs and streams drying up," she told BBC Walescast.

"If you're an arable farmer the heat and dry weather have also forced a lot of the crops to come to ripening a lot earlier than they normally would.

"It's unprecedented early harvesting this year and farmers are going to see lower crop yields."

Welsh Water emphasised that NRW's drought declarations were different to its own announcements.

The company has already brought in a hospipe ban for 33,000 properties in west Wales.

"NRW's drought status reflects environmental conditions, including factors such as rainfall, river flows and groundwater levels," a spokesperson said.

"By contrast, Welsh Water's Temporary Use Ban is an operational measure based on local water demand and our ability to replenish service reservoirs with drinking water at the same rate, or faster, than customers are using water.

"It is driven by the capacity of the local treatment works and distribution network to keep up with sustained demand.

"This means different parts of Wales can experience different operational pressures, even if they are not in the same environmental drought category declared by NRW."

Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability, Llyr Gruffydd, said: "This is an environmental drought classification. It's about the state of water levels in our rivers.

"It does not speak to public water supplies which I can assure people are there, there is sufficient supplies but we would of course urge people to be careful and diligent in their use of water so that that can be protected."

News.title: UK 'ready to defend itself' after Iran says bases are 'legitimate targets'
News.content:
The British government has said it "stands ready 24/7 to defend itself" after Iran said UK bases used by the US were considered "legitimate targets".

The UK has allowed the US to launch "defensive" operations from British bases hosting American personnel and aircraft, while refusing to cooperate in offensive operations against Iran.

Iran's foreign ministry said the UK was an "accomplice" in the US war, while the powerful Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) military wing said any country which supports the US militarily "will be responsible for the consequences and repercussions".

It came after the US carried out a 12th consecutive night of strikes against targets in Iran.

While US President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticised the British government and former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer for what he has deemed a lack of support for his war, Iran's comments on 23 July sought to paint the UK as a party to the campaign.

In March, days into the US-Israel led war, permission was given to the US for it to use British bases including RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire and Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean to target Iranian military infrastructure used to attack Gulf countries and vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

That policy has not been altered by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was notified last week that a decision had been taken to extend the agreement with the US.

In a statement published on the IRGC-linked Tasnim News Agency on 23 July, the group said American bombing missions had been launched from RAF Fairford two days earlier.

The UK Ministry of Defence has not commented on whether the base was used by the US for operations against Iran this week.

Responding to the Iranian threats, a UK government spokesperson said: "Our Armed Forces are ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it's on our soil or from abroad. The UK stands ready 24/7 to defend itself.

"This includes through operating a layered approach to air and missile defence, provided by Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force assets equipped with a range of advanced capabilities, working closely with our Nato allies.

"The UK's approach to the conflict remains the same - we are committed to defending our people, our interests and our allies, acting in accordance with international law and not getting drawn into the wider conflict."

Days after the war began on 28 February, Iran's ambassador to London, Seyed Ali Mousavi, said Iran would have the "right to self-defence" if the UK joined the war, and said it should be "very careful" about taking part.

On 19 March, Iran fired two ballistic missiles at the UK's Diego Garcia base in the Chagos Islands. One reportedly failed mid-flight, with the other shot down by a US airship.

There were doubts then over whether Iran had missiles which were capable of reaching the archipelago, which is about 2,360 miles (3,600km) from Iran.

The same month, Israel claimed Iran possessed missiles that could reach up to 4,000km (2,485 miles), which would theoretically mean they could reach the UK and mainland European countries.

However, then Housing Secretary Steve Reed told BBC News at the time there was "no specific assessment that the Iranians are targeting the UK - or even could if they wanted to".

Analysts have also raised doubts over the reliability and accuracy of Iran's missile arsenal, which the US says has been severely degraded by its strikes.

Iran has launched strikes against several countries in the Gulf which house US military bases in recent months, while attacks against civilian vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have effectively closed the vital shipping route.

News.title: Gary Lineker among millionaires asking Andy Burnham to tax them more
News.content:
Millionaires including former footballer Gary Lineker and music producer Brian Eno have written to new prime minister Andy Burnham asking to be taxed more.

In an open letter, 120 well-off Britons told Burnham: "We can afford it. We're not talking about higher taxes on those who get up and go to work for their income every day, but on the very richest whose income is derived from the wealth they hold."

Organised by Patriotic Millionaires, the letter said it would lead to a more equal society, and urged a "devolution of wealth and power from the very richest".

People can already give money or stocks voluntarily to the Treasury using a donation facility.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Lineker is "very welcome to pay more tax he can write a cheque to the Treasury, no one is stopping him."

Patriotic Millionaires support a 2% tax on wealth over Â£10m.

"Millionaires are a patriotic bunch," the letter states. "We love this country and we want it to succeed.

"But success requires investment and a primary source of untouched capital investment is sitting with us, in untaxed potential."

Other signatories include Richard Curtis, who wrote the film Notting Hill, and Ian Gregg, the former managing director of Greggs and son of the bakery chain's founder. Scottish crime writer Val McDermid and former financial trader-turned-equality campaigner Gary Stevenson also signed the letter.

Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds said she would welcome UK millionaires increasing the amount of tax they pay but said any major changes would be announced during a Budget.

"I welcome the fact that people of good means are saying that they want to pay more. They can pay more," she said and pointed to the Treasury's donation link.

The renewed call for higher tax on the wealthy follows a similar campaign in previous years.

Burnham did not rule out a wealth tax when asked about it by Lineker - formerly the BBC's highest paid presenter - a few days before he became prime minister.

He suggested he may have "to ask for a little more" tax at some point.

Lineker was paid around Â£1.3m a year before he left the BBC. He is worth a reported Â£30m.

In 2023, Lineker won his appeal against HMRC over a Â£4.9m tax bill, after the UK tax authority pursued him over taxes on income from both the BBC and BT Sport, from 2013 to 2014, and 2017 to 2018.

The latest call from Patriotic Millionaires said there is a "need to embrace a new kind of devolution of wealth and power, from the very richest in order to reinvest back into our greatest asset in every region".

It added that in its own poll, the majority of millionaires wanted a higher tax on themselves.

"There are a few people left with outdated economic thinking and few others desperate to hold onto every penny they can... Those that can't see past the end of their own self interest have no place in designing a Britain for the future," the letter said.

Musician Brian Eno told BBC Radio Lincolnshire the tax system was "very generous to rich people".

"If you're wealthy you don't pay very much tax but hire a clever bunch of accountants who somehow get you off that," he said.

He also dismissed the idea that lots of millionaires would leave the UK if they were taxed too much.

News.title: Southport killer Axel Rudakubana moved to psychiatric hospital
News.content:
Axel Rudakubana, who murdered three children at a dance class in Southport, has been moved from prison to a secure psychiatric hospital.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has confirmed he will be transferred from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor, the high-security psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Rudakubana murdered Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, and injured eight other children and two adults in an attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in July 2024.

He was given a 52-year prison sentence in January 2025 but the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to Rudakubana being 17 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

The then Attorney-General Lord Hermer said Rudakubana's sentence was the "second-longest sentence imposed by the courts in English history".

A spokesperson for the MoJ told PA: "The families of those murdered and injured in Southport will be in this country's heart forever and our thoughts remain with them.

"Any decision to transfer an offender is made following an independent, clinical assessment, under the Mental Health Act. Following rigorous security checks, the offender has been transferred to a high-security psychiatric unit, where he will remain until assessed fit to return to prison.

"Officials have approved this transfer, on behalf of Ministers. This transfer does not change his sentence â which remains at 52 years â and of which he will serve every single day."

The cost of keeping Rudakubana in hospital is likely to be much higher in Broadmoor than a prison.

According to the Centre for Mental Health the average secure hospital bed costs around Â£270,000 a year.

The average cost of keeping a prisoner in Belmarsh is Â£97,740 according to figures for 2023.

Broadmoor is the oldest of the UK's three high-security hospitals and has held some of the UK's most high-profile criminals.

It was renovated in 2017 and the BBC obtained pictures from inside the hospital. They show that older prison-like cells were replaced by more spacious rooms, though still with locks on the doors.

In May 2025 there was an investigation after Rudakubana, now 19, allegedly attacked a prison officer with boiling water.

The Southport Public Inquiry has heard evidence about his past mental health conditions.

A senior clinician at Alder Hey Children's Hospital described his "lack of empathy" combined with a "fascination with violence" and neurodiversity, which he said added up to a "really toxic mix".

According to West London NHS Trust, Broadmoor specialises in "providing assessment, treatment and care in conditions of high security" for men and is one of only three high secure psychiatric hospitals in England and Wales.

News.title: Pubs cheer business rates relief while other firms 'left out in the cold'
News.content:
Keith Bott, who runs the Titanic Brewery and nine pubs across the Midlands, said the government was "finally recognising the plight of the hospitality industry and trying to help".

He said pubs had been hit by a mix of employer National Insurance increases, the rising minimum wage, high inflation and the climbing cost of living.

Meanwhile, the sector is "heavily taxed", with around 35-40% of turnover going to the Treasury, he added.

"What I really liked in this announcement is they are recognising we need to look at a fairer tax system so we can all contribute to society," Bott told the BBC. He said online retailers that operate out of warehouses pay a "ridiculously low" amount of business rates in comparison, and "we need to make the system fair".

And Bott urged the government to go further in supporting the industry, cutting the duty on draft beer to target drinks sold in pubs.

News.title: Burnham tells Swinney independence is 'off limits' at Glasgow Commonwealth Games meeting
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has met the Scottish and Welsh first ministers ahead of the start of the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

Burnham spoke to John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth at a series of face-to-face meetings in Glasgow.

Downing Street later said a second Scottish independence referendum was "off limits".

Swinney said the new prime minister gave a commitment not to bypass Holyrood with his plans for further devolution of power, while ap Iorwerth said he set out the case for Wales to have parity of powers with Scotland.

A Downing Street spokesperson said the prime minister congratulated Swinney and the city of Glasgow on hosting the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

He said he was looking forward to the opening ceremony later in the evening.

However, the cross-government meetings were dominated by conversations about the relations between London, Edinburgh and Cardiff.

News.title: Police failed to check Manchester synagogue attacker's phones despite arresting him twice
News.content:
A police chief has apologised after admitting phones were twice seized from the Manchester synagogue attacker months before the car and knife assault but they were not examined.

Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, was on bail for an alleged rape when he carried out the attack on Heaton Park Synagogue in Crumpsall on 2 October 2025, in which two Jewish men were killed.

His devices, which contained evidence of his extreme views, were seized after he was arrested in February and September but not analysed.

Greater Manchester Police Chief Constable Sir Stephen Watson said he was "deeply sorry", conceding that "the information contained within these devices would have inspired further investigative action".

Sir Stephen said the end of legal proceedings against Mohammad Bashir, who has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 17 years for plotting a separate attack with Al-Shamie, meant rules around sharing information about a live criminal case had been lifted.

He said: "In conducting an internal review, it became apparent that GMP had seized Al-Shamie's mobile devices, at the point of each arrest.

"The significance of the data contents of these devices was substantial in respect of evidencing an extremist mindset.

"I am disappointed at the prospect of adding to the distress of all of those affected by the terrible events last October.

"For this, I am deeply sorry."

News.title: Shapps blocked from standing again for the Conservatives
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the BBC she leads "a brand new party full of new people" - after it emerged in the Spectator, external that the former cabinet minister and Tory party chairman Sir Grant Shapps has been rejected as a Conservative Party parliamentary candidate.

Sir Grant, who has declined to comment, served in nine ministerial roles in government as well as co-chairing the party.

In cabinet, he served as home secretary, defence secretary, transport secretary, business secretary, energy secretary and net zero secretary.

He was also a Foreign Office Minister, housing minister and international development minister, external.

He lost his Welwyn Hatfield seat to Labour's Andrew Lewin in 2024 by 3,799 votes after representing it since 2005.

But his application to stand again for the Conservatives at the next general election has been declined.

One party source told the BBC "it reflects badly on Kemi's temperament. North Korean purges don't work in British politics".

Badenoch told a news conference in central London: "We don't treat our former MPs or our candidates like tittle-tattle for Westminster gossip.

"What I will say is that we're going to be announcing candidates shortly, and you will see that this is a very different party from the one that was removed from government in 2024."

News.title: Johnson-Thompson and Asher-Smith out of Commonwealths
News.content:
Olympic silver medallist Katarina Johnson-Thompson has pulled out of the Commonwealth Games because of injury.

Dina Asher-Smith and 400m Olympic silver medalist Matt Hudson-Smith, who were both set to run relays for Team England in Glasgow, have also been replaced, as has Asher-Smith's sprint team-mate Daryll Neita and 400m runner Amber Anning.

Johnson-Thompson, 33, was due to compete in her third Commonwealth Games heptathlon, having won gold on the Gold Coast in 2018 and at Birmingham in 2022.

But she said she has "not been able to get back to the level" needed to compete and will instead focus on being fit for the European Championships next month.

"Missing a championship is never easy, but I know it's the right decision," she said.

Johnson-Thompson has been replaced in England's squad by Niamh Emerson, who took bronze behind Johnson-Thompson in 2018.

The withdrawal of such high-profile names is a significant blow to the event on the day the opening ceremony takes place.

Renee Regis, Ebuka Nwokeji, Tara Simpson-Sullivan and Tom Keen have all been added to England's athletics squad in Glasgow. The track and field competition begins on Monday.

News.title: Love Island: All Stars winners Molly Smith and Tom Clare marry
News.content:
Sharing more from their marriage ceremony, Molly posted a photo to her Instagram story of her hand on top of Tom's.

The snap showed their wedding rings along with a bouquet of flowers, with the caption: "Husband and wife".

The couple first got together two years ago, when they met on season one of Love Island: All Stars.

All Stars is a spin-off of the hit dating show, which sees past contestants return for a second chance at finding love in the villa.

During the reality dating show, the pair beat Molly's ex-boyfriend Callum Jones and his partner at the time, Jessica Gale, who finished as runners-up.

Molly previously starred in series six in 2020 and left the show with Callum, who she was in a relationship with for three years before they split.

While Hyde United footballer Tom previously came third place on the second winter edition of Love Island in 2023 with former partner Samie Elishi.

Earlier this year, Tom and Molly took over hosting duties of the NearlyWeds podcast from radio presenters and reality stars Jamie Laing and Sophie Habboo.

Fellow Love Island stars were among those to congratulate the couple, including former winner Casey O'Gorman who described it as the "best day".

Sophie Piper, who came third on their All Star season, and TikTok star GK Barry also shared their support with the newly weds.

News.title: MI5 to pay damages for illegal surveillance of journalist's phone
News.content:
MI5 and the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) have been ordered to pay Â£20,000 in damages to a journalist, after they illegally obtained his phone records.

Former BBC Journalist Vincent Kearney took a case at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) in London.

It is believed to be the first time that MI5 has been directed to pay compensation to a journalist.

Kearney was the subject of secret operations aimed at discovering his confidential sources while he worked at the BBC in Belfast.

In a statement welcoming the judgement, Kearney said: "I am delighted the court has penalised those responsible for breaking the law.

"The fact it decided to award damages reflects the seriousness of the case.

"It is important that agencies charged with upholding the law know that they are not above the law and will be held to account."

The BBC, which brought the case alongside Kearney, said: "Today's findings are welcome, necessary and significant.

"We hope that their effect will be to protect journalists and their freedom to report and investigate stories into the future."

Kearney worked for BBC Northern Ireland for 18 years until 2019, when he joined RTÃ, where he is currently its northern editor.

There were multiple operations targeting him between 2006 and 2014, when he was a BBC correspondent covering policing and security issues.

Four of them were run by the PSNI, who also created a "profile" on him, which included car registrations and the names of his wife and mother-in-law.

He suspects it was for surveillance purposes.

News.title: Marathon runners compete on drifting sea ice at North Pole
News.content:
Twenty-three runners from seven countries took part in races at the Arctic's geographic North Pole, organisers have said, in an event they dubbed as the "world's coolest marathon".

The races took place on drifting sea ice at the geographic North Pole in the Arctic, with competitors arriving from Norway aboard the French polar vessel Le Commandant Charcot.

They disembarked the ship to run laps of a 1,055 metre loop on the ice below, wearing thermal gear and life vests as a safety requirement, while armed guards kept watch for polar bears around the perimeter.

Denmark's Rikke Dam won the women's title with a time of 6:54:02 and Wang Shengxian of China won the men's race in 3:52:22. Organisers said the course disappeared with the ice just hours after the races ended.

The food arrives almost as steadily as the protesters.

Every few minutes, delivery riders on motorbikes pull up outside the protest site with bags of burgers, snacks and bottled water. Volunteers collect the food, stack it along other donated supplies and distribute it to demonstrators.

Supporters across India are helping sustain the country's “Cockroach” movement by ordering meals through online food delivery apps for protesters camped in the capital. The steady stream of food has become a visible sign of the growing support for a youth movement that has emerged as one of the biggest challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government in years.

Many contributors have never set foot at the protest site in New Delhi and don't know each other. Instead, they send meals directly to the demonstrators, often instructing delivery riders to hand them to any protester they see.

open image in gallery ( AP )

Shakti Vashisth, 24, sees every food delivery as a reminder that the protest extends far beyond those camped on the streets. Each meal, she said, is a sign of support from someone who cannot be there in person.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

“There are a lot of people that I can understand might not be able to come here, but they are sending their love,” she said.

The “Cockroach” movement, which started over repeated leaks of high-stakes medical college and government job entrance examinations, and led to some committing suicide, has expanded into a broader call for government accountability, drawing thousands to demonstrations at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in New Delhi that has become the movement’s base.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

Demonstrators at the protest site have stood their ground despite a major crackdown on Monday when police used tear gas and batons to stop them from marching toward Parliament. The violence fueled public anger and the crowds now extend beyond students, with young professionals, parents and others joining the sit-in.

Now, the growing crowd needs sustenance and the steady flow of donations helps sustain the protest camp. From home-style Indian meals to pizza, burgers and other fast food, volunteers hand out meals and bottles of water to protesters.

open image in gallery ( AP )

The support has been staggering, with protest organizers asking people to stop sending food orders as they have begun to exceed the number of protesters on site.

“The amount of food coming in is overwhelming. It’s difficult to even keep count,” said Bhoomi Kapoor, a volunteer.

open image in gallery ( AP )

Motorbike courier Neg Singh said he had already made 19 trips to the protest site. On one run, he picked up 70 pizzas, an order so large it took three delivery riders to carry it through the crowds. The order was placed from someone in Noida city, some 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) from the protest site.

For Singh, the protest has brought more than extra work. It has also drawn him into the movement itself.

“We also feel deeply connected to this protest. We support it wholeheartedly,” he said.
