The Tate brothers, who have publicly backed Trump, are prominent figures in the online "manosphere", a network of influencers often associated with hyper-masculine content that played a role in mobilising some young male voters during the 2024 US presidential election.

A judge scheduled a further hearing for 27 July. A district judge will decide whether the legal conditions for extradition have been met.

World.title: World Cup boosts Chinese tourists' interest in Spain: retailers prepare for Golden Week
World.content:
Spain's World Cup victory has fuelled interest among Chinese tourists in visiting the country and opens up an opportunity for retailers ahead of Golden Week, one of China's main holiday periods, according to data from travel platform Qunar compiled by Spanish company Stamp.

 

Searches for flights between Shenzhen and Barcelona rose thirty-three-fold in the hours following La Roja's triumph, while searches for Tenerife were up nineteen times and those for Malaga 10.5 times.

More broadly, according to a 2024 study by the University of Aberdeen published in the Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics, winning the World Cup raises the champion country's year-on-year GDP growth by at least 0.48% over the two quarters after the final, before the effect fades, even though the sample of winners analysed is inevitably small. Applied to the size of the Spanish economy, at 1.69 trillion euros, that estimated increase would amount to around 4 billion euros.

In the case of the Asian giant, however, the surge in interest is also underpinned by a trend that was already well under way. According to data from Aena, air traffic between Spain and China reached 707,530 passengers in the first half of 2026, 46.8% more than in the same period a year earlier. The launch of new air routes and the increase in travellers from cities such as Chengdu and Guangzhou have strengthened this recovery, which the World Cup has helped to accelerate.

With Golden Week scheduled from 1 to 8 October, Stamp has published a guide to help Spanish retailers adapt to Chinese consumers' preferences. The document highlights that 77.8% of these travellers plan their shopping before they travel via platforms such as Xiaohongshu, Weibo or WeChat, making online visibility crucial for attracting customers.

The Spanish company specialising in shopping tourism also stresses the importance of accepting payment methods such as Alipay and WeChat Pay, used in more than 90% of purchases made by Chinese tourists abroad, as well as simplifying the VAT refund process.

"Today's Chinese tourist does not have Tax Free, he has Tax Refund: he pays the full VAT at the till and, weeks later, if everything goes well, gets part of it back," explains Abel Navajas, co-founder and chief executive of Stamp. According to the executive, removing that friction and applying the discount at the time of purchase could prove decisive in helping Spanish retailers make the most of the rise in tourism from China.

World.title: Google fine 'creates uncertainty' for EU-US trade deal, US Trade Representative says
World.content:
The US government has hit back at Brussels after the European Commission slapped on Thursday a €890 million fine against Google for breaching the bloc's Big Tech rulebook, warning that the sanction puts the EU-US trade deal at risk.

 

The Commission announced the first fine against Google under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), concluding a two-year investigation into the company's alleged unfair practices — notably self-preferencing its own services in search results and unfairly treating app developers.

The sanction predictably drew the ire of Washington, which views the EU's digital rules as unfairly targeting American companies and has repeatedly equated the fines with trade tariffs.

"This is in addition to two recent actions by the Commission under the Digital Markets Act that target Google's Android operating system and Search services that pose serious risks for the privacy and security of users, represent a de facto forced technology transfer and intellectual property theft, and impose unreasonable financial penalties," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement after the news.

According to the senior US official, the various fines against Google alone amount to over 2% of the EU's budget, a contribution larger than that of many of the bloc's member states.

"The EU often claims that it is looking for stability and predictability in our trading relationship, but these actions are driving massive uncertainty for U.S. exports of goods and services to Europe," Greer added.

Ongoing dialogue attempts

In recent weeks, the Commission and the US government have launched a so-called digital dialogue, an attempt to revive transatlantic tech cooperation following the decline of the EU-US Trade and Technology Council under the Biden administration.

Critics see the initiative as offering Washington a privileged channel to lobby against EU digital rules, pressing Brussels to soften their application to American businesses under the threat of tariff retaliation.

Last year, Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič emerged as an outspoken voice in favour of postponing an antitrust fine against Google, fearing it could derail the trade negotiations that culminated in the Turnberry agreement.

While the fine was executed, the Commission refrained from making a big announcement and the Commissioner responsible for competition, Teresa Ribera, did not take questions from journalists. The EU Commission cited a scheduling conflict, even though records showed there wasn’t any.

Commission officials, by contrast, now argue the dialogue is meant to defuse tensions and prevent them from erupting into public spats, acknowledging that Washington will always lobby for its own companies, but using the channel as a chance to explain Brussels' reasoning.

Brussels has also been careful to show its rules don't target only US tech giants, alternating fines against American companies with sanctions against Chinese ones. On Monday, the Commission slapped AliExpress with a €550 million fine.

The US reaction comes despite these efforts, and the Commission giving US officials an heads-up on the upcoming conclusion of the investigation.

Pressure mounting

On both sides of the pond, pressure has been mounting over enforcement of the EU's digital rules, threatening to push Brussels and Washington towards confrontation.

In a letter sent earlier this week and seen by Euronews, 25 Republican members of the US Congress urged President Donald Trump "to encourage your administration to take decisive action before the EU further entrenches this anti-American regime."

The lawmakers argue that the EU's enforcement of the DMA contradicts commitments made to Washington on digital trade barriers, dismiss the ongoing dialogue as a "delay tactic," and go as far as naming companies that could be targeted in retaliation — Nokia, Axel Springer, Volkswagen, BMW, Ikea and Airbus.

Conversely, a cross-party coalition of MEPs has written to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urging faster enforcement of the DMA against Google.

"The EU has been very clear that we have the sovereign right to legislate, including in a digital sector," a Commission official said. "Today is the proof that when our case is ready, and it's always based on solid evidence, it's nondiscriminatory, we adopt a decision."

Big decision, few implications?

Still, critics point out that the fine is modest for a company of Google's size — just 0.22% of annual turnover — suggesting the EU executive is going easy on the American giant to avoid drawing Washington's ire.

"Plenty of people would fare-dodge if the fine were cheaper than the ticket. The size of the fine is disappointing and bears no relation to the damage Google has done to the European economy," MEP Alexandra Geese (Germany/Greens-EFA) told Euronews.

For the Commission, the point of the DMA is not primarily about hefty fines, but about forcing changes in behaviour to make digital markets fairer and more contestable for European consumers and businesses.

Google must comply with the Commission's decision within 60 days or face periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of its worldwide turnover. The company has already introduced some changes, which the EU executive is currently assessing.

"This implementation of the DMA continues to break everyday products. To comply, we are having to strip away real-time Search features Europeans love - like instant pricing and direct availability for hotels, flights, and restaurants - and dismantle safety protections on Google Play," Google President of Global Affairs Kent Walker said.

Trade fallout

Commission officials note that elements of the investigation — notably the treatment of app developers — are also under antitrust investigation in the US.

"Just as the US FTC and Justice Department pursue fair competition in digital markets, the DMA ensures those same shared principles are upheld in Europe. This is about market fairness and openness, not discriminatory trade friction and should not be looked at it with this perspective," MEP Brando Benifei (Italy/S&D) told Euronews.

Washington is preparing a fresh round of duties, with the current regime set to expire this week. The Commission has said it will not react to new tariffs as long as they stay within the 15% cap agreed in last year's EU-US trade deal.

The new tariffs are set to target goods allegedly produced with forced labour that harm US commercial interests. However, a long-floated retaliation targeting the digital tax currently in place in EU countries such as Spain, Italy and France is also rumoured to be in the cards.

"A real dialogue can only take place during a ceasefire. The EU's recent actions undermine these efforts and pose a real risk to the continuation of transatlantic stability with respect to trade," Ambassador Greer concluded.

World.title: Man jailed for life over terror plot targeting UK military academy
World.content:
A man has been sentenced to life in prison for plotting a terrorist attack on a British military academy with a friend who later carried out a deadly stabbing attack at a synagogue.

 

Mohammad Bashir, 31, pleaded guilty at Manchester Crown Court to preparing an act of terrorism and must serve a minimum of 17 years before he can be considered for parole.

Although he was not involved in the synagogue attack on Yom Kippur last October, the investigation into the stabbing uncovered evidence that he and the attacker had planned a similar assault on the UK's Defence Academy, believing it trained Israeli forces.

“Mohammad Bashir is a determined jihadist and dangerous individual who was planning an attack that could have caused devastation,” the Crown Prosecution Service said in a statement.

“His actions demonstrate a deliberate and sustained commitment to violent extremism.”

Two months before his friend Jihad Al-Shamie carried out the synagogue attack, Bashir drove him from Manchester to the Defence Academy in Shrivenham, Oxfordshire, to scout the site. The pair discussed how they would enter the base, what weapons they would use and how a fake suicide vest could be used during the attack.

Related Former UK water company CEO charged over alleged water test fraud

“I am sure that you and he anticipated that you would both be martyred and you intended to kill others,” Justice Bobbie Cheema-Grubb told Bashir during sentencing.

“This was a viable plan to attack the Defense Academy in a broadly similar way to that in which that Al-Shamie attacked the synagogue; using handheld weapons and a dummy suicide vest to cause as much bloodshed as possible.”

The planned attack was never carried out, and prosecutors said there was no evidence that Bashir was involved in the synagogue attack.

Greater Manchester Police said on Thursday messages between the two men were found on phones seized from Al-Shamie after earlier arrests in 2025.

The police apologised for failing to review the evidence before the synagogue attack and said the Independent Office for Police Conduct would examine whether the missed messages could have helped prevent it.

“It is clear that our not having reviewed the data available to us prior to the attack constitutes a missed opportunity,” Stephen Watson, Chief Constable of Greater Manchester Police, said.

“I am disappointed at the prospect of adding to the distress of all of those affected by the terrible events last October. For this, I am deeply sorry.”

World.title: Opera icons or birds? Europeans invited to pick new euro banknotes
World.content:
The future euro banknotes are taking shape and, this time, it will be European citizens themselves who have the final say. On Thursday, the European Central Bank presented the ten finalist designs from which the new banknotes will be chosen.

 

More than 1,200 proposals were examined, but in the end two major themes emerged, reflecting the continent's identity: European culture and the richness of nature.

On the one hand are figures who have left their mark on the history of art, music, science and literature. On the other are rivers and birds that cross the continent's borders, symbols of Europe's biodiversity and the need to protect it.

The ECB opens a public vote to choose the euro's new look

The ten finalist designs were presented by European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, who invited Europeans to take part in choosing the euro's new look.

You can vote here. For each of the two themes, five different designs have been created, ranging from modern and minimalist styles to more traditional depictions of the chosen subjects. Through a survey published on the ECB's website, citizens can express their preferences and help shape the final decision.

The "European culture" theme: six major historical figures

If the culture-themed option wins, the new banknotes will feature some of the most influential figures in European history.

The €5 banknote would feature Maria Callas, the renowned Greek-American soprano who revolutionised the world of opera.

The €10 banknote would be dedicated to the German composer Ludwig van Beethoven, while the €20 banknote would honour scientist Marie Curie, a Nobel Prize winner and pioneer of scientific research.

The €50 banknote would depict Miguel de Cervantes, author of Don Quixote, one of the most important novels in world literature.

The higher denominations would celebrate two emblematic figures of European thought: Leonardo da Vinci, who would feature on the €100 banknote, and Bertha von Suttner, the Nobel Peace Prize laureate chosen for the €200 banknote.

The nature-themed design for the €10 banknote, presented on Thursday 23 July 2026 in Frankfurt, Germany AP Photo

The other proposal: Europe's symbolic birds

The alternative theme focuses on nature. Each banknote depicts a different species of European bird set against a river landscape, while the reverse side features one of the European Union's main institutions.

The series includes the wallcreeper paired with the European Parliament, the kingfisher with the European Commission, the European bee-eater alongside the European Central Bank, the white stork with the Court of Justice of the European Union, the avocet with the European Council and the Council of the European Union, and, finally, the northern gannet with the European Court of Auditors.

When the new banknotes will arrive

The public vote is one of the stages in the process that will lead to the final selection of the euro's new design. Once the consultation is complete and the winning design has been selected, the ECB will move on to the technical steps required to produce the new banknotes, which are scheduled to enter circulation from the end of 2026.

The aim is to renew the look of the single currency while maintaining a strong link to Europe's shared values: its rich cultural heritage and the natural environment that unites all the member states.

World.title: Morrissey urges Sánchez to end bullfighting on return to Spain
World.content:
Few figures in the performing arts have woven animal-rights activism as tightly into their career as Morrissey. Even before stepping on stage, the former Smiths frontman is already making waves in Spain. Just days before performing in Barcelona and Madrid, the British musician has sent a letter to the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, urging him to help bring bullfighting to an end.

 

The singer, a vegetarian since his adolescence and one of the most combative voices in defence of animals for decades, asks the head of the Spanish government to use his "influence" to put an end to a tradition which, in his view, "still tarnishes" Spain's international image. "Please," he writes in the letter, "do something the whole world will love: end this barbarity".

The letter, released with the support of the animal-rights organisation PETA, comes at a time when bullfighting has returned to the centre of the political debate. On 15 July, a group of 52 MPs once again registered in the Congress of Deputies the citizens' initiative (source in Spanish) "Not My Culture", which calls for bullfights to be stripped of their status as protected cultural heritage. The proposal had already won the backing of more than 715,000 signatures.

PETA supports (source in Spanish) the campaign with an international petition addressed directly to Sánchez. The organisation says that each year thousands of bulls suffer "a slow and painful death" in Spanish bullrings and argues that public opposition to these shows continues to grow both inside and outside the country.

This cause, however, is not just a one-off reaction to his Spanish tour. It is part of Morrissey's artistic DNA. In 2014 he released "The Bullfighter Dies", one of the most talked-about songs on his album "World Peace Is None of Your Business". In it he uses irony to portray the bullfighter and repeats a refrain that went on to become a statement of intent: "The bullfighter dies and nobody cries" (in Spanish, 'El torero muere y nadie le llora').

Over the years, the musician has used interviews, concerts and statements to condemn meat consumption, factory farming, animal experimentation and bullfighting. He even, just as PETA itself did, went so far as to ask the late Pope Francis to issue a public condemnation of bullfighting.

For his followers, that commitment is an indivisible part of his persona; for his detractors, it is yet another example of his tendency to turn any public appearance into a controversy.

And he rarely goes unnoticed when he sets foot in Spain. Last March he cancelled the concert he was due to give in Valencia, claiming he was in a "catatonic" state after being unable to sleep because of the noise in the city, which was immersed in preparations for the Fallas festival. The explanation fuelled a reputation that has followed him for years: that of an artist as brilliant as he is unreliable.

It was not an isolated episode. In 2025 he also called off at the last minute his performance at Las Noches del Botánico in Madrid for medical reasons. According to specialist website Muzikalia, Morrissey has already clocked up more than 350 cancelled concerts over the course of his career. Now, even before his Spanish tour begins, he has once again managed to get people talking about him. And, once again, not just because of his music.

World.title: Modi adresses India's youth's 'Cockroach' movement as protesters hold capital sit-in
World.content:
Thousands of young people in India continued to protest on Thursday in what has been dubbed the "Cockroach" protest, demanding the resignation of India's Education Minister following a scandal involving leaked exams. The movement has now become a symbol of broader frustrations among India's youth.

 

In response, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the issue during a televised address on Thursday calling for fast-track court to handle examination paper leak cases.

Modi also took to X to express "Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth".

Meanwhile, one protester, law student Daksh Bhargava, said “Rather than providing solution which is convenient for him, he should work toward a solution which is convenient for the nation and set an example”.

Modi's biggest challenge yet

The over a month long protests, which were sparked by leaks around some of India's most competitive entrance exams for medical colleges and governmental jobs, have expanded beyond exam grievances.

Demands from protesters also include examination system reforms and compensation for the families of students who died by suicide after the exam paper leaks. The movement, which has gained a wider following from Indians of all ages over government accountability, unemployment and economic opportunity, is considered one of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government's biggest challenge yet.

Meanwhile, Thursday's overnight demonstrations in Jantar Mantar in New Delhi were met with police who used tear gas and batons to disperse crowds. On Monday, demonstrators had already experienced a similar situation when thousands defied restrictions and marched toward parliament.

Police officers detain a protester during a demonstration demanding educational reforms as part of the Cockroach Janta Party's protest movement in Mumbai, India, 22/07/2026. AP Photo / Rafiq Maqbool

Despite roadblocks, protesters regrouped on Thursday morning and returned to the protest site. Meanwhile, authorities closed down 16 metro stations across central New Delhi in efforts to limit access to the demonstrations.

Origins of the movement

The movement launched by the Cockroach Janta Party began as an online satirical campaign in May, however it gained ground when well known activist Sonam Wangchuk joined and began a hunger strike lasting more than three weeks. Leaders have said that they would not stop protesting until the education minister resigns. Meanwhile, Dharmendra accuses the opposition of exploiting students for political gain.

Opposition parties have shown support toward the protests, using the issue to challenge Modi's government in parliament, while other Indian cities have also backed the movement by holding events in solidarity. But demonstrations against Modi's government have led to a broader crackdown on activists, opposition figures and public protests.

World.title: ECB hostage to oil prices? Lagarde leaves door open for a September hike
World.content:
Just six weeks ago, the European Central Bank appeared to be winning its fight against inflation.

 

Oil prices had fallen sharply after a ceasefire between the US and Iran, inflation was cooling faster than expected and the eurozone economy was proving more resilient than initially feared.

By Thursday, the conversation in Frankfurt had changed completely.

Christine Lagarde mentioned energy prices, particularly oil, repeatedly during her press conference, underscoring how rapidly geopolitical developments have reshaped the ECB's outlook.

While policymakers insist their September decision will remain data-dependent, the message was clear: the path of oil prices may now be the single most important variable determining whether interest rates remain on hold or rise again.

From ceasefire optimism...

The ECB Governing Council left its three key interest rates unchanged, as estimated.

However, the tone of Lagarde's press conference was notably more cautious than the decision itself suggested.

Lagarde revealed that the Governing Council spent the past two days reconstructing everything that had changed since its June meeting.

Initially, the news had been encouraging.

Inflation slowed more than expected to 2.8%, economic activity held up better than anticipated and the Memorandum of Understanding between the US and Iran, followed by a ceasefire, pushed crude oil prices sharply lower.

"That was the first part of that period of time," Lagarde said, but then context changed.

...to a renewed oil shock

"The memorandum of understanding was short-lived. The ceasefire was broken several times and led to the current situation where we have clearly a flaring up of the conflict and serious development taking place on the commodity markets," Lagarde stated.

That abrupt reversal is precisely why the ECB decided not to move rates on Thursday.

Rather than reacting solely to June's encouraging inflation figures, policymakers are trying to assess whether the renewed energy shock will prove temporary or evolve into a broader inflation problem.

"The full inflationary impact of the energy shock has yet to play out," she said, adding that policymakers were closely monitoring the "intensity and duration of the shock" together with any indirect or second-round effects.

For now, however, Lagarde said the central bank is not seeing evidence that companies are responding with higher wage demands.

This is perhaps the development policymakers fear most because it could make inflation persist for much longer.

"We remain well positioned to navigate the uncertainty," Lagarde assured.

Oil prices are becoming the ECB's biggest concern

The timing of the ECB meeting could hardly have been more difficult.

As Lagarde spoke in Frankfurt, Brent crude surged more than 6% towards $100 per barrel, its highest level since May, after Iran-backed Houthi militants claimed attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, intensifying fears of supply disruptions.

The attacks followed renewed strikes around the Strait of Hormuz and growing concerns over shipping routes through one of the world's most important energy corridors.

Lagarde acknowledged that the latest attacks occurred after the Governing Council had already concluded its policy discussions, meaning they did not directly influence Thursday's decision.

Nevertheless, she described the developments as "alarming" and confirmed that ECB staff had already been instructed to carry out deeper analysis of different oil and gas price scenarios ahead of the September meeting.

She noted that policymakers are paying close attention not only to crude prices but also to natural gas markets, where inventories remain relatively low heading into winter.

September remains wide open

Perhaps the clearest signal from Thursday's press conference came when Lagarde revealed that today's decision had been unanimous, but not without debate.

She acknowledged that several Governing Council members questioned whether the ECB should already have considered another interest-rate increase.

Ultimately, policymakers agreed that waiting until September would allow them to assess two additional inflation reports, updated growth figures and fresh staff projections before deciding whether tighter policy is needed.

"The burden of proof is on data," Lagarde said when asked whether those arguing for another rate rise or those favouring unchanged policy faced the higher hurdle.

The message leaves every option on the table for September.

The ECB insists it is not pre-committing to any particular interest-rate path but Thursday's press conference suggested the institution's reaction function has become increasingly tied to developments in energy markets.

Lagarde also dismissed speculation that she could leave the ECB before the end of her term, saying, "You are not going to see the back of me before 2027," before adding that "when there are clouds on the horizon, the captain stays on the ship."

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Indian activist Sonam Wangchuk ends hunger strike
World.content:
Sonam Wangchuk has broken his hunger strike after 26 days, saying the decision follows a "long negotiation on various conditions and in view of possible violence in the country

Sonam Wangchuk has ended his hunger strike after 26 days, the Indian activist said Thursday on his X account.

"Just now in the presence of Union Ministers JP Nadda & Dr. Jitendra Singh and the senior leaders of Apex Body of Leh Ladakh I finally broke my fast after 26 days," Wangchuk wrote.

He added that 65 members of parliament from different political parties had visited or otherwise urged him to break the fast.

"This was done after a long negotiation on various conditions and in view of possible violence in the country," he wrote. "Meanwhile I urge you all to stay very vigillant about not allowing violence of any kind anywhere."

Earlier on Thursday, Wangchuk had offered to end his hunger strike if the government agreed not to harm student protesters.

He said he was seeking assurances from the government, including compensation for families of students who committed suicide, and the resignation of India’s education minister.

More to come on this developing news at dw.com...

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Germany seeks energy and trading partners in Africa
World.content:
Germany wants to boost relations with Africa. During his trip, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has promoted cooperation on energy, infrastructure and the economy. He also criticized US treatment of South Africa.

In a tent in the Nigerian metropolis of Lagos, two worlds collided: Three fashionable influencers sat on cushioned stools across from Germany's 63-year-old Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul. For half an hour, the senior politician met youth from Africa's creative scene.

These young people are among the stars of Nigeria's creative industry — in a country with a population of around 240 million and a median age of just under 18. Wadephul wanted to understand what moves the younger generation. What issues are on their minds? How do they view Germany? And what do they expect from a collaboration?

After a brief hesitation, they replied: Germany and Europe listen to their music, view their art, and want to collaborate with them. But anyone who wants to travel to the German capital for Fashion Week or the Berlinale film festival can hardly get a visa, said a young man in the audience.

A conversation gets underway; everyone enjoys the exchange and subsequently uploads upbeat videos to social media platforms — to the influencers' channels as well as those of the Federal Foreign Office. This is how German diplomacy is pursuing a direct line of communication with Africa's younger generation.

Nigeria as a valuable energy supplier

There is good reason for the Foreign Minister to be promoting Germany in Nigeria. "The country is an economic powerhouse and, as Africa's largest domestic market, also a key destination for German exports," he says. Nigeria is sub-Saharan Africa's second-largest economy and already imports machinery, chemicals, and food products "Made in Germany."

However, Nigeria's raw materials account for the largest share of the trade balance. They have become even more important since the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. "In June, 25% of jet fuel shipments to Europe came from Nigeria. But we can do significantly more," emphasized Wadephul.

Vital infrastructure support

Wadephul was accompanied by a business delegation on his third trip to Africa. The group includes major corporations like Siemens as well as small and medium-sized enterprises. One of these is VIDA , a Munich-based AI company that is finalizing a multi-million-euro contract with the Nigerian government. The focus is on AI-driven infrastructure planning.

"Our solutions help identify and evaluate new locations. AI allows us to determine much more quickly the economic potential of a site, as well as the local conditions regarding security, climate trends, and other key factors," explained VIDA founder Tobias Engelmeier. His company is already implementing projects in 20 African countries.

German support for infrastructure development is in demand in many places. Since the European Union launched a €290 million ($330 mio) package as part of its Global Gateway strategy, hopes have been rising — both in Africa and among European companies — for faster progress in expanding transport, energy, and utility networks. The Nigerian government is also actively lobbying for German investment to modernize its power supply.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and President of the ECOWAS Commission Omar Touray attended the Nigerian-German business roundtable Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

Underestimated economic and political significance

Yet Germany has long underestimated Nigeria's economic and political importance. Given the potential of what is Germany's second-most important trading partner in sub-Saharan Africa, the presence of around 100 German companies is comparatively small. Siemens is involved in expanding the power grid, while Bayer is planning pharmaceutical production facilities together with regional partners. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are also increasingly entering the market, though many complain about a lack of transparency in market and decision-making structures.

"It is a challenging market with high operating costs. That is why local partners who understand the diverse structures across the 36 states are essential," says Sabine Dal'Omo, Managing Director of Siemens Sub-Saharan Africa and Chairwoman of the German-African Business Association.

Renewable energy provider Enertrag is among the companies taking a wait-and-see approach. "For us, Nigeria holds great potential — there is strong domestic demand and favorable conditions for exporting green energy. However, the overall framework remains too uncertain for us to commit to a long-term investment," said board member Anne Bendzulla.

Instead, Enertrag has been successfully investing in South Africa for several years. There, the company states it is prepared to invest around €850 million in wind energy.

Missing out by arriving late

The security situation in Nigeria is a matter of concern for German business. Consequently, the federal government has made additional funds available for cooperation with Nigeria's police authorities.

Wadephul urges the German business community not to hesitate too long. "Anyone not present in Africa today risks missing out on crucial opportunities," he told reporters. The country, with its young population, possesses immense potential and abundant resources, he added. "It would be grossly negligent of us to overlook that."

On the final day of his third trip to Africa this year, Wadephul visited South Africa, Germany's most important economic partner on the continent.



At a press conference in the capital Pretoria, South African Minister for International Relations Ronald Lamola praised the fact that "some 600 German companies operate in our country [South Africa] and employ approximately 100,000 people."

In April 2026, the two countries had elevated their relationship to a Strategic Partnership and adopted a Joint Action Plan, which focuses on strengthening cooperation in the areas of trade and investment, security and energy transition. Today, about 80% of South Africa's electricity is still generated from coal.

While in the South African capital, Wadephul criticized US President Donald Trump for not inviting South Africa, which he described as "an indispensable member of the G20," to the group's next summit.

"To exclude South Africa means sidelining an important African voice and a regional economic and political powerhouse," the German foreign minister said. "This can be in no one's interest. As — particularly at a time of growing global economic uncertainty — we need more cooperation, not less!"

He added that he was confident that "South Africa will be able to participate again as a full member of the G20 next year."

He also agreed that African states were underrepresented in the United Nations. "There can be no representative United Nations without permanent African representation on the Security Council," he said.

Wadephul's four-day diplomatic offensive in Africa is evidence of Germany's desire to engage more with democracies and middle powers around the world amid a crisis of multilateralism. As Chinese and Russian influence on the continent increase, Germany with Europe wants to offer an alternative to the Global South.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Sweden eases mining permits to cut China minerals reliance
World.content:
Sweden has declared the mining of critical minerals and rare earths a national security interest. This will ease and expedite the permit process. The government said the step was needed to counter dependence on China.

Sweden on Thursday announced plans to try to boost its mining sector, particularly when it comes to rare earths, and counter European dependence on China.

Resource-rich Sweden is already home to Europe's largest iron ore mine, and has since found considerable rare earth deposits at the same Arctic Circle site in Kiruna.

Rare earth minerals are essential for renewable energy generation, defense and electric vehicle production, modern computer manufacturing and other core industries. China accounts for roughly 70% of global mining and refining.

What did the Swedish government say about the plan?

The government in Stockholm on Thursday declared the mining of critical metals and rare earth minerals to be a national security interest.

This should ease and accelerate the permit process for new extraction projects and help attract investments, according to Energy Minister Ebba Busch, who is also deputy prime minister.

"Sweden must become a leading mining nation," she said as she outlined the new strategy, saying the government intended to "streamline authorization procedures so decisions can be taken more quickly."

Ebba Busch said that despite the country's vast mineral wealth and mining operations, only 1% of global mining investment currently found its way to Sweden Image: Viktoria Bank/TT/picture alliance

"We believe that this can contribute significantly to both Sweden's the EU's and NATO's defense capabilities," Busch said, calling European industry's dependence on China a "systemic risk."

Busch also said the move would make it easier for the state to assign land for mining projects, an area of tension with the Sami reindeer-herding indigenous people, who say the expansion of mining could spell the end for their traditional way of life.

The energy minister also said the government was looking into setting up a state-owned investment company for the mining sector.

"Today, to put it plainly, the governemnt lacks concrete tools to wisely contribute to accelerating and attracting investments in crucial strategic projects," she said.

A special train carries the Kiruna mine's minerals to a nearby port for further transit Image: Andreas Werth/imageBROKER/picture alliance

What are Sweden's existing mining credentials?

Sweden has been a European mining giant since the 10th century and the opening of the vast Falun copper mine, which at one point produced as much as two-thirds of the continent's copper. The distinctive deep red color that adorns many houses, churches and other buildings in the country is called Falun Red and hails from the disused mine. It's now a museum and UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Sweden's modern-day Falun is the vast LKAB iron ore mine in Kiruna in the Arctic Circle. Sweden holds around 60% of Europe's known iron ore deposits and, as of 2021, was responsible for around 90% of the continent's iron ore extraction, around one-third of that from Kiruna alone.

The vast frozen mining town made headlines in recent years because of the need to relocate various homes and buildings — including the church — in Kiruna because of subsidence as the giant operation literally undermines the city.

Kiruna's chuch was put on wheels and moved last summer in the more clement weather, attracting international attention Image: Fredrik Sandberg/TT/picture alliance

More than 90% of Sweden's mines operate in the sparsely populated and resource-rich Norrland region in Sapmi, the traditional territory of the Sami.

Near the Kiruna mine is the Per Geijer find, a flagship EU project seeking to reduce mineral reliance on China. This is an area where around 1.2 billion tons of mineral resources, including around 2.2 million tons of rare earth oxides, have been identified.

Mining group LKAB is examining the potential of the deposit but estimates that obtaining permits to excavate on Sami land could take 10 years.

Four of the EU's 47 strategic projects aimed at reducing mineral dependence on China are located in Sweden.
