World.title: Indonesia's baby traffickers target poor families as demand grows
World.content:
Indonesia's Child Protection Commissioner has described recent revelations about illegal adoptions and baby trafficking as just the "tip of the iceberg" after 19 Indonesians were sentenced over the issue earlier this week.

On Tuesday, 70-year-old Lie Siu Luan was sentenced to seven years in jail over her role as the ringleader of a baby-trafficking adoption syndicate that involved a group of 19 people.

At least 28 babies were trafficked, many of whom were adopted by parents in Singapore.

Baby trafficker sentenced to seven years Lie Siu Luan, 70, was the leader of a group of 19 people accused of trafficking babies in Indonesia and Singapore.

Prosecutors told the court that Lie was asked to find babies by a Singaporean man who offered about $20,000 for each child.

They alleged she accepted and used a network of individuals to find young boys and girls.

Prosecutors said vulnerable mothers were targeted across West Java, with members of the syndicate offering money in exchange for their newborn babies.

Nannies were paid a monthly wage to care for the babies, while members of the syndicate falsified birth certificates for the infants and forged documents to get passports.

Some in the syndicate posed as fake parents, accompanying babies to Singapore for adoptions.

The case is considered to be one of several suspected trafficking syndicates in Indonesia operating over the past few years.

One of the worst in recent memory involved at least 57 people who were found caged on a palm oil plantation in North Sumatra province in 2022.

Figures from the Ministry of Women Empowerment and Child Protection show a concerning number of reports of children being trafficked in Indonesia, with more than 1,400 recorded between 2020 and 2025.

However, Indonesian Child Protection Commissioner Diyah Puspitarini said the official data did not represent the full picture of trafficking or illegal adoption cases.

Diyah Puspitarini says there may be more child trafficking cases than what is known. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

"This is only the tip of the iceberg, either in illegal adoption or baby trade," she said.

"The parents who sell their babies are embarrassed to report it to us."

Ms Puspitarini said many people chose to remain silent because the parents who sold their babies were usually those "who can't accept" them.

Indonesia's child trafficking underbelly

West Java Police Senior Commissioner Ade Sapari said the parents of infants trafficked in the recent case were experiencing financial hardship.

"It looks like the root cause is economic … our investigation shows the victims needed money, so they gave up their babies for others to take care of," he said.

Babies sold online in Indonesia An infant was allegedly sold by his father to a married couple desperate to have children in one of the latest cases of baby trafficking in Indonesia.

The case was only revealed because a parent complained to police that the family had not received payment for their child.

The enormous financial pressures on Indonesian families can play a huge role in trafficking, with poverty seen as a root cause for families and mothers selling or giving away their children outside of the state care system.

"The majority of the parents are financially in need, so most of them have economic reasons to sell their babies … they're poor, they can't afford it," Ms Puspitarini said.

She said the process could sometimes begin while the baby was still in their mother's womb.

"The buyer would already tell the mother they want to buy the baby, so the mother will give birth. Then the baby is gone," Ms Puspitarini said.

Mother describes painful decision to give up child

While social media is commonly used by syndicates to contact families to give up their children, some are contacted in person.

Dewi, whose name has been changed by the ABC to protect her identity, is a young mother of four living in Jakarta who made the difficult decision to give up her child because she could not afford to look after him.

Dewi says her family struggled financially. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

"Life was really hard," she said. "My husband was sick, we had nothing to eat, we couldn't even afford gas for cooking."

"When the newborn needed a warm bath, I used the rice cooker to heat the water.

"All I could think about was the baby, plus I had a two-year-old who still needed me.

"I felt like I wasn't capable of being a mother to four kids."

Dewi lives in Jakarta but her family has been doing it tough. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

Dewi said she gave her newborn son to a woman who approached her at her home, accepting $400 to help feed her other children.

She immediately regretted the decision, tracking down the woman the next day, but she was told her son had been taken to Kalimantan.

"The evening I gave him away, I went home and felt so empty," she said.

"My baby wasn't there, only his pillow and mattress … that's when I broke down."

She contacted the police and other agencies to help find her son and eventually her baby was returned after several months.

Trafficking networks can be 'national or international'

Peri Sopian, who runs an orphanage in Bandung, has been helping to care for some of the infants who were taken by the trafficking syndicate.

Peri Sopian runs the Bandung orphanage. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

"From our experience, based on what we see in the field and the number of referrals we've received, there have been a lot of human-trafficking-related cases," he said.

"These networks can be national or international, and they happen quite often, especially because many parents aren't aware of the government's childcare system."

Bandung's Deputy Mayor Erwin said that many trafficking cases had involved teenagers who were kicked out of home for having children outside of marriage.

"That's why we often do raids in apartments and rented rooms, because kids as young as 16 or 17 are already having sex," he said.

"Some end up pregnant, and when their parents kick them out, they end up on the streets while still pregnant; that's when these middlemen get to them.

"Sometimes the middlemen also use social media to find them.

"It's a complex problem, and we need a comprehensive social approach, not just legal measures, but also social ones."

The orphanage in Bandung is responsible for children caught in trafficking operations. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

Senior Commissioner Sapari has called for greater economic welfare, noting the government "needs to pay more attention" to the trafficking issue to prevent it from happening.

"Agencies like the Manpower Office should also pay closer attention to the welfare of the people," he said.

"Aside from stronger efforts from the central government, we'll also focus on raising public awareness, educating communities about the law so people don't end up falling victim to the same kind of crime again."

The case has also prompted Singaporean authorities to pledge a review of child adoption processes.

World.title: Adelaide now fourth most expensive capital for buying a house
World.content:
Adelaide's housing market is bucking national trends, with median prices rising 4.8 per cent in the June quarter.

According to Domain's latest House Price Report, Adelaide's median house price is now a record $1.125 million, up from $970,165 a year ago.

It was the fastest-rising market among Australia's capitals in the past quarter.

Dr Nicola Powell, chief of research and economics for Domain, told 891 ABC Adelaide that the city was "bucking the national trend".

"We saw an acceleration in house price growth, with momentum strengthening both over the quarter and over the year, and that is not what we've seen in other capital cities," Dr Powell said.

Adelaide is now the fourth most expensive capital to buy a house, behind Sydney, Brisbane and Perth.

Adelaide's housing market is bucking recent national trends, according to Domain's latest data. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

Adelaide supply lagging behind other capitals

Dr Powell said increased housing supply across Australia was driving fluctuations in price changes.

Year on year, supply has increased around 17 per cent across the nation's capital cities.

Housing market enters downturn Australia's property market has entered a downturn after both house and unit prices fell for the first time in more than three years, bringing an end to the recent housing boom.

But Adelaide trails the nation for growing its local supply – only a six per cent increase in the past 12 months.

"Adelaide also still has one of the tightest rental markets in Australia, and that has flow-on effects also to pushing demand quicker into purchasing," Dr Powell said.

Despite the apparent demand for Adelaide housing shown by the latest report, real estate agents are starting to see changes on the ground.

John McRostie, principal of Belle Property Real Estate, saw no interested buyers at one inner city terrace on Thursday morning.

He told the ABC that local buyer confidence was lacking and turnout at open inspections and auctions across the city was low, particularly among investors. It may mean sellers are forced to reconsider how they price properties.

"The numbers are less, so now, you've got some nice properties, you've got to price them properly, you've got to be prepared to adjust them, and you've got to work hard with the buyer," Mr McRostie said.

There was little difference at another open inspection in Parkside on Thursday morning, where the only person in attendance was local John Albanese.

"I live in the area, I saw this open, and thought I would pop in and have a look," Mr Albanese said. "I thought there would be more than just myself."

John McRostie says confidence is down among prospective buyers. (Olivia Mason)

High price a credit to lifestyle, but not sustainable

Mr McRostie said Adelaide's lifestyle and livability was a major appeal for buyers.

Along with Melbourne and Sydney, the city was recently named in the top 10 of the world's most liveable cities in the Economist Intelligence Unit's annual ranking.

"It's great to see the average price in South Australia to be quite buoyant," Mr McRostie said.

"Adelaide is a great place to live. It's just a nice lifestyle; it's different from Melbourne and Sydney. Adelaide deserves it."

High median prices might be welcome for sellers, but for buyers struggling to find a home it may be a different story.

Greg Nield has been searching for a bigger home for his family. (ABC News: Rachael Merritt)

Greg Nield attended one open inspection in Adelaide inner north on Thursday afternoon. Already a home owner, he wants a bigger house to meet the needs of his family as his school-age children grow older.

"It's a bit hard to find a property that ticks all the boxes we want and is still in the area that we need," said Mr Nield.

"The ones that are nice go very, very quickly. And often someone puts in an offer before it goes to auction.

"Then other houses, I think people put a higher price above, trying to get something within the market and capitalise on the interest, and those ones sometimes stay on the market for a bit longer."

Dr Powell described Adelaide as a long-term "quiet achiever" when it came to property prices, but it would likely see declines in future reports.

"What I'm expecting is that a 5 per cent increase each quarter is not sustainable and I think what we will see is higher borrowing costs will start to help to slow down the pace of price growth," she said.

World.title: Violence by a son-in-law left Maria 'homeless and hopeless' at 72
World.content:
Maria (not her real name) stood shivering outside her home for hours on a winter's day after she was kicked out by an abusive son-in-law and had her belongings dumped on the driveway.

The then-72-year-old had nowhere to go, anxiously waiting for help from police, who she called three times.

Family and domestic violence support services: If you need help immediately, call emergency services on Triple Zero. Elder Abuse Hotline: 1800 353 374

1800 Respect National Helpline: 1800 737 732

Women's Crisis Line: 1800 811 811

Men's Referral Service: 1300 766 491

Lifeline: 131 114

It was 2022, and Maria lived at a property in Brisbane she co-owned with her 35-year-old daughter, who then moved in with her would-be husband.

While Maria knew he was "hot-headed", she never anticipated the violence that would be brought into her home.

"They started breaking the door to the other room because he wanted to make a big ensuite," Maria said.

"And while I'm asleep, he just kept banging on the wall."

National plan to tackle elder abuse delayed by more than two years The National Plan to Respond to the Abuse of Older Australians lapsed in 2023 and the government has not given a timeline for the release of its replacement.

Maria said her son-in-law frequently swore and screamed at her, made aggressive hand gestures, and put his "face in my face" in fits of rage.

Through it all, her daughter remained a bystander.

"She'd just sit there and observe," Maria said. "He called all the shots. Whatever he says, she agrees."

When her possessions were thrown out, Maria managed to contact a friend on the Gold Coast who offered to help at short notice.

But the now-76-year-old said she hoped police would have better supported her through what was a conspicuously abusive domestic environment.

It was not until Maria reached out to a support service that she said she felt her experience was taken more seriously, and carried forward in court.

"It's as if a big [burden] was taken off my back because I was just hopeless," she said.

" Homeless and hopeless. "

Maria said she wanted people in situations like hers to know seeking help made a difference.

'Everyone's responsibility'

Defined as occurring within a relationship of trust, elder abuse can take various forms including neglect, financial, physical, sexual, and psychological abuse.

One in six Australians over the age of 65 experiences abuse, according to a 2021 Australian Institute of Family Studies (AIFS) study, with adult children being the most common perpetrators.

In Queensland, notifications of abuse to the Elder Abuse Prevention Unit have increased 82 per cent in the past five years, with 2,794 notifications made in 2025 from more than 4,800 calls.

However, with research showing more than 60 per cent of victims choose not to report their experiences or seek help, advocates say the broader community needs to step in.

"Sometimes, the person that changes an older person's life and helps them access support isn't an expert or a professional, it's simply someone who noticed," Caxton Community Legal Centre senior lawyer Nicky Mitchell said.

Nicky Mitchell says caring for seniors is everyone's responsibility. (Supplied)

" Silence protects abuse … [while] conversations create opportunities for support. "

Ms Mitchell said that because older people did not always recognise their mistreatment as such, it was crucial for anyone who noticed red flags to check in and help empower them with knowledge about their rights.

"It is everyone's business. It is everyone's responsibility," she said.

Ms Mitchell said more government funding was needed for dedicated elder-abuse support services.

"Elder abuse should be treated and funded to the same level as family and domestic violence in partner abuse, and anything less than that is ageist," she said.

Addressing ageism, investing in support

A Queensland parliamentary inquiry last year called on the government to improve elder abuse data collection and reporting, develop a national definition of elder abuse, and leverage educational assets to foster respect for older members of the community, among other recommendations.

Aged and Disability Advocates (ADA) Australia CEO Geoff Rowe said there was a lack of public understanding about the extent and impact of elder abuse in Australia, with ageism a key factor.

"Older people don't tend to count … they're often seen as a burden on the community rather than the people that have built the foundations of the community that we all enjoy," he said.

Geoff Rowe says the small number of available elder abuse support services are in high demand. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"So, it's very easy to discount the impact. It's seen as someone else's problem. 'It's a family matter. It's not something that's going to impact on you or me.'"

Mr Rowe said the sector was frustrated with the failure of governments to implement recommendations from a landmark Australian Law Reform Commission report into elder abuse in 2017.

Resource to help 'invisible' older women victim-survivors Experts say sexual violence against older women is "grossly underestimated" as victim-survivors face additional barriers to disclosing the abuse.

"It would be wonderful if some of our community leaders showed leadership on this issue," he said.

" We need to change the way that we look at older people. "

Many advocacy and legal bodies have been calling for elder abuse to be criminalised, with a debate on the issue to take place at a national Elder Abuse Conference on the Gold Coast next week.

Queensland Police said it had "no reliable data" on how many elder abuse cases it had dealt with given its lack of classification as a standalone criminal offence.

The Queensland attorney-general's office said in a statement "work is progressing to implement specific recommendations" from last year's inquiry.

Maria's real name has not been disclosed to protect her safety.

World.title: Fast food key to farmers making more with their dairy calves
World.content:
Every day, Evan Nicholas and his family milk around 600 black-and-white Friesian cows in the Upper Murray region of Victoria.

He has another 900 head of cattle on his farm, many of them calves born from the milking herd each year.

Historically, those calves were sold on quickly, but Mr Nicholas is among a growing number of dairy farmers in Australia finding viable ways to keep them longer.

And as fast food companies make plans to increase the amount of dairy beef they are using, farmers are capitalising on the surge by cross-breeding their cows with beef genetics.

"It makes the bobby calf a viable asset," Mr Evans said.

"The beauty about dairy beef is now you can choose the best genetics … and you can get the most meat," he said.

Dairy calves are crossbred with beef breeds like Charolais, Hereford and Angus. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

Beefing up bobby calves

Dairy cows generally need to calf every 12 months, to keep milk production going.

Of the 1 million dairy calves born in Australia each year, about a third are sold as "bobby calves" or "non-replacement calves" from as young as five days old.

They are used for veal meat or hides.

The younger members of Mr Nicholas's herd are part of the Dairy Australia and Meat and Livestock Australia Calfways project, to transform dairy calf management by 2035.

Bec Barnewall from Dairy Australia said calves were historically an "issue" to deal with, but now were an "opportunity".

"We're trying to find them viable pathways, whether that be through to weaning and going to backgrounders and feedlotters," Dr Barnewall said.

"One of the surprising findings has been, regardless of the cost to get the animals weaned, farmers were able to compensate for that cost when they sold them, which is really positive."

Bec Barnewall says there is growing interest for dairy beef from big food companies. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

Fast food wants dairy beef

The Fulton Market Group (FMG) is the main buyer of beef and pork for McDonald's restaurants around the world.

Earlier this year, the company announced it wanted to increase the amount of dairy beef it used in Australia by 2030 and beyond.

Speaking at the Australian Dairy Conference in February, FMG Global strategic sourcing manager Andrew Ralph said high-quality beef could be created from dairy cows "if it's done right".

"We want to take 100,000 of those [300,000 non-replacement calves] and move them out of that non or low-value market and move them into a high-value market," he said.

"Our goal is now to work with processors to get their confidence in these cattle and start scaling supply chains up to that 100,000 head by 2030."

McDonald's Australia was contacted for comment.

McDonald's plans to increase the amount of dairy beef in its burgers. (AP: Mike Stewart)

It is not just the fast food sector that is keen to use more dairy beef.

"It's a hot topic at the moment," Dr Barnewall said.

"It's encouraging to see big companies come forward and make that kind of commitment.

"We've started to see a lot more announcements from bigger companies and a lot more positive conversations around dairy beef in Australia."

There has also been a rise in the purchasing of beef genetics by dairy farmers.

Genetics company Semex said in 2021 they sold 5,700 doses of Angus semen, and in 2025 that had risen to 60,000 straws.

Semex Australia general manager Tyson Shea said that number was expected to rise.

"I think now with the use of the right genetics over dairy herds, people are seeing it as a revenue type of opportunity," Mr Shea said.

"This beef market can play a huge role, as beef herd numbers drop around the world."

No phasing out of bobby calf market

Dr Barnewall said the move to dairy beef genetics did not mean the bobby calf market would be phased out.

"We're really just looking to give dairy farmers options if they would like to keep the animals on farm for longer," Dr Barnewall said.

Evan Nicholas spends every day with his cows. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

Mr Nicholas agreed the bobby calf market needed to stay for now, but said changes may come in the future.

"My thoughts are that in time something will change [with bobby calves] and we'll have to keep them for a certain period of time," he said.

He said the opportunities in dairy beef would protect farmers and the industry going forward.

"This has given us something that we're trying to make a viable industry for," Mr Nicholas said.

World.title: This footy club wants better for its women's team but is in a pinch
World.content:
Macedon Football Netball Club president Ron Rutledge says his club does things a bit like Ted Lasso.

The "Lasso Way", inspired by the popular TV show, is a leadership style centred on kindness, personal growth and human connection, often over winning.

"Our number one thing is 'thank you' and our number two thing is 'please'," Rutledge tells ABC Sport.

"We're a very easy club to get on with … But we are in a desperate pitch now for our female participants."

The club is in the heart of the Macedon Ranges in central Victoria, about 60 kilometres north-west of Melbourne.

Ron Rutledge says the club has worked hard to grow its women's and girls' teams. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Founded in 1887 as an original member of the Riddell District Football League, its clubrooms contain cabinets filled with trophies won by generations of men's teams.

The latest additions are the two premiership trophies won by the senior women's side.

Six years ago, the club underwent a significant change when it established a women's team, followed by a girls' team.

"A lot of people before me worked very hard on getting a junior program going for females, particularly in the AFL sense. It's been a netball club for many years, and that has continued to grow and grow and grow," Rutledge says.

The senior women's team is again among the premiership favourites this season.

MFNC female participation keeps on growing. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

But, like many long-standing clubs across the country, Macedon encountered a significant problem as female participation grew: its facilities were neither large enough nor suitable for the new women's and girls' teams.

The Cats' home ground, Tony Clarke Reserve, is also used by the local bowling, cricket and tennis clubs.

The football teams also train around the corner at JD Clifford Reserve during the week.

On Thursday nights, the youth boys, youth girls, senior men's and senior women's sides all train across the two grounds.

'Made for men'

Reigning senior women's club best and fairest winner Ruby Watts has played football since 2017, the year AFLW started.

Now 21, she played Auskick as a child but stopped after a year because she "didn't like playing with the boys", which was then the only option available.

She returned to the sport as a teenager when her local club, Gisborne Football Netball Club, established a girls' team. But she was forced to leave in 2024 when the club could no longer field a women's side.

Ruby Watts won the best and fairest last year. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

She joined Macedon with about six other players from Gisborne. The difference between the clubs' facilities was immediately noticeable.

"At Gisborne it was fine. Like, the facilities are perfect, they're clean, they're nice, but the ones here are a bit… they're just old and they're mainly made for men," Watts says.

"It's open urinals and just open showers, and it's just disgusting. There's one toilet with a door, so it's a big struggle.

"We have to use it after the men's teams, and it's not their fault. Like, they clean it nicely, but it's still disgusting. It just smells gross and it's not right. In 2026 we should be doing better, I reckon."

Women's players say the toilet situation in the change rooms isn't good enough. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Watts says the club does its best to make sure the women's side is included, but understands sometimes it is constrained by a lack of space.

At Thursday night selection dinners, for example, the women are encouraged to get their food first, while the men listen and cheer as the women's team is announced.

The club has also had several pride rounds this year for the women's competition, in which the shared space gets decorated with streamers and posters.

The away rooms for Macedon's home ground have just the one open showers room. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

But during training beforehand, the women have only a small section of the oval to use if one is rained out.

"There is quadruple the amount of them than there is of us. It would be nice to get half of the ground, but we don't need it in comparison," she says.

The same imbalance means the men fill the clubroom on shared nights, while the women leave their belongings on nearby benches. By dinner, the men have showered and changed, while the women remain in their wet training clothes.

"You can't walk on the ground without your socks getting wet, like we don't have a locker to put our stuff in. A girl, a few weeks ago, lost all of her clothes, because there's nowhere safe to put them," Watts says.

Women's players have to leave their belongings on benches while they train. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

"She literally lost her jumper, her pants, like everything. And she still hasn't gotten her clothes back, just because we have no locker or nothing to put them in, nowhere safe.

"We put our clothes on the chairs and just along the fence and it gets nice and wet and dewy … Then the boys shower after training, but all of us girls have to go fully kitted, fully in our wet socks and everything.

"The boys have comfy jumpers and pants on because they don't care, they'll shower around anybody. We don't have a shower to get changed in. It's different for us."

MFNC has a successful women's program. But the players still have nowhere to get changed. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Eve Moait, 19, plays in the senior women's side and coaches the under-14 girls.

She loves the club and has embraced its Ted Lasso philosophy. A "Believe" sign hangs above the door to the home change rooms.

"My junior girls love it, they think it's hilarious … They think it's the thing that won them their first game because they all tapped it on the way out and truly believed it," Moait says.

Some of the younger players could not quite reach it.

"They were actually really good jumpers, but we had some really, really small girls and they'd lift each other up to tap it. They're so sweet."

There is a "BELIEVE" sign above the door at MFNC's change rooms. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Before training, she gets changed in her car and then heads onto the ground.

She says the main club room is good, particularly since indoor artificial turf was installed, even if it's "terrible to clean as a coach".

"But then when we come to the toilet side, the girls just don't want to go in there," she says of her junior team.

"It's smelly because we come in on a Sunday after all the senior men have played the day before, and then all of the boys' teams have played the morning, so we come in during the afternoon at about one o'clock and it is disgusting.

" It smells, and there's grass, and there's underwear, and pee in the corner. It is so gross. "

The junior girls' team at Macedon Football Netball Club. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Moait often takes the junior players to a public toilet block 200 metres away, but says that can be difficult when she is responsible for all 18 members of the team.

"It's also a very awkward age for these girls," Moait says.

"We've noticed when they first come to the team, when they're at the very bottom age, so 11 or 12, they're typically fine. They'll go to the toilet, or try and avoid it if it's dirty, but it won't bother them as much.

"But when they hit the upper end and they start going into that time [puberty], they just shut off when it comes to the toilet, be like, 'nah, don't want to', and it's like I can't provide them with much better, so it's frustrating.

"There's no sanitary bin, it's dirty, and there's only one toilet there. It's not working for them, that's the problem."

MFNC train on cold and foggy Thursday nights. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

The push for an upgrade

Rutledge has been lobbying the council and state government for help upgrading Tony Clarke Reserve, attracting visits from politicians across the political spectrum.

Macedon Ranges Shire Council has allocated $380,000 in its 2026–27 budget to upgrade the change rooms.

The away rooms at Macedon Football Netball Club. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

The council's assets and operations director, Dom Testoni, told the ABC: "The proposed project, valued at approximately $650,000, would bring the facilities up to current standards and better support the needs of the growing number of participants using the reserve.

"While Council's recent application to the Victorian Government's Country Football Netball Program was unsuccessful, a number of funding avenues remain available.

"Council will submit a new application through the Victorian Government's Local Sports Infrastructure Program, which is currently open, and will continue to pursue other state and federal grant opportunities as they become available."

Macedon Football Netball Club home rooms. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

But Macedon Ranges Shire Mayor Kate Kendall said that funding "falls a little bit short".

She described the facilities as "absolutely prehistoric" and in "such a dire state" that they deterred local girls and women from participating in sport.

"We look at inclusion and a lot of people talk about inclusion, but if we don't have the very basic needs met, where people can go to the toilet safely and privately, then it's just, you know, a poor tale," Kendall told ABC Sport.

MFNC president Ron Rutledge in the club's away rooms. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Macedon MP Mary-Anne Thomas told the ABC she had visited the club and it was clear the facilities were past their use-by date. She said she had pressed the council to find a short-term solution while it pursued grant funding.

Rutledge hopes portable change rooms can be installed while the club identifies a long-term solution.

Victorian Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell said the situation demonstrated the consequences of cutting the Office for Women in Sport and Recreation from last year's state budget.

Girls players getting changed on the benches outside the football field. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Purcell said the office was not merely symbolic and had provided important support to sporting clubs, particularly those with relatively new women and girls' teams.

"It's not enough to just say women can play and think everything is going to magically resolve overnight. It requires commitment and work from the government," she told ABC Sport.

"I think the big problem with women in sport, and what we confront now, is women worked really hard and clubs worked really hard to let women into the spaces, but letting women into the spaces doesn't necessarily mean that they feel welcome or supported, or that the facilities and access are there for them to feel comfortable and like they're taken seriously.

" We say women are welcome in sport. We have women's sporting teams, but we just don't have the access or the facilities to allow those teams and club cultures to thrive. "

Macedon senior women's team are going for the three-peat this year. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

The Macedon way

Rutledge says he feels he is letting down the club's women's and girls' programs.

"I feel personally disappointed as president of the organisation. One of my commitments on the day that we had the election was that I want to make female participation one of our main goals," he says.

"We define outcomes not necessarily as premierships, but as participation and doing things for the community as well. We are a community club and we're very focused on letting the community judge us rather than us judging them.

"We've got a very powerful and energetic committee that works very closely with all parts of our operation… but we sit here tonight in a draconian position with our change rooms for our women."

Players say the culture at Macedon is different. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

The women want better facilities and are not quiet about it. But they are not going anywhere.

Even after Gisborne re-established its women's team, players such as Watts decided they would rather make the longer drive to keep doing things "the Macedon way".

World.title: Labor warned regional funding woes will drive One Nation support
World.content:
A stoush over local council funding could end in a rare showdown on the Labor conference floor amid a warning the "sleeper issue" is central to the frustration driving regional voters to One Nation.

The rise of Pauline Hanson was a prominent feature of the first day of the ALP's 50th National Conference in Adelaide, where senior Albanese Government ministers established One Nation as a central challenge for Labor heading into the next election.

Multiple speeches criticised One Nation's use of grievances to blame minorities for problems in Australia and sought to tie the minor party to the Coalition.

Now an influential Labor figure has declared an unlikely fight over a push to raise funding for local governments to 1 per cent of Commonwealth revenue cannot be separated from the cost-of-living pressures fuelling One Nation's rise.

Sydney's Inner West Mayor Darcy Byrne has warned the lack of local government funding was a "sleeper issue" that went to the "very heart" of frustration in regional communities worried about basic services the rest of the country can "take for granted".

"It's contributing to the very febrile atmosphere in the bush, where people are turning away from big parties, from the National Party, and parking their vote with One Nation," he said.

Mayor Darcy Byrne warned lack of local government funding was a "sleeper issue" driving regional communities to One Nation. (ABC News: Paul Pandoulis )

"If the Labor Party chooses to step in and say there will be a pathway to sustainable funding for local government, we'll then be able to say to those regional communities in particular, that we are stepping in to support them in a practical, meaningful way that no other party in Australian politics could do."

Lifting the funding would cost the federal government $3.6 billion a year, but Mr Byrne said advocates were willing to negotiate a staged approach to the 1 per cent goal.

"We're very confident we can win," he said.

Backroom negotiations on the sidelines of the conference scuppered a hyped-up push for a debate on a gas tax and landed compromises on other issues like the fuel tax credit and AI, while talks are ongoing to settle amendments on gambling reform and Gaza.

But Mr Byrne said there was a majority of conference delegates "willing to debate this on the floor" when the issue comes up on Saturday.

"We're very confident that we can win," he said.

Mr Byrne said council budgets were under immense pressure, with many forced to step up and fund essential services like aged and childcare, or recruit and subsidise a local GP to keep their towns alive.

"We're going to see councils have to shutter their doors … if we don't fix this financial crisis," he said.

United Services Union national secretary Graeme Kelly said he was not prepared to compromise or back down from the 1 per cent funding ask.

ALP national conference's first day wraps up A much-anticipated floor fight over calls for a gas export tax has failed to materialise at the ALP national conference. Take a look back at how the day's events unfolded.

Mr Kelly said he had a letter signed by the presidents of every local government association in Australia, representing 538 councils, that warned of a "crisis in our suburbs … in our region and rural communities" without the funding boost.

"It cannot get any more dire than that," he said.

"We need funding, and we need it increased at this conference.

"It's quite clear from our discussions that there is a majority of conference delegates who are ready to vote to direct our party to increase funding for local government."

Albanese takes aim at One Nation

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese used his speech at the opening of the conference to celebrate Labor's achievements and take aim at One Nation, the Liberals and Nationals.

He argued regardless of whether the three parties ever formalised cooperation, "in every way that matters" they were "already a Coalition".

"It's not just that they need each other to form government," he said.

"They agree with each other about what they want to do in government."

Housing Minister Clare O'Neil said "whatever distance" the Liberals tried to put between themselves and Ms Hanson, the Coalition would "not be able to govern without One Nation".

Housing Minister Clare O’Neil said the Coalition would “not be able to govern without One Nation”. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

"Imagine Pauline Hanson around the cabinet table, with real power to take away paid parental leave and childcare," she said.

Ms O'Neil also warned that unlike the Liberals, who "never pretended to represent working people", One Nation promoted a "dangerous deception".

"One Nation tries to use the language of working people to sell an agenda that works against them. But when the pressure is on, the mask slips," she said.

Closed-door talks land deals on AI, superannuation and fuel tax credit

Negotiations on the sidelines of the conference meant every amendment to Labor's draft policy platform debated on Thursday passed without dissent.

Delegates voted to add under-18s in a pledge to ensure superannuation was paid on "every dollar earned," and to establish a national Fair AI Taskforce to give workers a greater say on how artificial intelligence impacts the nation.

Labor conference to test PM's AI pitch Labor insiders expect ongoing debate about artificial intelligence when party faithful gather to hash out a policy platform to guide the next three years.

An amendment to "remove disincentives for orderly decarbonisation" — a reference to a tax break provided to off-road diesel users like mining companies and farmers — was also waved through on the conference floor.

But behind that efficient and seamless vote was months of work by the Labor Environment Action Network (LEAN) to pass motions calling for an end to the fuel tax credit through 355 local ALP branches in the lead up to the national conference.

LEAN national co-convenor Louise Crawford said the amendment put forward at the national conference "speaks to the principle" behind the group's push for reform on the diesel tax credit.

"We'd rather see that investment [from the tax credit] go into things like electric trucks and renewables," she said.

Speaking in favour of the amendment, Labor MP Jerome Laxale said widespread support within the party on the issue "cannot be ignored".

"There are tough decisions to be made to reform existing disincentives to decarbonisation," he said.

Tax debate runs out of gas

Despite anticipation of a major stoush over the popular push to tax gas exports, no last-ditch proposal reached the conference floor on Thursday.

The closest debate got to the issue was when Australian Workers Union national secretary Paul Farrow criticised the flow of resource profits offshore during a motion endorsing the government's domestic gas reservation plan.

Mr Farrow railed against Australia's gas being used to "supercharge the profits of multinational gas exporters" rather than support local industry.

Speaking on the sidelines of the conference ahead of the debate, gas tax proponent and Labor MP Ed Husic said there were a lot of delegates with "strong views that reflect the position of the broader public" on the issue.

"I think there is an expectation that we do need to move," he said.

But no explicit attempt to adjust the tax treatment of gas was proposed.

Labor's draft platform, which was negotiated ahead of the conference, instead includes a pledge to ensure the Australian people receive a "fairer return from their natural resources including through appropriate taxation arrangements".

One party source said this vague wording was already reflective of where consensus rested on the issue of a gas tax, and they were "not surprised" further amendments had not progressed.

World.title: Chinese research ships that visit Australia under US surveillance
World.content:
Two Chinese polar research ships that make regular port visits in Australia have come under increased scrutiny by US authorities targeting "any detected malign activity".

It comes as the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade have rejected a Freedom of Information request regarding the vessels' access to Australian ports, saying disclosure could impact national security.

The Xue Long (Snow Dragon) and Xue Long 2 are icebreakers that undertake missions in Antarctica and the Arctic on behalf of the Polar Research Institute of China (PRIC).

The ships have docked in Hobart four times over the past two years after the Tasmanian government invited PRIC to resupply its vessels in the city during trips to and from Antarctica.

The Xue Long docked in Hobart on its way to Antarctica. (ABC News)

The icebreakers had previously been using the Port of Fremantle in Western Australia to stock up on supplies.

Last week, as the ships headed to the Arctic, the US Coast Guard issued a statement saying it had been monitoring them as part of an operation to "protect American sovereign rights".

It said the ships were tracked within the US exclusive economic zone (EEZ) — within 200 nautical miles of the shore — and over the US extended continental shelf in the Bering Sea.

"In response, the U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Munro executed Operation Frontier Sentinel to actively monitor the vessels during their northbound transit," it said.

"This operation is designed to protect American sovereign rights, ensure consistency with international law, and position the Coast Guard to rapidly respond to any detected malign activity."

The Xue Long transits north through the US EEZ and over the US extended continental shelf in the Bering Sea in July 2026. (Supplied: US Coast Guard)

Foreign vessels are permitted to travel in those waters, but the US Coast Guard said it needed "to ensure their activities comply with established international law."

"In particular, conducting marine scientific research within the U.S. EEZ and/or on the U.S. extended continental shelf would require advance permission from the United States and subsequent sharing of information collected," it said.

It is the second year in a row that US authorities have kept a close watch on China's activities in the region after the Xue Long 2 was spotted 290 nautical miles off the Alaskan coast in 2025.

A US Coast Guard aircraft captures an image of the Xue Long 2, about 290 nautical miles north of Alaska in 2025. (Supplied: US Coast Guard)

The Canadian military also tracked the ship last year, with a spokesperson telling CBC that competitor nations were exploring Arctic waters and the sea floor, "probing our infrastructure, and collecting intelligence using dual-purpose research vessels and surveillance platforms".

The increased activity of Chinese and Russian research vessels in the Arctic prompted two US senators to table a bipartisan bill last month to keep what they described as "spy ships" from conducting "research and espionage operations in American waters".

Vigilance needed in Australian waters, analysts say

Elizabeth Buchanan, a senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute who specialises in polar security, said nothing should be taken for granted in Australia.

"We should be concerned along the same lines of what the US Coast Guard is concerned about," Dr Buchanan said.

Dr Elizabeth Buchanan says Australia should also monitor what the ships are doing. (Supplied: Elizabeth Buchanan)

Dr Buchanan recommended Australian authorities monitor the Chinese icebreakers when in Australian waters.

"We know that these vessels have various submersibles, crewed submersibles, that can stay undetected under the polar ice cap, under the water, for up to 12 hours," she said.

"They have all sorts of capabilities: sonar, imaging, recording, robotic hands to lay cables, to add devices to the seabed floor.

"So, we don't actually know what activity is going on in these research expeditions."

Jennifer Parker, an adjunct professor at the University of Western Australia's Defence and Security Institute, said Australia should be vigilant about the ships' activities and capabilities.

Dr Jennifer Parker says the US's statement on the ships is meant to convey a message to China. (Supplied: LinkedIn)

But the former naval officer said there was no current reason to prevent them from accessing Australian ports.

"We should pay more attention to what they're doing, yes, but that doesn't mean we should blanket ban them from our ports," Professor Parker said.

She said the US posture towards the Xue Long and Xue Long 2 was specific to issues in the US and the Arctic region.

"This is about messaging China to highlight that the US knows exactly where they are and what they're doing and intends to respond, but also messaging the global audience that the US has concerns about China's activities in the Arctic and whether they are truly for scientific research purposes," Professor Parker said.

She said while the research ships had a range of dual-use technologies that could be used for non-scientific purposes, it was not enough to warrant significant concern in regard to port visits in Australia.

"Just because they are here and just because they have the capability, it doesn't mean that they necessarily pose a threat," Professor Parker said.

Government refuses to release port documents

The ABC submitted a Freedom of Information (FOI) request to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) in May seeking documents relating to Australian port access for the Xue Long and Xue Long 2.

The request also sought correspondence between the Australian and US governments about the same topic.

The application was rejected by a DFAT FOI officer earlier this month, who said the documents were exempt because public disclosure could affect national security.

"Having examined the documents, I have decided that disclosure of some material contained within the documents would cause damage to the security of the Commonwealth, in particular because the disclosure of some material could be taken advantage of by those conducting activities which are hostile to the Commonwealth's interests," the officer said.

The officer said the public release of the documents could also damage international relations.

Several other reasons for refusal were also outlined, including that the material had been communicated in confidence and was subject to deliberative processes — both of which are considered exemptions under the FOI Act.

China says voyages are for scientific research

The ABC sought comment from the Chinese Embassy in Australia and the PRIC, but did not receive a response.

Earlier this month, China's Ministry of Natural Resources said the purpose of the ships' Arctic mission was scientific research.

"Sustained comprehensive Arctic expeditions serve as a critical foundation for addressing global climate change and advancing the sustainable development of the Arctic region," it said.

China's Foreign Ministry has previously rejected concerns about its fleet of research vessels as "groundless suspicion and speculations".

It says the country carries out "normal activities at sea in accordance with international law".

The Tasmanian government said the Antarctic gateway city of Hobart regularly welcomed research vessels and scientists from around the world.

"Questions regarding national security are a matter for the Australian government," a spokesperson said.

"The Tasmanian government receives briefings and advice regularly from Commonwealth agencies."

The ABC has contacted DFAT for comment.

World.title: First nursery for babies of Ebola victims opens in Congo
World.content:
When the sun starts to set, Wivine Kabala makes her final rounds at the first nursery for infants and children whose parents have been struck down by Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

Ebola cases surge There have been 2,344 cases of Ebola recorded across the DRC to date.

Of that number, there have been 930 deaths.

476 children have contracted the disease, with189 dying. Source: Ministry of Public Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

"Several children are waiting there, others are asking for their parents," Ms Kabala said.

"I bring them a smile, a few comforting words and the certainty that they are not alone."

Ebola has resurfaced in the DRC in Central Africa in the first major outbreak in more than a decade, with the World Health Organization declaring it a public health emergency.

In the DRC, Ebola is a fatal viral disease driven by the rare Bundibugyo virus strain.

The first UNICEF-supported emergency Ebola nursery has opened in the Ituri province in the north-eastern part of the DRC, where 135 children have been orphaned by the outbreak.

The province is at the epicentre of the outbreak, accounting for 90 per cent of cases and 85 per cent of deaths.

Wivine Kabala provides psychosocial support to patients, their relatives and caregivers. (Supplied: UNICEF/Benekire)

Children with confirmed Ebola make up 15 per cent of total cases and are almost twice as likely to die from the disease as adults, according to UNICEF.

Ms Kabala said many children were scared and needed support.

The nursery offered a safe space for children and infants separated from their caregivers, providing them with care and psychosocial support.

"Behind these figures lies a deeper reality. Every day, psychosocial workers like me re-establish dialogue when fear takes over," she said.

Mapenzi, 17, with her three-month-old baby brother Eliya, at the UNICEF-supported nursery. (Supplied: UNICEF/Benekire)

UNICEF chief Catherine Russell said there was a need for extra support for children affected by the outbreak.

"Children are especially vulnerable because they depend on caregivers and cannot distance themselves from a sick parent or sibling in the same way that an adult can," Ms Russell said.

"Our teams in Ituri have met children who have lost their mothers, and in some cases both parents, to Ebola."

Attacks on health facilities

Rubble set on fire as concerns grow over health workers involved in Congo's Ebola response centres. (AP: Constant Same Bagalwa)

At least a dozen attacks on health facilities have sparked safety fears for healthcare workers.

Many of the attacks have been carried out by angry mobs who have stormed treatment centres or targeted response teams in the field, according to incident manager at Congo's National Institute of Public Health, Pierre Akilimali.

Officials said the attacks were not limited to healthcare teams and they also affected frontline workers such as burial teams.

The outbreak has unfolded amid widespread insecurity and displacement due to ongoing war and conflict, while the country grapples with limited access to basic services and fragile health systems.

UNICEF regional director for West and Central Africa, Gilles Fagninou, who just returned from a mission in Ituri province, said five provinces were affected by Ebola amid a turbulent time.

"This geographical increase, in a context of conflict, insecurity, population displacement, and limited access, makes the response both more complex and more urgent," Mr Fagninou said.

Mental health support for children

UNICEF set up treatment centres and other spaces to help children struggling with grief and anxiety. (Supplied: UNICEF/Benekire)

The impact of the outbreak on children's mental health has been immense, with more than 4,000 children in Ituri receiving mental health and psychosocial support, according to Save the Children.

Organisations such as UNICEF and Save the Children have set up spaces to help those struggling with grief and anxiety after losing family to the outbreak.

Save the Children staff in Ituri said the disease had also changed how some children interact, with many now avoiding close contact and keeping their distance from others.

Dr Babou Rukengeza, Save the Children's Ebola Response lead in the DRC, said children in Ituri were carrying an enormous emotional burden.

"Many have witnessed violence, lost loved ones because of the Ebola outbreak or lived through repeated displacement," he said.

"Child Friendly Spaces give them a safe environment where they can express themselves, rebuild confidence and simply be children again."

The effects of prolonged stress and distress during childhood can extend far beyond the immediate crisis.

Save the Children said without adequate support, repeated exposure to adversity can have lasting consequences for children's cognitive development, emotional wellbeing and long-term physical and mental health.

World.title: ASX set to slump as oil surges over $US100, Tesla and Alphabet tumble
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slump as oil surges over $US100, Tesla and Alphabet tumble Stan Choe Updated July 24, 2026 — 6:31am ,first published 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brent oil shot to its highest price since May after increased fighting in the Middle East on Thursday threatened to slow the global flow of crude. At the same time, sharp drops for two of Wall Street’s most influential companies, Alphabet and Tesla, yanked the US stock market to its worst loss in a month. The S&P 500 fell 1.2 per cent and is on track for its first back-to-back weekly loss since March. The Dow Jones dropped 506 points, or 1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 2.2 per cent. Rising oil prices and a slump for Alphabet and Tesla weighed down Wall Street. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to fall, with futures at 5am AEST pointing to a loss of 61 points, or 0.7 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.2 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was 0.5 per cent lower to US69.64¢. Stocks fell under the pressure of rising oil prices, which raise costs for businesses and erode their customers’ ability to spend. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, jumped 7 per cent to settle at $US100.69.



It touched $US102 during the day, the highest price since May for the most actively traded Brent contract in the market. The cause: attacks on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. That threatens another avenue that oil companies use to move their crude from the Middle East to customers worldwide, along with the Strait of Hormuz. Underscoring the importance of the sea route for the economy, President Donald Trump threatened “major military punishment” against the Houthi rebels in Yemen, who are backed by Iran, if they keep attacking ships. It was just a few weeks ago that Brent had dropped below $US72 per barrel, roughly back to where it was before the United States and Israel attacked Iran to begin their war, on hopes that a wind-down in the war would fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The jumps in oil prices will worsen inflation, just when it had begun to decelerate by more than economists expected. That in turn could push the Federal Reserve and other central banks to raise interest rates, which would slow economies and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. The European Central Bank held its main interest rates steady at its meeting Thursday. But traders are betting on a 36 per cent chance the Fed will hike the federal funds rate at its meeting next week. That’s up from the nearly 12 per cent probability seen a week ago, according to data from CME Group.



Related Article Opinion

Executive shake-up Eat what you kill: Macquarie’s first-ever female CEO is a tough act to follow Elizabeth Knight Business columnist An increase by the Fed would be the first since 2023. Higher oil prices pushed the yield of the 10-year Treasury up to 4.69 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Wednesday and from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began. That’s a significant increase, and it’s already brought long-term US mortgage rates to their highest levels in nearly a year. Gasoline prices tend to follow oil prices higher, and a gallon of regular costs an average of $US4.09 across the United States, according to AAA. That’s still below highs of roughly $US4.56 in May, but it was at just $US3.93 a month ago. On Wall Street, stocks of companies with big fuel bills fell to sharp losses on worries about higher expenses.



American Airlines fell 8.4 per cent even though it reported a much bigger profit for the spring than analysts expected, something that usually sends a stock’s price higher. It raised airfares, which helped it offset its higher fuel prices, during the latest quarter. Southwest Airlines lost 6.2 per cent, even though it also reported better profit and revenue than analysts expected. One of the heaviest weights on the US stock market was Tesla, which tumbled 14.5 per cent after Elon Musk’s electric-vehicle company reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Because it’s one of the largest stocks in the S&P 500 by market value, its stock has more influence on the index than nearly every other. One of the few that’s larger is Alphabet, and its stock fell 7.1 per cent even though the parent company of Google delivered stronger profit and revenue than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on how much Alphabet is planning to spend on artificial-intelligence investments. Alphabet raised its forecast for capital spending over the full year after its investments last quarter doubled to nearly $US45 billion ($64.6 billion) from a year earlier.



CEO Sundar Pichai said AI helped its cloud revenue growth accelerate to 82 per cent last quarter, but unease nevertheless remains about whether all the money going into AI will pay off in terms of productivity and profits. Related Article Opinion

AI Money to burn? Big Tech’s AI splurge is blowing out Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Such worries have been shaking the AI industry broadly in recent weeks, leading to big swings for the overall stock market. All told, the S&P 500 fell 90.66 points to 7,408.30. The Dow Jones dropped 506.93 to 51,711.65, and the Nasdaq composite sank 553.21 to 25,137.69. In stock markets abroad, indexes fell sharply in Europe after oil prices jumped. France’s CAC 40 dropped 1.6 per cent for one of the larger losses.



Indexes in Asia were stronger earlier in the day, and South Korea’s Kospi jumped 4.4 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Qantas plane set to arrive in Australia today - direct from France
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Qantas plane set to arrive in Australia today - direct from France Chris Zappone July 24, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Qantas’ Project Sunrise plane will land in Australia today, after making a direct 20-hour plus flight from the factory in France. The specially adapted Airbus A350-1000ULR is expected to land in Melbourne on Friday after performing a flight test designed to push its range capability. It’s coming to Australia: The Project Sunrise A350-1000 ULR in Toulouse, France. Chris Zappone It is fitted with an additional 20,000 litre fuel tank, extending the range of the plane beyond 18,000 km. The Airbus plane is designed to fly non-stop for up to 22 hours, the longest commercial flights in the world, and will connect Australia to London and New York direct.



When active in Qantas’ fleet, the A350-1000 ULR will be able to travel directly between Sydney and London, either flying up over parts of the Eurasia, across Europe or over the Pacific and then the North Pole. The fastest Sydney-to-London flight would be 19 hours and 25 minutes, and the slowest is about 21 hours, Qantas officials have said. From London to Sydney, it would take between 18-20 hours. The Airbus plane is designed to fly non-stop for up to 22 hour and is designed to connect Australia with London and New York. iStock The time of the flight would vary “from day to day” and its “hugely influenced by winds,” Qantas’ chief technical pilot Alex Passerini told a gathering in Toulouse in June. The plane, still in its primary coating, is being flown to Melbourne by four Airbus flight test pilots, and five flight test engineers, who will put “the aircraft’s systems through their paces”. Two Qantas pilots will join the Airbus flight test crew for the return journey to France.



The aircraft completed its first flight on June 2, 2026. In the weeks since, Airbus’ test teams have carried out extensive testing on the ground and in the air in Toulouse, including of the aircraft’s redesigned fuel system. Related Article Aviation Why European summer holiday fares haven’t fallen in line with petrol Sydneysiders feeling cut out of the first sighting of the Project Sunrise plane, don’t despair. The Project Sunrise plane is expected to begin flying between London and Sydney from October 2027. There are no currently no plans to schedule Project Sunrise routes to and from Melbourne. World.title: Tens of thousands forced to flee French holiday spot as fires spread across Europe
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeBushfires Tens of thousands forced to flee French holiday spot as fires spread across Europe David Crowe July 24, 2026 — 5:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: More than 20,000 people are fleeing a wildfire in southern France after flames spread rapidly through a bayside area busy with families on school holidays, in the latest emergency of a European summer marked by intense heat and dry conditions. French authorities said more than 700 firefighters were trying to contain the blaze around the Bay of Arcachon, west of Bordeaux, as they asked families at beachside campsites to leave overnight to avoid being trapped by the flames. People on the beach in Biscarosse, southwestern France as a cloud of smoke rises from a fire raging in the northern part of the Arcachon Basin. AFP A water bomber fighting wildfires in the Lège-Cap-Ferret region in western France on Thursday. AP Photo/Caroline Blumberg Wildfires have also spread in Spain and Italy after the heatwaves of the northern summer, while a fire also spread in a district south of Paris, blamed on arsonists who lit the flames in the Fontainebleau forest near the capital.



The emergencies highlight the ongoing threat from the intense heat when the French public health agency has estimated an “excess mortality” of 5764 deaths between June 17 and July 2, when temperatures soared above 30 degrees. The death toll remains below the statistics reported during a similar heatwave in 2003, although the estimate is yet to reflect the impact over the full summer. Wildfires broke out in several parts of the Italian island of Sicily this week. Anadolu via Getty Images French authorities have ordered the evacuation of about 12,000 people from the area around the Bay of Arcachon, while another 8800 are being moved as a precaution.



“Overnight, the fire spread more quickly than we had imagined,” said Philippe de Gonneville, the mayor of Lège-Cap Ferret. In ​neighbouring Spain, authorities were still working to put out fires which have raged for several days, while in Italy, a 59-year-old firefighter died after falling ill while battling ⁠a large wildfire near San Cataldo in Sicily. Smoke rises in the Lège-Cap-Ferret region. AP Photo/Caroline Blumberg A fire burns in San Martin de Valdeiglesias, Spain, on Thursday. Europa Press via Getty Images Lège is the only one of the peninsula’s 11 villages that is currently threatened by the fire, but Gonneville said authorities had evacuated 5200 people overnight. He said access ​was completely closed, and contingency plans were in place to evacuate the entire peninsula by both road and sea if necessary.



The fire later reached the edge of Lège, forcing the evacuation of several campgrounds and neighbourhoods close to the forest. Wildfires ​remained a major challenge across Spain on Thursday, with authorities tackling several significant blazes. Firefighters use a helicopter to combat wildfires in Rome on Tuesday. Francesco Benvenuti/LaPresse via Train traffic on Spain’s Madrid-Barcelona high-speed rail line resumed on Thursday after a wildfire near the tracks prompted the suspension of services between Mejorada del Campo and Alcalá ‌de Henares, east ⁠of Madrid. Europe is bearing the brunt of ⁠a rapidly warming climate, with temperatures rising more than twice as fast as the global average.



In Italy, arsonists were reported to have tied rags to the tails of cats and set them alight, causing wildfires. Investigators also candles and delayed ignition devices in the aftermath of the fire, according to The Telegraph. The fire spread through the Pollino national park in Calabria in southern Italy this week. “These animals were released into the fields, running around and spreading the fire,” said Domenico Costarella, of Calabria’s civil protection agency. The Reuters Climate Monitor, an interactive tool tracking weather patterns, showed the average high across Western Europe is forecast to be 26.5 degrees on Thursday, which is 2.9 degrees above the normal high for July 23 over the period from 1961 to 1990. World.title: The 30 best movies to watch on Stan right now
World.content:

The depths of winter demand a night in with a great movie. The problem? Choice paralysis. Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great hand-picked movies on Stan* right now. Don’t have Stan? Check out our guides on Netflix, Amazon Prime Video and HBO Max. 12 Years a Slave (2013) Chiwetel Ejiofor in 12 Years A Slave. A true story where slavery’s horror weighs on the very will to live, Steve McQueen’s Oscars best picture winner stars Chiwetel Ejiofor as Solomon Northup, a free black man kidnapped into southern slavery. Masterfully made and uncompromising. Animal Kingdom (2011) Told with nightmarish economy and Aussie vernacular, David Michod’s debut charts a Melbourne crime clan’s deadly eruption. With Ben Mendelsohn as a paranoid killer and Jacki Weaver the controlling matriarch, this is a can’t-look-away crime drama. Timothee Chalamet in Call Me By Your Name. Sony Pictures Classics



Call Me by Your Name (2017) Audiences at large discovered Timothee Chalamet with this heart-rending depiction of first love as director Luca Guadagnino captures every turning point for Chalamet’s Elio and Armie Hammer’s Oliver. Discovery, joy and loss are intertwined. Clueless (1995) Jane Austen’s Emma is relocated to Beverly Hills in a teen comedy so enjoyable that it rightly still populates our shared cultural idiom. Alicia Silverstone’s Cher Horowitz is the preposterously perfect student whose life comes unstuck when she discovers matchmaking. Stacey Dash and Alicia Silverstone in Clueless. Paramount Pictures Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000) Ang Lee delivered the wuxia martial arts genre to the world with this thrilling 18th century adventure in which Chow Yun-fat and Michelle Yeoh’s stoic Chinese warriors seek a stolen sword and possibly each other. Gravity and genre-defying.



Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022) And here’s the Michelle Yeoh double-bill, with the Malaysian as the anchor in this inter-dimensional epic in which immigrant family trauma, freaky bureaucrats and apocalyptic fates intermingle. It’s both delightfully absurd and undeniably tragic. Michelle Yeow in Everything Everywhere All At Once. Erin Brockovich (2000) Director Steven Soderbergh and star Julia Roberts gave the legal drama a memorable underdog heroine in this real-life story of a Californian legal clerk who uncovered deadly corporate crimes and refused to take a backwards step. Fargo (1996) With thick North Dakota accents and a subtle reading of evil’s ease with the mundane, the Coen brothers follow a pregnant sheriff (Frances McDormand) diligently unwinding a botched kidnapping. It is the quintessential laugh-until-you-cry black comedy.



Frances McDormand as Marge Gunderson in Fargo. Related Article Cinema Every Christopher Nolan movie ranked: How does The Odyssey compare to Oppenheimer? Fight Club (1999) The true end of the 20th century bug was this subversive satire from David Fincher in which a corporate drone (Edward Norton) finds purpose via a badass bestie (Brad Pitt). Fighting each other and the audience’s morality, the film coolly runs amok. The Fugitive (1993) With Tommy Lee Jones as his hard-charging pursuer, Harrison Ford is the grieving husband on the run after being framed for his wife’s murder. This is one of the great Hollywood action-thrillers – edge-of-your-seat momentum meets heroic recklessness. The Godfather (1972)



The gangster film as American epic, Francis Ford Coppola’s masterpiece about a 1940s New York mafia clan combines indelible performances – Al Pacino, Marlon Brando and more – with starkly tragic image-making. Godland (2022) The physical and philosophical worlds combine to harrowing heights in this 19th century drama about a Danish priest (Elliott Crosset Hove) tasked with founding an Icelandic parish. Specks of the harshest humour dot spiritual doubt and colonial guilt. Al Pacino in Heat. Heat (1995) Michael Mann’s monumental crime drama stars Robert De Niro and Al Pacino as respectively a brilliant master thief and obsessive police detective drawn together in a Los Angeles punctuated by cataclysmic shootouts and flawed personal relationships.
