World.title: From $6 flat whites to $10 Gen Z drinks: You can’t put a price on the breadth and brilliance of Melbourne’s cafes
World.content:
When Melburnians do head out for brunch, many are stepping away from the familiar in favour of trying new dishes and new cultures, such as the Mexican-meets-British-caff menu at Aftermath in Prahran.

For its annual 100 Essential Cafes and Bakeries guide, Good Food asks what going out for brunch looks like in 2026, from new-wave coffee orders to the rise of the queue.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne’s coffee – and by extension, its cafe scene – is often declared among the best in the world. After spending the past 12 months hitting up hundreds of cafes to compile the 100 Essential Cafes and Bakeries of Melbourne Guide, I find it hard to disagree. From Frankston to Caroline Springs, we’re spoiled by our choice of specialty brews, brunch plates, foamy signature drinks, matcha and pastries. It’s why Australians spent nearly as much in cafes last year ($99 on average a month) as they did in restaurants ($111 a month), as shown in Lightspeed’s 2026 State of Hospitality Industry Report. Related Collection Good Food’s 100 Essential Melbourne Cafes & Bakeries But what is the hallmark of a good cafe in 2026? Do Gen Z and other groups want different things from a cafe? And what does it take to survive as a cafe in today’s economy? The answers – at least to the first question – are found in Good Food’s second annual Essential Melbourne Cafes and Bakeries Guide. It’s a creme de la creme collection of 100 businesses, baristas, servers, roasters and chefs that make our days (and even our nights) that little bit better. Narrowing it down to just 100 anonymously reviewed venues wasn’t easy in such a cafe and bakery-dense city that continues to grow. But visit any of the spots on this list, and we guarantee you’ll be happy, whether you’re a long-black drinker or a banana cream matcha obsessive. Fifteen years ago, cafes stood out by crafting an impressive menu catering to vegans and paleo diets, typically featuring some kind of avocado toast, an OTT “freakshake” and edible flowers – things designed to capture views on Instagram in its embryonic stages. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up



There’s a generational divide between those who order matcha (left) and those who prefer flat whites. Today, cafes pour their creativity into tall, foam-capped signature drinks. These wildly inventive creations reveal a generational divide in how Melbourne likes its coffee. “The older generations are still coming in for a classic coffee – a latte, cappuccino, long black or espresso – but the younger generation looks at coffee as a cultural product,” says Byoung-Woo Kang, founder of Acoffee in Collingwood. Matcha is still ubiquitous, but it’s the cream-capped, einspanner-style coffee that has taken over nearly every breakfast, brunch and coffee menu in our city. Inspired by the two-tone Viennese coffee drink combining espresso and fresh cream, variations are many and madcap: tiramisu, banana pudding, Biscoff and Earl Grey creams and foams are blended with cold brew coffee all over Melbourne, even in the dead of winter. ACoffee’s signature einspanner (left) and cameo caramel drinks. Acoffee is joining in, too. Despite serving a minimalist line-up of single origin filter and drip coffees for nearly 10 years, it now also offers a range of einspanners, matchas and creamy teas. “I actually didn’t want to have signature drinks because of my passion for specialty coffee,” Kang says. “But people are very sensitive to the price of coffee.”



Tiramisu, banana pudding, Biscoff and Earl Grey creams and foams are blended with cold brew coffee all over Melbourne, even in the dead of winter. With supply chain costs leading to a rise in green coffee expenses, he says something had to give. “It’s difficult to increase the price of a latte or a long black, but if we have signature drinks, younger generations are willing to spend a bit more.” At the chic inner-north cafe, a flat white will set you back $6.30, while an einspanner is priced at a premium of $9.50. It’s unsurprising that trends driven by younger generations are showing up on cafe menus. Gen Z are dining out more than any other generation, according to Lightspeed’s report. Those in their 20s might not be able to afford a three-course degustation, but a weekly fun drink and a sweet treat isn’t out of the question. “They aren’t going to be loyal customers; they’re moving around and looking for something new all the time,” says Kang. For now, it keeps new customers coming through the doors.



Related Article The small Carlton cafe selling 6500 Mont Blanc signature coffees per week Award-winning barista Junnie Phyu recently opened her first cafe, More Coffee in Hawthorn, with a two-speed menu that speaks to old- and new-school coffee drinkers. Sticking to her passion for quality brews, Phyu offers an entire menu of specialty pourovers and continues to run her coffee workshops in Burwood East. But catering to a broader audience allows her to have a bit of fun, offering signature drinks in all colours of the rainbow: sparkling orange and grapefruit coffee; taro matcha; pandan cloud coffee, to name a few. “Even if we add extra sugar or foam, we really try not to overwhelm or take away the coffee flavour,” Phyu says. Signature drinks at More Coffee. More’s signature drinks might contain lots of flashy extras, but they’re actually cheaper to make than a good quality pourover coffee due to the cost of ingredients, equipment and labour. Despite this, Phyu prices them all around $10. “Some people really don’t want to drink coffee as much any more,” Phyu says. “It’s more about the experience.” How much that experience should cost is a hot topic (just read this controversial opinion piece published by The Age). While the 100 Essential Cafes list celebrates the venues we know and love today, it’s difficult to ignore those that are shutting their doors each week in the face of rising costs, wages and other overheads. Meanwhile, customers battling the enduring cost-of-living crisis can no longer afford to splash out regularly on dining. It’s a catch-22. There’s a reason why you’re less likely to sit down for a leisurely breakfast, and more likely to see queues for takeaway pastries and sandwiches.



Charlie Duffy’s debut bakery, Daybreaker, attracts queues. Eddie Jim Earlier this year, Mordor Intelligence found takeaway was driving the fastest growth in the foodservice market – projected to expand at nearly 12 per cent a year until 2031. It might seem like a death sentence for the average hospitality business, but most cafe and bakery owners across Melbourne are already adapting. Grab-and-go is the new daytime business model. In Carlton North, ever-popular cafe Florian this year added a takeaway-only shop next door for its bestselling sandwiches, salads and cakes. “The takeaway element honestly really saved us,” Florian owner Dom Gattermayr says. “We’ve noticed now we can actually afford to do things rather than breaking even.” Owners Dom Gattermayr and Rose Richards outside Florian To-Go. Penny Stephens Removing the limitation of finding space for customers has also meant welcoming a new demographic – those who might have been daunted by the crowded doorways or disappointed by the lack of grab-and-go options by lunchtime. And of course, those that don’t want to spend too much. New bakeries such as Vandels in Brunswick and Abbotsford’s Daybaker have opened to instant crowds, while Chinese breakfast spot Wow Crepes on Bourke Street has expanded to a second, hole-in-the-wall shopfront opposite Flinders Street Station – this time without seating available. Could a sit-down breakfast or brunch soon become a premium product with a pricetag to match?

World.title: The fruit that connects 200 years of Australian history
World.content:
CultureBooksReview The fruit that connects 200 years of Australian history Thuy On July 24, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Short History of Longans is a historical novel that spans two centuries and follows the twisted branches of an Irish-Chinese family in Australia. Mirandi Riwoe’s latest book, her sixth, explores similar themes tackled in her previous works: cross-cultural identities, interracial relationships, immigration, racism and colonial history. Following a preface about a Chinese bushranger named Ah Yang, the novel is divided into four seasonal sections, each helmed by one of his successors. This multigenerational saga begins at the end. Its reverse chronology opens in the near future, in winter 2049, when elderly Daniel finds his beloved longan tree toppled by a storm. It seems like an apt metaphor for his own life, as he fears a “shambolic, exhausting sprint to the finish line – a race that he somehow finds himself ill-equipped for”. The longan appears in all four sections of the book as a linking motif. Getty Images He has long lived alone, but his solitude is disrupted by a widowed neighbour, Olivia Quong, who is piqued with curiosity by the dusty, red-lacquered altar in his house. This neglected heirloom once belonged to Daniel’s late father and offers a clue as to his distant Asian ancestry. So indeed does his cat, who is named after a Chinese emperor, despite Daniel’s general indifference towards his family history.



He used to be a carpenter; now he potters around, creating sculptures from mosaics of inherited letters, photos and crockery. He finds satisfaction in reassembling these shards into new formations, and also likes the shape he’s becoming through his slowly growing friendship with Olivia. But his peace is broken when a stranger turns up, requesting that Daniel delve into his shameful past. Before we can find out more about this mystery, Riwoe ends the section. This abrupt closure may dismay readers who are primed for narrative resolution, or at least for more information, but the author has jumped even further back in time. The second section settles in autumn on New Year’s Day in 2000, and focuses on another branch of the family tree. Like Daniel, Wendy is also of advanced years, but aside from the usual physical ailments, she’s experiencing early onset dementia. Unlike Daniel, who was busy cutting up his family’s paraphernalia for his art projects, Wendy is an aspiring writer trying to bring together pieces of her Irish immigrant forebears to document them. However, her “honeycomb” brain, with its gaps in memory, makes research difficult. Riwoe writes perceptively about this collapse of time: “The multiplying particles of herself – child, adolescent, adult, demented woman – assembling, competing, squirming, for room beneath her skin.” Novelist Mirandi Riwoe’s new book is a multigenerational epic.



The narrative then jumps back another 60-odd years, leaving Queensland behind to follow Ruby in Los Angeles. She’s a Chinese-Australian actress chasing the American dream in the 1940s. The nuances of race are particularly potent in this section. Ruby has missed out on playing Shakespearean heroines because her complexion was “too dusky, as usual”. And yet, she’s found a way to take advantage of her mixed ancestry, leaning into the market’s proclivity for fetishising “Orientalists” by changing her surname to her mother’s “Wong”and preparing lectures about “the usual spiel about Chinese recipes and superstition …” even though she’s never been to China. Editor's pick Literature The Australian author who went from rejection letters to global bestseller The final section of A Short History of Longans loops us back to the start and explains how the bushranger Ah Yong inadvertently planted the seed for this mixed-race family tree. This last segment includes a cacophony of voices from extended members of the clan, but it’s primarily the story of Maria Barrett, an 18-year-old Irish pauper who arrives in Australia at the turn of the century. It’s appropriately set in spring, a time of birth and beginnings. The novel moves adeptly between each family member; in terms of time and place and social norms, the world-building for these varied and disparate characters has been meticulously researched. With her Eurasian background, a mix of Chinese-Indonesian and Irish-English heritage, Riwoe knows what it’s like to straddle cultures, to live as racially bifurcated: divided and wholly of neither east nor west, but a brew of both. Her lived experience informs her books and offers verisimilitude to the stories.



The longan, a fruit native to South-East Asia, with its historical cultivation dating back to China, appears in all four sections of the book as a linking motif. Though the bloodline flows through the chapters, sometimes the connection between them may feel tenuous, and each quarter can pass as a short story or the beginning of a novella and be read as a discrete unit on its own. But together they present a beguiling, detail-rich narrative that tracks the fortunes and fates of several generations, replete with secrets and lies, but also with hope. At the end of Daniel’s narrative, there’s a discovery of infant longan leaves in his garden. These slender saplings, offspring of the destroyed parent plant, look to the future. What else is happening in the book world? A split-second mistake sent author Jaclyn Moriarty on a two-decade literary odyssey.

The legendary cinematographer for Blade Runner 2049, Fargo and Skyfall takes us behind the lenses in his new memoir.

Here’s why you should keep re-reading your favourite book (without feeling guilty).

And there’s a new word for when a media empire targets you.

World.title: ASX set to slump as oil surges over $US100, Tesla and Alphabet tumble
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slump as oil surges over $US100, Tesla and Alphabet tumble Stan Choe Updated July 24, 2026 — 6:31am ,first published 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brent oil shot to its highest price since May after increased fighting in the Middle East on Thursday threatened to slow the global flow of crude. At the same time, sharp drops for two of Wall Street’s most influential companies, Alphabet and Tesla, yanked the US stock market to its worst loss in a month. The S&P 500 fell 1.2 per cent and is on track for its first back-to-back weekly loss since March. The Dow Jones dropped 506 points, or 1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 2.2 per cent. Rising oil prices and a slump for Alphabet and Tesla weighed down Wall Street. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to fall, with futures at 5am AEST pointing to a loss of 61 points, or 0.7 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.2 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was 0.5 per cent lower to US69.64¢. Stocks fell under the pressure of rising oil prices, which raise costs for businesses and erode their customers’ ability to spend. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, jumped 7 per cent to settle at $US100.69.



It touched $US102 during the day, the highest price since May for the most actively traded Brent contract in the market. The cause: attacks on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. That threatens another avenue that oil companies use to move their crude from the Middle East to customers worldwide, along with the Strait of Hormuz. Underscoring the importance of the sea route for the economy, President Donald Trump threatened “major military punishment” against the Houthi rebels in Yemen, who are backed by Iran, if they keep attacking ships. It was just a few weeks ago that Brent had dropped below $US72 per barrel, roughly back to where it was before the United States and Israel attacked Iran to begin their war, on hopes that a wind-down in the war would fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The jumps in oil prices will worsen inflation, just when it had begun to decelerate by more than economists expected. That in turn could push the Federal Reserve and other central banks to raise interest rates, which would slow economies and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. The European Central Bank held its main interest rates steady at its meeting Thursday. But traders are betting on a 36 per cent chance the Fed will hike the federal funds rate at its meeting next week. That’s up from the nearly 12 per cent probability seen a week ago, according to data from CME Group.



Related Article Opinion

Executive shake-up Eat what you kill: Macquarie’s first-ever female CEO is a tough act to follow Elizabeth Knight Business columnist An increase by the Fed would be the first since 2023. Higher oil prices pushed the yield of the 10-year Treasury up to 4.69 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Wednesday and from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began. That’s a significant increase, and it’s already brought long-term US mortgage rates to their highest levels in nearly a year. Gasoline prices tend to follow oil prices higher, and a gallon of regular costs an average of $US4.09 across the United States, according to AAA. That’s still below highs of roughly $US4.56 in May, but it was at just $US3.93 a month ago. On Wall Street, stocks of companies with big fuel bills fell to sharp losses on worries about higher expenses.



American Airlines fell 8.4 per cent even though it reported a much bigger profit for the spring than analysts expected, something that usually sends a stock’s price higher. It raised airfares, which helped it offset its higher fuel prices, during the latest quarter. Southwest Airlines lost 6.2 per cent, even though it also reported better profit and revenue than analysts expected. One of the heaviest weights on the US stock market was Tesla, which tumbled 14.5 per cent after Elon Musk’s electric-vehicle company reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Because it’s one of the largest stocks in the S&P 500 by market value, its stock has more influence on the index than nearly every other. One of the few that’s larger is Alphabet, and its stock fell 7.1 per cent even though the parent company of Google delivered stronger profit and revenue than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on how much Alphabet is planning to spend on artificial-intelligence investments. Alphabet raised its forecast for capital spending over the full year after its investments last quarter doubled to nearly $US45 billion ($64.6 billion) from a year earlier.



CEO Sundar Pichai said AI helped its cloud revenue growth accelerate to 82 per cent last quarter, but unease nevertheless remains about whether all the money going into AI will pay off in terms of productivity and profits. Related Article Opinion

AI Money to burn? Big Tech’s AI splurge is blowing out Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Such worries have been shaking the AI industry broadly in recent weeks, leading to big swings for the overall stock market. All told, the S&P 500 fell 90.66 points to 7,408.30. The Dow Jones dropped 506.93 to 51,711.65, and the Nasdaq composite sank 553.21 to 25,137.69. In stock markets abroad, indexes fell sharply in Europe after oil prices jumped. France’s CAC 40 dropped 1.6 per cent for one of the larger losses.



Indexes in Asia were stronger earlier in the day, and South Korea’s Kospi jumped 4.4 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Qantas plane set to arrive in Australia today - direct from France
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Qantas plane set to arrive in Australia today - direct from France Chris Zappone July 24, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Qantas’ Project Sunrise plane will land in Australia today, after making a direct 20-hour plus flight from the factory in France. The specially adapted Airbus A350-1000ULR is expected to land in Melbourne on Friday after performing a flight test designed to push its range capability. It’s coming to Australia: The Project Sunrise A350-1000 ULR in Toulouse, France. Chris Zappone It is fitted with an additional 20,000 litre fuel tank, extending the range of the plane beyond 18,000 km. The Airbus plane is designed to fly non-stop for up to 22 hours, the longest commercial flights in the world, and will connect Australia to London and New York direct.



When active in Qantas’ fleet, the A350-1000 ULR will be able to travel directly between Sydney and London, either flying up over parts of the Eurasia, across Europe or over the Pacific and then the North Pole. The fastest Sydney-to-London flight would be 19 hours and 25 minutes, and the slowest is about 21 hours, Qantas officials have said. From London to Sydney, it would take between 18-20 hours. The Airbus plane is designed to fly non-stop for up to 22 hour and is designed to connect Australia with London and New York. iStock The time of the flight would vary “from day to day” and its “hugely influenced by winds,” Qantas’ chief technical pilot Alex Passerini told a gathering in Toulouse in June. The plane, still in its primary coating, is being flown to Melbourne by four Airbus flight test pilots, and five flight test engineers, who will put “the aircraft’s systems through their paces”. Two Qantas pilots will join the Airbus flight test crew for the return journey to France.



The aircraft completed its first flight on June 2, 2026. In the weeks since, Airbus’ test teams have carried out extensive testing on the ground and in the air in Toulouse, including of the aircraft’s redesigned fuel system. The Project Sunrise plane is expected to begin flying between London and Sydney from October 2027. There are no currently no plans to schedule Project Sunrise routes to and from Melbourne. World.title: Tens of thousands forced to flee French holiday spot as fires spread across Europe
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeBushfires Tens of thousands forced to flee French holiday spot as fires spread across Europe David Crowe July 24, 2026 — 5:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: More than 20,000 people are fleeing a wildfire in southern France after flames spread rapidly through a bayside area busy with families on school holidays, in the latest emergency of a European summer marked by intense heat and dry conditions. French authorities said more than 700 firefighters were trying to contain the blaze around the Bay of Arcachon, west of Bordeaux, as they asked families at beachside campsites to leave overnight to avoid being trapped by the flames. People on the beach in Biscarosse, southwestern France as a cloud of smoke rises from a fire raging in the northern part of the Arcachon Basin. AFP A water bomber fighting wildfires in the Lège-Cap-Ferret region in western France on Thursday. AP Photo/Caroline Blumberg Wildfires have also spread in Spain and Italy after the heatwaves of the northern summer, while a fire also spread in a district south of Paris, blamed on arsonists who lit the flames in the Fontainebleau forest near the capital.



The emergencies highlight the ongoing threat from the intense heat when the French public health agency has estimated an “excess mortality” of 5764 deaths between June 17 and July 2, when temperatures soared above 30 degrees. The death toll remains below the statistics reported during a similar heatwave in 2003, although the estimate is yet to reflect the impact over the full summer. Wildfires broke out in several parts of the Italian island of Sicily this week. Anadolu via Getty Images French authorities have ordered the evacuation of about 12,000 people from the area around the Bay of Arcachon, while another 8800 are being moved as a precaution.



“Overnight, the fire spread more quickly than we had imagined,” said Philippe de Gonneville, the mayor of Lège-Cap Ferret. In ​neighbouring Spain, authorities were still working to put out fires which have raged for several days, while in Italy, a 59-year-old firefighter died after falling ill while battling ⁠a large wildfire near San Cataldo in Sicily. Smoke rises in the Lège-Cap-Ferret region. AP Photo/Caroline Blumberg A fire burns in San Martin de Valdeiglesias, Spain, on Thursday. Europa Press via Getty Images Lège is the only one of the peninsula’s 11 villages that is currently threatened by the fire, but Gonneville said authorities had evacuated 5200 people overnight. He said access ​was completely closed, and contingency plans were in place to evacuate the entire peninsula by both road and sea if necessary.



The fire later reached the edge of Lège, forcing the evacuation of several campgrounds and neighbourhoods close to the forest. Wildfires ​remained a major challenge across Spain on Thursday, with authorities tackling several significant blazes. Firefighters use a helicopter to combat wildfires in Rome on Tuesday. Francesco Benvenuti/LaPresse via Train traffic on Spain’s Madrid-Barcelona high-speed rail line resumed on Thursday after a wildfire near the tracks prompted the suspension of services between Mejorada del Campo and Alcalá ‌de Henares, east ⁠of Madrid. Europe is bearing the brunt of ⁠a rapidly warming climate, with temperatures rising more than twice as fast as the global average.



In Italy, arsonists were reported to have tied rags to the tails of cats and set them alight, causing wildfires. Investigators also candles and delayed ignition devices in the aftermath of the fire, according to The Telegraph. The fire spread through the Pollino national park in Calabria in southern Italy this week. “These animals were released into the fields, running around and spreading the fire,” said Domenico Costarella, of Calabria’s civil protection agency. The Reuters Climate Monitor, an interactive tool tracking weather patterns, showed the average high across Western Europe is forecast to be 26.5 degrees on Thursday, which is 2.9 degrees above the normal high for July 23 over the period from 1961 to 1990. The depths of winter demand a night in with a great movie. The problem? Choice paralysis. Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great hand-picked movies on Stan* right now. Don’t have Stan? Check out our guides on Netflix, Amazon Prime Video and HBO Max. 12 Years a Slave (2013) Chiwetel Ejiofor in 12 Years A Slave. A true story where slavery’s horror weighs on the very will to live, Steve McQueen’s Oscars best picture winner stars Chiwetel Ejiofor as Solomon Northup, a free black man kidnapped into southern slavery. Masterfully made and uncompromising. Animal Kingdom (2011) Told with nightmarish economy and Aussie vernacular, David Michod’s debut charts a Melbourne crime clan’s deadly eruption. With Ben Mendelsohn as a paranoid killer and Jacki Weaver the controlling matriarch, this is a can’t-look-away crime drama. Timothee Chalamet in Call Me By Your Name. Sony Pictures Classics



Call Me by Your Name (2017) Audiences at large discovered Timothee Chalamet with this heart-rending depiction of first love as director Luca Guadagnino captures every turning point for Chalamet’s Elio and Armie Hammer’s Oliver. Discovery, joy and loss are intertwined. Clueless (1995) Jane Austen’s Emma is relocated to Beverly Hills in a teen comedy so enjoyable that it rightly still populates our shared cultural idiom. Alicia Silverstone’s Cher Horowitz is the preposterously perfect student whose life comes unstuck when she discovers matchmaking. Stacey Dash and Alicia Silverstone in Clueless. Paramount Pictures Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000) Ang Lee delivered the wuxia martial arts genre to the world with this thrilling 18th century adventure in which Chow Yun-fat and Michelle Yeoh’s stoic Chinese warriors seek a stolen sword and possibly each other. Gravity and genre-defying.



Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022) And here’s the Michelle Yeoh double-bill, with the Malaysian as the anchor in this inter-dimensional epic in which immigrant family trauma, freaky bureaucrats and apocalyptic fates intermingle. It’s both delightfully absurd and undeniably tragic. Michelle Yeow in Everything Everywhere All At Once. Erin Brockovich (2000) Director Steven Soderbergh and star Julia Roberts gave the legal drama a memorable underdog heroine in this real-life story of a Californian legal clerk who uncovered deadly corporate crimes and refused to take a backwards step. Fargo (1996) With thick North Dakota accents and a subtle reading of evil’s ease with the mundane, the Coen brothers follow a pregnant sheriff (Frances McDormand) diligently unwinding a botched kidnapping. It is the quintessential laugh-until-you-cry black comedy.



Frances McDormand as Marge Gunderson in Fargo. Related Article Cinema Every Christopher Nolan movie ranked: How does The Odyssey compare to Oppenheimer? Fight Club (1999) The true end of the 20th century bug was this subversive satire from David Fincher in which a corporate drone (Edward Norton) finds purpose via a badass bestie (Brad Pitt). Fighting each other and the audience’s morality, the film coolly runs amok. The Fugitive (1993) With Tommy Lee Jones as his hard-charging pursuer, Harrison Ford is the grieving husband on the run after being framed for his wife’s murder. This is one of the great Hollywood action-thrillers – edge-of-your-seat momentum meets heroic recklessness. The Godfather (1972)



The gangster film as American epic, Francis Ford Coppola’s masterpiece about a 1940s New York mafia clan combines indelible performances – Al Pacino, Marlon Brando and more – with starkly tragic image-making. Godland (2022) The physical and philosophical worlds combine to harrowing heights in this 19th century drama about a Danish priest (Elliott Crosset Hove) tasked with founding an Icelandic parish. Specks of the harshest humour dot spiritual doubt and colonial guilt. Al Pacino in Heat. Heat (1995) Michael Mann’s monumental crime drama stars Robert De Niro and Al Pacino as respectively a brilliant master thief and obsessive police detective drawn together in a Los Angeles punctuated by cataclysmic shootouts and flawed personal relationships. World.title: From $6 flat whites to $10 Gen Z drinks: You can’t put a price on the breadth and brilliance of Melbourne’s cafes
World.content:
When Melburnians do head out for brunch, many are stepping away from the familiar in favour of trying new dishes and new cultures, such as the Mexican-meets-British-caff menu at Aftermath in Prahran.

For its annual 100 Essential Cafes and Bakeries guide, Good Food asks what going out for brunch looks like in 2026, from new-wave coffee orders to the rise of the queue.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne’s coffee – and by extension, its cafe scene – is often declared among the best in the world. After spending the past 12 months hitting up hundreds of cafes to compile the 100 Essential Cafes and Bakeries of Melbourne Guide, I find it hard to disagree. From Frankston to Caroline Springs, we’re spoiled by our choice of specialty brews, brunch plates, foamy signature drinks, matcha and pastries. It’s why Australians spent nearly as much in cafes last year ($99 on average a month) as they did in restaurants ($111 a month), as shown in Lightspeed’s 2026 State of Hospitality Industry Report. Related Collection Good Food’s 100 Essential Melbourne Cafes & Bakeries But what is the hallmark of a good cafe in 2026? Do Gen Z and other groups want different things from a cafe? And what does it take to survive as a cafe in today’s economy? The answers – at least to the first question – are found in Good Food’s second annual Essential Melbourne Cafes and Bakeries Guide. It’s a creme de la creme collection of 100 businesses, baristas, servers, roasters and chefs that make our days (and even our nights) that little bit better. Narrowing it down to just 100 anonymously reviewed venues wasn’t easy in such a cafe and bakery-dense city that continues to grow. But visit any of the spots on this list, and we guarantee you’ll be happy, whether you’re a long-black drinker or a banana cream matcha obsessive. Fifteen years ago, cafes stood out by crafting an impressive menu catering to vegans and paleo diets, typically featuring some kind of avocado toast, an OTT “freakshake” and edible flowers – things designed to capture views on Instagram in its embryonic stages. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up



There’s a generational divide between those who order matcha (left) and those who prefer flat whites. Today, cafes pour their creativity into tall, foam-capped signature drinks. These wildly inventive creations reveal a generational divide in how Melbourne likes its coffee. “The older generations are still coming in for a classic coffee – a latte, cappuccino, long black or espresso – but the younger generation looks at coffee as a cultural product,” says Byoung-Woo Kang, founder of Acoffee in Collingwood. Matcha is still ubiquitous, but it’s the cream-capped, einspanner-style coffee that has taken over nearly every breakfast, brunch and coffee menu in our city. Inspired by the two-tone Viennese coffee drink combining espresso and fresh cream, variations are many and madcap: tiramisu, banana pudding, Biscoff and Earl Grey creams and foams are blended with cold brew coffee all over Melbourne, even in the dead of winter. ACoffee’s signature einspanner (left) and cameo caramel drinks. Acoffee is joining in, too. Despite serving a minimalist line-up of single origin filter and drip coffees for nearly 10 years, it now also offers a range of einspanners, matchas and creamy teas. “I actually didn’t want to have signature drinks because of my passion for specialty coffee,” Kang says. “But people are very sensitive to the price of coffee.”



Tiramisu, banana pudding, Biscoff and Earl Grey creams and foams are blended with cold brew coffee all over Melbourne, even in the dead of winter. With supply chain costs leading to a rise in green coffee expenses, he says something had to give. “It’s difficult to increase the price of a latte or a long black, but if we have signature drinks, younger generations are willing to spend a bit more.” At the chic inner-north cafe, a flat white will set you back $6.30, while an einspanner is priced at a premium of $9.50. It’s unsurprising that trends driven by younger generations are showing up on cafe menus. Gen Z are dining out more than any other generation, according to Lightspeed’s report. Those in their 20s might not be able to afford a three-course degustation, but a weekly fun drink and a sweet treat isn’t out of the question. “They aren’t going to be loyal customers; they’re moving around and looking for something new all the time,” says Kang. For now, it keeps new customers coming through the doors.



Related Article The small Carlton cafe selling 6500 Mont Blanc signature coffees per week Award-winning barista Junnie Phyu recently opened her first cafe, More Coffee in Hawthorn, with a two-speed menu that speaks to old- and new-school coffee drinkers. Sticking to her passion for quality brews, Phyu offers an entire menu of specialty pourovers and continues to run her coffee workshops in Burwood East. But catering to a broader audience allows her to have a bit of fun, offering signature drinks in all colours of the rainbow: sparkling orange and grapefruit coffee; taro matcha; pandan cloud coffee, to name a few. “Even if we add extra sugar or foam, we really try not to overwhelm or take away the coffee flavour,” Phyu says. Signature drinks at More Coffee. More’s signature drinks might contain lots of flashy extras, but they’re actually cheaper to make than a good quality pourover coffee due to the cost of ingredients, equipment and labour. Despite this, Phyu prices them all around $10. “Some people really don’t want to drink coffee as much any more,” Phyu says. “It’s more about the experience.” How much that experience should cost is a hot topic (just read this controversial opinion piece published by The Age). While the 100 Essential Cafes list celebrates the venues we know and love today, it’s difficult to ignore those that are shutting their doors each week in the face of rising costs, wages and other overheads. Meanwhile, customers battling the enduring cost-of-living crisis can no longer afford to splash out regularly on dining. It’s a catch-22. There’s a reason why you’re less likely to sit down for a leisurely breakfast, and more likely to see queues for takeaway pastries and sandwiches.



Charlie Duffy’s debut bakery, Daybreaker, attracts queues. Eddie Jim Earlier this year, Mordor Intelligence found takeaway was driving the fastest growth in the foodservice market – projected to expand at nearly 12 per cent a year until 2031. It might seem like a death sentence for the average hospitality business, but most cafe and bakery owners across Melbourne are already adapting. Grab-and-go is the new daytime business model. In Carlton North, ever-popular cafe Florian this year added a takeaway-only shop next door for its bestselling sandwiches, salads and cakes. “The takeaway element honestly really saved us,” Florian owner Dom Gattermayr says. “We’ve noticed now we can actually afford to do things rather than breaking even.” Owners Dom Gattermayr and Rose Richards outside Florian To-Go. Penny Stephens Removing the limitation of finding space for customers has also meant welcoming a new demographic – those who might have been daunted by the crowded doorways or disappointed by the lack of grab-and-go options by lunchtime. And of course, those that don’t want to spend too much. New bakeries such as Vandels in Brunswick and Abbotsford’s Daybaker have opened to instant crowds, while Chinese breakfast spot Wow Crepes on Bourke Street has expanded to a second, hole-in-the-wall shopfront opposite Flinders Street Station – this time without seating available. Could a sit-down breakfast or brunch soon become a premium product with a pricetag to match?

World.title: The fruit that connects 200 years of Australian history
World.content:
CultureBooksReview The fruit that connects 200 years of Australian history Thuy On July 24, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Short History of Longans is a historical novel that spans two centuries and follows the twisted branches of an Irish-Chinese family in Australia. Mirandi Riwoe’s latest book, her sixth, explores similar themes tackled in her previous works: cross-cultural identities, interracial relationships, immigration, racism and colonial history. Following a preface about a Chinese bushranger named Ah Yang, the novel is divided into four seasonal sections, each helmed by one of his successors. This multigenerational saga begins at the end. Its reverse chronology opens in the near future, in winter 2049, when elderly Daniel finds his beloved longan tree toppled by a storm. It seems like an apt metaphor for his own life, as he fears a “shambolic, exhausting sprint to the finish line – a race that he somehow finds himself ill-equipped for”. The longan appears in all four sections of the book as a linking motif. Getty Images He has long lived alone, but his solitude is disrupted by a widowed neighbour, Olivia Quong, who is piqued with curiosity by the dusty, red-lacquered altar in his house. This neglected heirloom once belonged to Daniel’s late father and offers a clue as to his distant Asian ancestry. So indeed does his cat, who is named after a Chinese emperor, despite Daniel’s general indifference towards his family history.



He used to be a carpenter; now he potters around, creating sculptures from mosaics of inherited letters, photos and crockery. He finds satisfaction in reassembling these shards into new formations, and also likes the shape he’s becoming through his slowly growing friendship with Olivia. But his peace is broken when a stranger turns up, requesting that Daniel delve into his shameful past. Before we can find out more about this mystery, Riwoe ends the section. This abrupt closure may dismay readers who are primed for narrative resolution, or at least for more information, but the author has jumped even further back in time. The second section settles in autumn on New Year’s Day in 2000, and focuses on another branch of the family tree. Like Daniel, Wendy is also of advanced years, but aside from the usual physical ailments, she’s experiencing early onset dementia. Unlike Daniel, who was busy cutting up his family’s paraphernalia for his art projects, Wendy is an aspiring writer trying to bring together pieces of her Irish immigrant forebears to document them. However, her “honeycomb” brain, with its gaps in memory, makes research difficult. Riwoe writes perceptively about this collapse of time: “The multiplying particles of herself – child, adolescent, adult, demented woman – assembling, competing, squirming, for room beneath her skin.” Novelist Mirandi Riwoe’s new book is a multigenerational epic.



The narrative then jumps back another 60-odd years, leaving Queensland behind to follow Ruby in Los Angeles. She’s a Chinese-Australian actress chasing the American dream in the 1940s. The nuances of race are particularly potent in this section. Ruby has missed out on playing Shakespearean heroines because her complexion was “too dusky, as usual”. And yet, she’s found a way to take advantage of her mixed ancestry, leaning into the market’s proclivity for fetishising “Orientalists” by changing her surname to her mother’s “Wong”and preparing lectures about “the usual spiel about Chinese recipes and superstition …” even though she’s never been to China. Editor's pick Literature The Australian author who went from rejection letters to global bestseller The final section of A Short History of Longans loops us back to the start and explains how the bushranger Ah Yong inadvertently planted the seed for this mixed-race family tree. This last segment includes a cacophony of voices from extended members of the clan, but it’s primarily the story of Maria Barrett, an 18-year-old Irish pauper who arrives in Australia at the turn of the century. It’s appropriately set in spring, a time of birth and beginnings. The novel moves adeptly between each family member; in terms of time and place and social norms, the world-building for these varied and disparate characters has been meticulously researched. With her Eurasian background, a mix of Chinese-Indonesian and Irish-English heritage, Riwoe knows what it’s like to straddle cultures, to live as racially bifurcated: divided and wholly of neither east nor west, but a brew of both. Her lived experience informs her books and offers verisimilitude to the stories.



The longan, a fruit native to South-East Asia, with its historical cultivation dating back to China, appears in all four sections of the book as a linking motif. Though the bloodline flows through the chapters, sometimes the connection between them may feel tenuous, and each quarter can pass as a short story or the beginning of a novella and be read as a discrete unit on its own. But together they present a beguiling, detail-rich narrative that tracks the fortunes and fates of several generations, replete with secrets and lies, but also with hope. At the end of Daniel’s narrative, there’s a discovery of infant longan leaves in his garden. These slender saplings, offspring of the destroyed parent plant, look to the future. What else is happening in the book world? A split-second mistake sent author Jaclyn Moriarty on a two-decade literary odyssey.

The legendary cinematographer for Blade Runner 2049, Fargo and Skyfall takes us behind the lenses in his new memoir.

Here’s why you should keep re-reading your favourite book (without feeling guilty).

And there’s a new word for when a media empire targets you.

World.title: How New Zealanders are cutting the cost of their insurances
World.content:
RNZ national

Insurance costs have been a major pain point for many households in recent years, but data from insurers shows many of us are finding solutions.

It was reported mid last year that insurance had the largest increase of any item in the consumer price index since 2000, up 916 percent.

Insurance experts told RNZ that some health insurance policies lifted 50 percent last year.

But while there are signs that premium rises may be moderating, some policyholders are finding other ways to reduce their costs.

What if you don't want a slice of the AI hype? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 13m

Higher excesses

Generally, if your insurance policy has a higher excess, you may be able to pay lower premiums.

Excess is the amount that a policy-holder pays when they make a claim, before the insurer chips in the rest.

Vero said its research showed 57 percent of the 1172 insured homeowners it surveyed had home insurance excesses of more than $500, even though "standard" was $300 to $500.

Nichola Young, executive manager of pricing and underwriting, said Vero had noticed customers had been opting for higher excesses since mid-2022.

She said more people were choosing an excess of $1000 excess, while $400 excesses were becoming less popular.

She said a very high excess, for example of more than $5000, could reduce the cost of an average premium by about $300 a year, although other factors would affect it.

"We've seen more customers voluntarily increasing their excess, and we noticed that this shift coincided with broader cost-of-living pressures."

Vero's research found affordability was the main driver for the higher excesses, and 66 percent of homeowners who had increased their excesses said they did so to lower the cost of their insurance.

"It shows that our customers are making trade-offs to balance the cost of premiums with the level of risk they're willing to carry. The choice ultimately sits with the customer, but the important thing is understanding what that means if you ever need to make a claim."

Young said it would not help in every situation.

"It's important to understand that increasing your excess won't necessarily offset every driver of rising insurance costs. Premium increases in recent years have been influenced by factors such as the growing cost of natural hazards, and increased taxes and levies. If your premium is higher because your home faces greater flood or weather risk, increasing your excess is unlikely to significantly reduce your premium."

The research showed 9 percent of people who had a higher excess said it was a temporary measure.

Justin Lim, founder of insurance comparison website Quashed, said his site had recorded a 19 percent increase in excesses for house insurance year-on-year, a 14 percent increase for car insurance and 6 percent for contents cover.

Changing cover type

Lim said people were also looking for cheaper insurance options.

He said some vehicle owners were considering third-party covert rather than comprehensive insurance.

"While most consumers still ultimately purchase comprehensive car insurance, year-on-year growth in comparison activity for third-party was double that of comprehensive. Consumers are actively exploring cheaper, more basic options."

Dropping cover

Some people are dropping policies completely. Southern Cross reported a drop in membership numbers in the year to June 30, 2025, of 3493 members, bringing total membership to 951,808.

The Insurance Council said surveys showed New Zealanders still had relatively high levels of insurance cover overall, and the percentage of homes with house insurance was in the mid-90 percent range.

Shopping around

Lim said people could often save money by comparing their options.

He said people who looked at what else was on offer could find they could save up to $1500 a year.

He said the chances of finding a cheaper policy were eight out of 10 for car cover, seven in 10 for contents, and six in 10 for home insurance.

Reducing risk

You may sometimes be able to reduce your insurance costs by reducing the risk to the insurer.

For health or life cover, that could mean quitting smoking.

For vehicle insurance, you might be able to install an immobiliser or park in a garage rather than on the street.

The Insurance Council said home insurance rose only 0.4 percent in the year to March and vehicle insurance was down 2 percent.

World.title: 'Oozing pain': Plea for politicians to tackle hate speech
World.content:
Political parties are being urged to go back to hate crime and hate speech recommendations laid out by the inquiry into the Christchurch terrorist attacks.

The Law Commission released the final report from its review on hate crime laws this week, calling for a strengthening of the system rather than new offences.

But Federation of Islamic Associations (FIANZ) spokesperson Abdur Razzaq told RNZ that although the Law Commission had done a thorough job, it was far too constrained by its terms of reference, which kept hate speech as well as anything not already considered an offence out of scope.

"The Law Commission had an excellent engagement process, I mean, A+. But their hands were tied," Razzaq said.

FIANZ has for years been pushing for the work of the Royal Commission of Inquiry to be continued, with Razzaq saying that would be "the baseline" for safety for all New Zealanders.

"We know there's a direct connection between hate speech and hate crime. Even the Royal Commission emphatically said so, and then also the Human Rights Commission, in their report, said an extraordinary link.

"The latest police data is there's one hate crime against a Muslim ... every 54 hours."

The data he referred to points to a 7 percent increase in recorded hate crimes against Muslims in New Zealand - the most targeted religious group - from 2024 to 2025 (September to August).

Razzaq said he met recently with some of the victims of the Christchurch terror attack who survived.

"They still have the bullets in their body, and it's oozing pain ... the thing is, every single case of terror in the last eight years, every single one, bar none, there was hate rhetoric before."

Successive governments had failed to implement the hate speech changes the Royal Commission of Inquiry recommended, with Labour having botched two attempts, first having "absolutely made a hodge" of explaining hate speech then "just went in a totally different tangent".

"Then National came in: too-hard basket," Razzaq said. "Not just 'too hard' basket, it's a 'never-never' basket".

"It's a political hot potato. They said, 'oh, we have to have the the balance between ... free speech'. We totally agree, but we've had hate speech legislation since 1993. It just does not cover faith, it covers all the others.

"Look, other countries have done it ... even in the United States where they have freedom of information, the First Amendment. States also have limits."

The Free Speech Union on Wednesday backed the Law Commission's report which "landed where we and thousands of submitters urged it to".

"This is a win for every New Zealander who took the time to speak up," said Free Speech Union chief executive Jill Heather said in a statement.

"What we opposed was building new, vaguely defined crimes on top of a concept as slippery as hate, and that is exactly what the Commission has declined to do."

Free Speech Union chief executive Jill Heather. Supplied / Free Speech Union

Heather pointed to more than 4000 New Zealanders responding "through our submission tool, adding to the thousands who have consistently rejected attempts to turn subjective judgements about 'hate' into new criminal offences."

Razzaq however rejected the suggestion the original efforts to introduce hate speech laws had faced pushback other than from the Free Speech Union.

"They came up with a report that 'we had 10,000 people who were against the legislation', now who were the 10,000, it was click and send.

"I asked the Free Speech Union, were there 10,000 different people? They said, 'look, we don't know, it's just one site'. So somebody could have sat there and just click, click, click, click, click ... that is not public opinion."

He urged action, saying the risk of failing to make changes would allow hate speech - particularly against religious groups - to continue.

"The risk is we'll have a lot more Brian Tamakis. The risk is we're going to have a fractured society. The risk is people will be able to incite violence against faith communities, and they'll get away with it."

Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki last month called on followers to "purge" Muslims, Sikhs and Hindus from New Zealand.

Police are investigating, and Prime Minister Christopher Luxon dismissed Tamaki's comments, saying he did not listen to him, while Labour leader Chris Hipkins called him a "thug".

Political parties had mixed stances on hate speech reform, with the Greens and Te Pāti Māori saying they supported legislating against hate speech, National saying it did not, ACT calling for more enforcement of current laws, and Labour promising to share a detailed policy in due course.

RNZ sought comment from Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith, but he said he had nothing to add at this stage to his statements about the Law Commission's findings.

RNZ has also sought comment from Labour.

FIANZ in 2024 published a report outlining definitions of hate speech, including:

Racial or Ethnic Hate Speech: Expressions that denigrate or demean individuals or groups based on their race or ethnicity

Religious Hate Speech: Speech that vilifies or promotes hostility towards individuals or communities based on their religious beliefs or practices

Disability-Based Hate Speech: Expressions that mock, belittle, or demean individuals with disabilities.

Xenophobic Hate Speech: Speech that fosters animosity, prejudice, or discrimination against individuals or groups based on their nationality or immigration status.

World.title: Beehive bunker laptops malfunctioned during destructive storm
World.content:
Documents show with a destructive storm bearing down on the South Island last October, some laptops in the Beehive bunker could not access the emergency management system.

The National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) says now that it didn't matter, that staff had other devices that did work.

The problem has come to light in a Department of Internal Affairs review released under the Official Information Act of how NEMA was shifted from the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet to the DIA late last year.

The reshuffle, costing just over its $2 million budget, was effective but done hastily over three months and a host of difficulties were underestimated.

"The transfer was framed as a 'lift and shift of NEMA' ... The reality was substantially different to 'lift and shift'," said the review done last November.

"The post-transfer technology support and project structure was underestimated."

In one case this meant that a vendor company failed to fully finish a job leading to the problem with new DIA laptops staff had been issued.

This was not apparent till states of emergency were declared in late October in Canterbury, Southland and parts of Otago.

"It became apparent in the lead-up to an emergency activation that some aspects of the transfer had not been adequately completed by the vendor, meaning NEMA staff were unable to access the emergency environment in the bunker through their DIA devices," said the short review.

But other laptops linked to the National Crisis Management Centre (the bunker under the Beehive) did work.

"Our response activities weren't impacted, which is a good thing," NEMA told RNZ.

"Staff had full access to all applications and tools required to support response activities, and there were no impacts to response operations, support to [Civil Defence] groups or access to systems."

Emergency Management Minister Mark Mitchell at Kaikōura District Council during a storm earlier this month. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

DIA said it was accountable for making sure the tech worked. Since then it had got Datacom to make technical changes to allow access.

NEMA made the shift between departments in just 10 weeks when it had a lot on its plate.

It had recently embarked on a five-year overhaul of old, fragmented disaster response technologies and introducing new ones, such as a new national warning system, in response to Cyclone Gabrielle. An internal report suggested alongside the tech it must also helm a really big and uncertain cultural shift to be sure of lasting change in the previously fragmented sector.

Last week the agency's fledgling tech failed under pressure, with the civil defence website crashing during a tsunami alert near Te Anau, and its just-launched emergency mobile alert map not quickly updating about either the tsunami or flooding the previous week in Wairoa.

Emergency Management Minister Mark Mitchell said he would be meeting NEMA this week to make sure the website was fixed.

Last year's shift demanded that four agencies cooperated, including Treasury.

Cabinet agreed in April 2025 on the shift and wanted it done fast, starting in June and done by September 25.

"Agencies successfully completed a significant level of work to transfer people, data, and

information," said the 10-page review.

"The overwhelming feedback from NEMA staff is the transfer was well communicated, the

products and services are of a high standard, and the project was delivered by DIA in a

very tight timeframe with minimal disruption to NEMA's core business."

However, there was a very big "but" - the review's section on what went well had seven bullet points and what did not go well had 28 bullet points, for instance:

"As the project progressed, major issues arose relating to information technology and

"Outgoing host agencies [primarily DPMC] were unprepared for the level of work required to transfer NEMA's data out of their agencies and were slow to provide data necessary for a transfer, had not checked data for accuracy, prevented access to trusted vendors to assist with the work, and were critical of DIA for creating more work on limited resources."

"When DIA took over the project leadership, very little of the detailed discovery had been undertaken, requirements were not gathered and a clear scope had not been documented or agreed. This left insufficient time to determine the best transfer approach."

"The budgets did not fully capture the scale of the work."

About half-a-dozen homes flooded in the South Island overnight.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) crews responded to flooded homes in Greymouth, Cobden, Brunner and Runanga in the Grey District.

"Please take care as first light arrives."

Images uploaded by Grey District Council showed surface flooding in Greymouth.

Surface flooding in Greymouth, July 2026. Grey District Council

MetService head of weather Heather Keats told Morning Report the heavy rain would head up the west of the country over the next couple of days.

"Sunday's okay, but today and tomorrow, very much looking messy," she explained.

"We've got a bunch of fast-moving features and fronts tied up and that will be thunderstorms, snow, heavy rain, maybe even some small tornadoes and water spouts. And that'll race up and over the country - the North Island - tomorrow, and then it kind of races away.

World.title: Tornadoes, cold snaps, heavy rain and some sun: 'Every type of weather' forecast this weekend
World.content:
Heather Keats with details of this weekend’s cold snap Morning Report Download MP3 4m

It is shaping up to be a wintry weekend with a blast of polar air set to bring snow, severe frost and icy conditions across parts of the country.

Heavy rain and strong winds are also expected, with the potential to spark tornadoes. Weather watches were already in place for parts of the South Island and lower North. About half-a-dozen homes flooded overnight in the Grey District, and there was a slip on a road on Cobden, with more heavy rain likely on the way.

MetService head of weather Heather Keats agreed with suggestions it could be an 'inside' end to the week' - at least on Friday and Saturday.

"Sunday's okay, but today and tomorrow, very much looking messy," she told Morning Report on Friday morning.

"We've got a bunch of fast-moving features and fronts tied up and that will be thunderstorms, snow, heavy rain, maybe even some small tornadoes and water spouts. And that'll race up and over the country - the North Island - tomorrow, and then it kind of races away.

"But then we're left with a very cold southerly flow. So we've got every type of weather coming over the next sort of 48 hours."

Overnight already thunderstorms hit Westland Fiordland, she said with about 250 lightning strikes.

"Nothing crazy, but that's just the start of it."

Presently the heavy rain was hitting Buller and Nelson Lakes.

A formal heavy rain watch was in place Friday and Saturday for the Tararua Ranges, north of Wellington, with a moderate chance of being upgraded to a warning. More were likely to come, with tornadoes possibly in the mix, Keats said.

"The entire western coastline of New Zealand, I'm talking all the way up around Northland and the Coromandel Peninsula and then it'll track a little bit over to the eastern side as well.

"Thunderstorms, really strong wind gusts and the conditions are right to see some water spouts and some small tornadoes. We don't say that lightly. Not all thunderstorms produce thunder, not all thunderstorms produce tornadoes. But we are seeing that signal in the models. So it's going to be a watch-this-space today.

"If you are anywhere sort of near those western coastlines, keep an eye on your app because if we do see a severe thunderstorm, we will put out that warning. opportunity for you to get safe."

As for temperatures, among main centres Christchurch was likely to get bragging rights for the coldest, with it dipping below zero.

Snow was likely for Ruapehu and possibly the Desert Road, Keats said, and a couple of centimetres on Crown Range Road. The latter and Milford Road (10-15cm) both had road snowfall warnings in place.

"But because it's fast-moving, won't be hanging around for long.

"But then once it clears out on Sunday, and we will have sun, we will have some nice weather coming for most of the country on Sunday, it just drops to be freezing. So we're talking -4C for Christchurch.

World.title: Explainer: What is RSV and why is it making so many people sick this winter?
World.content:
Explainer: RSV may not quite have the name recognition that influenza and Covid do, but it's actually causing more winter illness.

New Zealand has some of the world's highest rates of serious illness caused by the virus, and health experts are calling for a national childhood vaccination programme to be instituted.

The Public Health Communication Centre issued a briefing this week asking for the government to approve RSV vaccines being used in Australia and other countries, which it says will also relieve the enormous burden put on doctors and hospitals each winter.

"It's an awful experience for families to see their children struggling to breathe," Emma Best, an associate professor of paediatric and youth health at Auckland University, told RNZ's Morning Report.

What exactly is RSV?

Dr Hasan Bhally is an infectious diseases specialist Supplied

Respiratory syncytial virus - RSV for short - is exceedingly common, particularly in the winter months from May to October.

It causes infections in the lung and respiratory tract. For some people it'll have symptoms similar to the common cold and fade after 10 days or so.

But for children and older people with compromised immunity, it can be much more serious.

Dr Hasan Bhally, an infectious disease doctor at North Shore Hospital, told RNZ's Nine To Noon that RSV is actually causing more cases than Covid-19 or influenza according to recent data.

"RSV is the most common of those troublesome three with about 45 percent, versus 25 percent for Covid and 30 percent for influenza."

Winter ills and RSV vaccinations Nine To Noon Download MP3 13m

"When you look at the viruses being seen over the last weeks amongst hospitalised people, RSV is much more than flu at the moment," Best added.

RSV spreads through the air when people sneeze or cough. People are typically infectious for about 10 days after symptoms have started.

There's plenty of chatter on social media about people suffering long illnesses lately, and much of that could be attributed to RSV, Best said.

"With RSV peaking at the moment it is likely the cause of the comment 'a lot of people talking about being sick recently,'" she noted.

The Respiratory Illness Dashboard run by PHF Science shows a steady rise in illnesses typically reported through July and into September.

Currently trends are "rising toward high so not at peak winter illnesses yet," Best said.

Is it worse for children?

Around 1800 to 2000 children every year are hospitalised with RSV, the Public Health Communication Centre report said.

About half of those are infants, particularly those under 6 months.

"Beyond the immediate illness, there is increasing evidence that RSV infection in infancy is associated with recurrent preschool wheeze and asthma, further adding to the long-term burden on families and the health system," the report noted.

RSV so far isn't actually worse than in previous years, but it is rising at typical levels for winter.

"It is predictably high at this time of year and leading to children under 5 and particularly under 1 being hospitalised," Best said.

Māori and Pasifika children are three to five times more likely to be hospitalised, the Cardiac and Respiratory Foundation NZ says.

Thousands of babies born each year "are healthy but acquire RSV, have an awful wheezing illness, they need oxygen, they need support with their feeding, they need hospitalisation essentially," Best said.

"It's really predictable for us, we see RSV coming, beds are full in hospitals."

But adults can get it too?

Definitely, and it can cause life-threatening complications.

"It is true that it's predominantly a virus of babies, especially infants, but there is a significant burden in adults also, especially the older adults, which I will define as 65 years and more," Bhally said.

"Our immunity wanes from natural infections as we all age," he explained.

Adults who have chronic health problems like asthma are also highly at risk, he said.

"Infections in these people can be quite severe, meaning it can lead to hospitalisation."

Babies are particularly affected by RSV. 123RF

How is it treated?

"There's unfortunately no antiviral treatment for RSV," Bhally said.

Because it's a viral infection, not bacterial, antibiotics don't work on RSV.

For adults the general recommendations is to isolate yourself, drink fluids, rest and take painkillers as needed.

For children, it's important to monitor their health closely - infants may not show symptoms as obviously as adults.

A medicine called palivizumab is available for some infants and children who are at high risk of severe illness, Health NZ says. Palivizumab is given by injections repeated once a month during the RSV season. A healthcare provider can determine if a child is eligible.

Anyone who shows signs of trouble breathing should seek immediate medical attention, as complications like pneumonia or bronchiolitis can develop.

Is there a vaccine?

There's no universal childhood vaccine programme in New Zealand, although there are growing calls to start one.

There are childhood vaccines already available in the US, UK, and Australia, but they have not yet been approved for use in New Zealand yet, a fact which has angered medical experts.

Paediatricians push for funded RSV vaccine Morning Report Download MP3 4m

"We just feel disappointed really, because it's been almost two years now in Australia that they've had some prevention for RSV," Best said.

In Australia, the ABC reported New South Wales are hailing the vaccination program launched in 2024 that's nearly halved hospitalisations ahead of the winter peak as a "fantastic" success.

Vaccines for RSV are relatively recent developments - there are long-acting monoclonal antibodies given to newborns, and maternal vaccination given during pregnancy.

"The landscape of RSV vaccinations is changing rapidly," Bhally said. "It's very exciting times if we look at what's happening globally with RSV vaccinations."

"We have to make the vaccines available, funded and accessible," he said.

Both Best and Dr Bhally called upon the government to approve and fund them for use in New Zealand.

"These have been licensed in Europe, US and Australia for several years already, so again we don't know why these things take longer when we've already got international agencies that have licensed them," Best said.

There is also a vaccine aimed at adults over 60 or those between 50 to 59 who are at increased risk, called Arexvy.

However, it's not funded by Pharmac and runs more than $400.

World.title: Kiwi's experiment shows need for new UK passport 'pointless'
World.content:
New figures show people applying from overseas for United Kingdom citizenship and passports has soared after a change in rules for dual citizens.

New Zealanders with British heritage or families were caught by surprise at the start of the year, when they found they could no longer travel back to the UK on their New Zealand passport.

From late February, Britain and Ireland required all its citizens to use only passports issued by those countries when travelling to them, or pay more than $1300 for a 'certificate of entitlement' to use in their New Zealand passport.

UK Home Office figures show overseas passport applications almost tripled to more than 300,000 in the first quarter of 2026. The British passport office had more than half-a-million applications in total in its system, the highest on record.

For some New Zealanders, it was the first time that they discovered they were classed as British citizens, as they had never previously owned a UK passport.

The policy change also coincided with the highest number of UK citizenship applications on record, in the 12 months to March. In the first three months of this year, 118,000 people applied - almost double the number at the same point last year.

Data from the UK's 2021 census shows New Zealanders were the most likely migrants to have dual citizenship (49.2 percent), ahead of South Africa (49.0 percent), and Australia (47.4 percent).

The British Foreign and Commonwealth Office found that at least 80 percent of New Zealanders had some British ancestry - higher even than Australia.

Dual nationals' travel

RNZ has heard from dual nationals who have travelled to the UK without a British or Irish passport, as well as those not able to get one because of documents they could not track down or the high cost of applying and postage.

Many queries centred on whether border officials would have any way of border staff checking whether a New Zealand passport holder also had UK citizenship.

Steve Horrell decided to try a real-world experiment, using an ETA (a $37 visa-waiver) he received last year to to fly to London with his New Zealand passport. He took along the UK passport ($320 including postage) he purchased in February - in case it went wrong.

At two airport check-in points no-one queried whether he had dual citizenship, then he used the Smart Gate at border control in Heathrow without issue.

"I was actually very angry that my New Zealand passport was just accepted and I got the big green tick to enter the country," he said in a formal complaint to the British Home Office. "Travel back to NZ was not an issue and I used my NZ passport throughout. So, my nice new shiny UK passport stayed in my travel wallet and has yet to see the light of day.

"How did the system not pick up that I was the holder of a valid UK passport and why did it not ask me to present it? Is the real reason that I was not challenged due to a shortage of staff to effectively police the border, or is it down to an ineffective computer system that is not fit for purpose?"

He told RNZ he planned to show an expired UK passport first if he was challenged at the border - to see if it was true that would be accepted as proof of his citizenship - then to produce his new British passport if that failed.

"It turned out to be a pointless exercise. The whole scenario is a complete nonsense and I am now absolutely sure that the UK authorities introduced this as a money-making scheme, because it would appear they were more interested in getting people through immigration by using Smart Gates so that they do not need to employ so many staff to check everyone manually."

He sent follow-up emails after only receiving an automated acknowledgement to his complaint in May, which had promised a response in 20 working days. He said he felt conned, describing the Government's statements about not allowing entry to British citizens using third-country passports to enter the UK as 'fearmongering'.

The UK Home Office said British and Irish citizens are no longer able to get ETAs and the onus is on the individual to apply for the appropriate permission to travel. Its advice is still that it is the airline's decision whether to allow dual citizen travellers to use an expired UK passport, if they also have a valid New Zealand passport.

The British government had described the expired passport as a "short-term transitional measure" but it is not clear how long it will last. An article by an immigration lawyer on the UK law website Free Movement argues that ETAs issued to British dual citizens before online changes were made remain valid.

In research by the House of Commons library, it noted speculation that some British dual nationals would continue using their foreign passport by not declaring their British citizenship.

"Other dual nationals may travel to the UK as a foreign passport holder unaware that they have British citizenship. For example, a person who has never lived in the UK might have automatically acquired British citizenship through one of their parents by automatic operation of the law, without having had any formal interaction with the UK Government.

"In either situation, transport providers and staff at UK passport control wouldn't necessarily know that a person travelling on a foreign passport also has British citizenship if the person didn't volunteer that information. There is no central register of British citizens or dual nationals, and information about a person's place of birth isn't enough to confirm if they are British."

The Home Office stressed that while British people would not be detained or separated from family at the border, the best way to ensure a smooth journey was travelling with a valid UK passport or a certificate of entitlement.
